lessons.title: What Electricity Is: Charge, Conductors and Circuits
lessons.content:
Imagine the load-shedding moment. You are reading at night, the fan is spinning, the phone is charging, and suddenly everything stops at once. The fan slows down, the light dies, the charger icon disappears. Ten minutes later the power comes back and everything wakes up again. What exactly came and went? Not water, not air, not anything you can see. It was a flow of tiny charged particles pushed through wires. This whole course is about that invisible flow: how to describe it, how to calculate it, and how to control it. And since every computer, phone and router is built from circuits, this is the ground floor of all the hardware you will ever touch as a CSE student.

What electricity is: Electricity is the name we give to everything that happens because of electric charge, especially charge that moves. When charge sits still we call it static electricity, like the crackle when you pull off a woollen sweater in winter. When charge moves steadily through a path we call it electric current, and that is what runs your fan. In this course we mostly care about moving charge, because moving charge can carry energy from a power station or a battery to a bulb, a motor or a processor.

Atoms and electrons: Everything is made of atoms. An atom has a tiny heavy centre called the nucleus, which holds positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, and around it move light, negatively charged electrons. Normally an atom has the same number of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel and the atom is neutral. In metals like copper, the outermost electron of each atom is only loosely held. These loose electrons can wander from atom to atom, so we call them free electrons. A copper wire is full of them, like a crowded Dhaka street full of people who are ready to move as soon as someone gives a push.

Electric charge and the coulomb: Charge is a basic property of matter, and it comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The charge of one electron is very small, about 1.602 × 10^-19 coulomb, and it is negative. The coulomb (symbol C) is the unit of charge. One coulomb is a huge crowd of electrons: about 6.24 × 10^18 of them. You can check this yourself: 1 divided by 1.602 × 10^-19 gives roughly 6.24 × 10^18. A small fact worth remembering is that charge is conserved. It is never created or destroyed in a circuit, it only moves from one place to another. This idea will come back when we study Kirchhoff's current law.

Conventional current versus electron flow: Here is a historical twist. Scientists decided the direction of current long before anyone knew about electrons. They guessed that positive charge flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal. Later it turned out that in metal wires it is actually the negative electrons that move, and they move the other way, from negative to positive. We kept the old rule anyway. So in circuit diagrams, current arrows always show conventional current, from + to - through the outside circuit. The maths works out exactly the same either way, so do not worry; just use conventional current everywhere in this course.

Conductors: A conductor is a material that lets charge move easily. Metals are the classic conductors. Silver is the best ordinary conductor, copper is very close and much cheaper, which is why house wiring and phone chargers use copper. Aluminium is lighter and cheaper still, so the big overhead power lines you see along highways are mostly aluminium, often with a steel core for strength. Salt water and the human body also conduct, which is exactly why wet hands and electric switches are a dangerous mix.

Insulators: An insulator holds on to its electrons tightly, so charge cannot flow through it easily. Rubber, plastic, glass, dry wood, porcelain and air are insulators. The coloured plastic around a wire is an insulator that keeps the current inside the copper and keeps your fingers safe. Those white or brown porcelain cups on electric poles are insulators too; they hold the live wire without letting current leak into the pole. No insulator is perfect, though. If the voltage is high enough, even air breaks down and lets a spark through, which is what lightning is.

Semiconductors: Between conductors and insulators sit semiconductors such as silicon and germanium. Pure silicon conducts poorly, but adding a tiny amount of another element, called doping, changes its behaviour a lot. That controllable behaviour is what makes diodes and transistors possible, and billions of transistors make a processor. You will study semiconductors properly in the Electronic Devices course. In this course we just need to know they exist and that they are the reason computers can be built from circuits.

The water pipe analogy: Engineers love to explain circuits with water. Think of a water tank on the roof of a building, connected by a pipe to a tap on the ground floor. The height of the water gives it pressure; that is like voltage. The amount of water flowing per second is like current. A narrow or partly blocked pipe resists the flow; that is like resistance. The pump that lifts water back up to the tank is like a battery or generator. The analogy is not perfect, but it gives a very good first feeling for how voltage, current and resistance relate, and we will lean on it in the next few lessons.

What a circuit is: An electric circuit is a closed path through which current can flow. It needs at least three things: a source of energy such as a battery, a load that uses the energy such as a bulb or a motor, and connecting wires that make a complete loop. Often there is also a switch to open or close the loop. If the loop is broken anywhere, current stops everywhere in that loop. This is why a torch light goes off when you slide the switch: the switch simply creates a gap in the path.

Open circuit and closed circuit: When the path is complete we call it a closed circuit, and current flows. When the path is broken we call it an open circuit, and no current flows. Notice the funny language: a closed switch means ON, and an open switch means OFF. This is the opposite of a door, where open means you can pass. Many students mix this up in the first week, so remember: closed circuit, current flows; open circuit, nothing flows.

Short circuit: A short circuit happens when current finds a path with almost no resistance, skipping the load. For example, if the two wires of a lamp cord touch each other because the insulation melted, current rushes straight through the touching point instead of going through the bulb. With almost nothing to limit it, the current becomes very large, wires heat up quickly, and fires can start. That is why houses have fuses and circuit breakers, which we will meet in the last lesson of this course.

Circuit diagrams and symbols: Drawing real wires and real parts would be slow and messy, so engineers use a schematic, a drawing made of standard symbols. A battery or cell is drawn as a pair of parallel lines, one long and one short; the long line is the positive terminal. A resistor is drawn as a zigzag line in the American style or as a small rectangle in the IEC style used in many Bangladeshi textbooks. A switch is a small line that can lift away from a contact. A bulb is a circle with a cross inside. A wire is just a straight line, and a dot where lines meet means they are joined. Learning to read these symbols is like learning the alphabet before reading a story.

Ideal wires: In circuit problems we usually treat connecting wires as perfect, with zero resistance. In real life a long thin wire does have some resistance, which is why an extension cord can get warm under heavy load. But for most textbook circuits, the wires are short and thick enough that we safely ignore them. This simplification lets us focus on the components that matter.

DC and AC in one breath: Current that always flows in one direction is called direct current, or DC. A battery, a power bank and the output of your phone charger give DC. Current that keeps reversing direction is called alternating current, or AC. The wall socket in Bangladesh gives AC that reverses 50 times every second in each direction cycle, which we say is 50 hertz. The first half of this course focuses on DC because it is simpler, and later lessons build up the tools for AC.

Real life example 1, a torch light: Open a simple torch. Inside you find two or three cells, a small bulb or LED, a switch and some metal strips that act as wires. When you slide the switch on, the metal strips touch, the loop closes, and current flows from the positive end of the cells, through the bulb, and back to the negative end. The bulb glows because the current carries energy into it. When the cells get weak, the push becomes smaller, less current flows, and the light becomes dim. That one little torch shows source, load, wires, switch, open circuit and closed circuit all at once.

Real life example 2, a rickshaw's battery lights: Many battery-run easy-bikes and auto-rickshaws in Bangladesh carry a set of lead-acid batteries. The same batteries power the motor, the headlight and the small indicator lights. Each light is part of a circuit that starts at the battery, runs through a switch on the handle, through the lamp, and returns to the battery. If a wire gets loose from the vibration on a bumpy road, that circuit opens and that light stops, while the others keep working because they have their own paths. Mechanics who fix these vehicles are, without calling it that, doing circuit analysis.

Where students go wrong: The first common mistake is thinking current gets used up in a bulb. It does not. The same amount of charge that enters the bulb leaves it; what the bulb uses up is energy. The second mistake is mixing up open and closed circuits. The third is forgetting that conventional current flows from + to - outside the source, even though electrons move the other way. Exams in the first chapter usually ask you to define charge, current, conductor and insulator, give the charge of an electron, count how many electrons make a given charge, and draw a simple circuit with standard symbols.

A tiny worked problem: How many electrons pass a point if 3.2 coulombs of charge flow? Number of electrons = 3.2 / (1.602 × 10^-19), which is about 2.0 × 10^19 electrons. That is twenty billion billion electrons, and yet it is only the charge that flows through a small phone charger cable in a few seconds. Electrons are tiny and there are unbelievably many of them.

Recap: Charge comes in positive and negative kinds and is measured in coulombs. Free electrons in metals make conductors; tightly held electrons make insulators; semiconductors sit in between. A circuit is a closed loop with a source, a load and wires. Open means off, closed means on, and a short circuit is a dangerous shortcut. In the next lesson we put numbers on the flow and the push: current, voltage, power and energy.
key_points: Electric charge comes in two kinds; like charges repel, unlike attract.
One electron carries about -1.602 × 10^-19 C; 1 C is about 6.24 × 10^18 electrons.
Charge is conserved: it moves around a circuit but is never used up.
Conductors (copper, aluminium) let charge flow; insulators (plastic, rubber) block it; semiconductors sit in between.
Conventional current flows from + to - in the external circuit.
A circuit needs a source, a load and a complete path; open = off, closed = on.
A short circuit bypasses the load and can cause dangerous currents.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page sheet of circuit symbols now and keep it in your notebook; you will use it in every lesson.

lessons.title: Current, Voltage, Power and Energy
lessons.content:
Every month a paper or SMS arrives from DESCO, DPDC or your local Palli Bidyut office, telling your family how many "units" of electricity you used and how many taka you owe. What is a unit? Why does the AC raise the bill so much more than the fan? And why does a 5 V phone charger feel so harmless while the 220 V socket can kill? To answer these questions we need four measuring words that every circuit problem uses: current, voltage, power and energy. This lesson gives each one a clear meaning, a unit and a small formula.

Current: Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point. If you stand beside a wire and count how many coulombs pass you every second, that number is the current. We write i = dq/dt, which simply means change in charge divided by change in time. For a steady flow, I = Q / t. The unit is the ampere (A), named after André-Marie Ampère, and 1 ampere means 1 coulomb per second. Example: if 30 coulombs pass a point in 10 seconds, I = 30 / 10 = 3 A.

Feeling the size of amperes: A phone charging cable often carries 1 to 3 A. A ceiling fan in Bangladesh draws well under half an ampere. An electric kettle can draw around 7 to 9 A. Inside electronics we often meet milliamperes (mA, one thousandth of an amp) and microamperes (µA, one millionth). An LED glows nicely at around 10 to 20 mA. These prefixes, kilo (10^3), milli (10^-3), micro (10^-6), nano (10^-9) and mega (10^6), will appear in almost every problem, so get comfortable with them early.

Charge from current: We can also go backwards. If you know the current and the time, the charge that moved is Q = I × t. A power bank rated 10,000 mAh can, in principle, give 10,000 mA (10 A) for one hour, or 1 A for 10 hours. Since 1 hour is 3600 seconds, 10 Ah is 10 × 3600 = 36,000 coulombs. So the mAh number on a battery is actually a measure of charge, not energy. To know the energy you also need the voltage, which brings us to the next idea.

Voltage: Voltage is the energy given to each coulomb of charge to push it from one point to another. Formally, v = dw/dq, energy per unit charge. The unit is the volt (V), named after Alessandro Volta, and 1 volt means 1 joule of energy per coulomb. A 9 V battery gives each coulomb that passes through it 9 joules of energy. In the water picture, voltage is the pressure difference that makes water want to flow. Another common name is potential difference, because voltage is always measured between two points.

Voltage is always between two points: This is a key habit. You never say "the voltage at the bulb" without meaning "the voltage across the bulb", that is, between its two ends. When we say a point has a voltage of 5 V, we secretly mean 5 V relative to a chosen reference point, usually called ground and given 0 V. In a phone, ground is the negative side of the battery. Without a reference, a single point has no voltage, just like the height of a hill means nothing until you say height above what, such as sea level.

Polarity: Voltage has a direction, shown with + and - signs on the diagram. If the + terminal of an element is 3 V higher than its - terminal, we write v = 3 V. If we had labelled the signs the other way round, the same voltage would be written v = -3 V. Both describe the same physical reality. A negative answer in a circuit problem is not wrong; it just means the real polarity is opposite to the one you assumed. This same idea applies to current direction too.

Sources and loads in terms of energy: A battery takes chemical energy and gives it to charges, raising their energy. A resistor or bulb takes energy away from the charges and turns it into heat or light. So when current goes through a battery from its - to its + terminal, energy is supplied. When current goes through a load from + to -, energy is absorbed. Charges come back to the battery with low energy, get re-energised, and go out again, like a rickshaw puller resting at a tea stall before the next trip.

Power: Power is how fast energy is supplied or used, energy per second. The formula is p = dw/dt. Combining it with the definitions of voltage and current gives the most useful equation of this lesson: p = v × i. The unit is the watt (W), named after James Watt, and 1 watt means 1 joule per second. A 9 V battery supplying 0.5 A delivers 9 × 0.5 = 4.5 W. A 220 V line feeding a 0.3 A fan supplies about 66 W. That is why fans in Bangladesh are often rated around 60 to 80 W.

The passive sign convention: Circuit books use a fixed rule to decide whether a positive p means power absorbed or power supplied. The rule is called the passive sign convention: if the current arrow enters the element at its + terminal, then p = v × i is the power absorbed by that element. If the current enters at the - terminal, then p = -v × i is absorbed. A positive absorbed power means the element is consuming energy, like a resistor. A negative absorbed power means it is actually supplying energy, like a battery that is discharging.

Worked example on sign convention: A battery has 12 V across it, with + on top. A current of 2 A comes out of its + terminal and flows into a lamp. For the battery, the current enters at its - terminal, so absorbed power = -(12 × 2) = -24 W, which means the battery supplies 24 W. For the lamp, the current enters at its + terminal, so absorbed power = +12 × 2 = +24 W. Notice something lovely: total power in the circuit is -24 + 24 = 0. Power supplied equals power absorbed. This is called conservation of power, or Tellegen's theorem in more advanced books, and it is a great way to check your answers.

Energy: Energy is power multiplied by time: w = p × t when the power is steady. In SI units, watts times seconds gives joules. But a joule is tiny for household use. One 60 W fan running for one hour uses 60 × 3600 = 216,000 joules. So electricity companies use a bigger unit: the kilowatt-hour (kWh). One kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for one hour, which equals 3.6 million joules. On your bill, one "unit" means one kWh.

Calculating an electricity bill: Suppose your home has four LED bulbs of 10 W each running 6 hours a day, two fans of 70 W each running 12 hours a day, and a refrigerator averaging about 100 W all day. Daily energy: bulbs 4 × 10 × 6 = 240 Wh, fans 2 × 70 × 12 = 1680 Wh, fridge 100 × 24 = 2400 Wh. Total is 4320 Wh, or 4.32 kWh per day. In a 30-day month that is about 130 units. If the tariff were, say, 6 taka per unit, the energy charge would be around 780 taka, plus any fixed charges and VAT. Real tariffs in Bangladesh use slabs, where the price per unit rises as usage rises, so the exact numbers change, but the method stays the same.

Why the air conditioner dominates: A 1.5 ton AC can draw roughly 1500 to 2000 W while its compressor runs. Running 8 hours a day at 1500 W gives 12 kWh daily, almost three times the entire rest of the house in our example. Power multiplied by time is what you pay for. A high-power device used for a few minutes, like an electric iron, may cost less than a low-power device left on all day and night.

DC and AC currents in a picture: If you draw current against time, DC is a flat horizontal line, for example a steady 2 A. AC is a wave that goes up and down, positive in one half and negative in the other, because the direction keeps reversing. There are also other shapes: a current that rises steadily, a current that jumps on and off like a digital clock signal inside a computer, and so on. Most of this course uses DC first, then sinusoidal AC from lesson 19 onwards.

Why high voltage is dangerous: What harms the body is current flowing through it, especially through the heart. Your skin has quite a high resistance when dry, so a 5 V USB supply cannot push a meaningful current through you. The 220 to 230 V mains can push enough current through a wet hand to be deadly. So voltage is the push that decides whether a dangerous current can flow at all. This is why chargers that convert mains to a few volts are safe to touch at the cable end, while the socket itself is not.

Real life example 1, comparing chargers: A basic charger is labelled 5 V, 1 A. A fast charger is labelled 9 V, 2 A. Their maximum power outputs are 5 × 1 = 5 W and 9 × 2 = 18 W. Charging a phone battery that holds about 15 Wh of energy would take at least 3 hours with the first and under 1 hour with the second, ignoring losses and the fact that charging slows near 100 percent. The labels on chargers are just voltage and current, and multiplying them tells you the power story.

Real life example 2, an IPS during load-shedding: Many Bangladeshi homes keep an IPS with a battery, say 12 V and 100 Ah. Stored energy is roughly 12 × 100 = 1200 Wh. If during load-shedding you run two fans of 70 W and three 10 W lights, the load is 170 W. Ideal backup time is 1200 / 170, about 7 hours. In practice the inverter wastes some energy and you should not drain a lead-acid battery fully, so real backup might be about half of that. Still, the whole estimate came from p = v × i and w = p × t.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse mAh (charge) with Wh (energy), forget to convert minutes into seconds or hours, and mix up the sign convention. Another classic error is saying "current flows across a resistor" and "voltage flows through it". Current flows through; voltage exists across. Typical exam questions: find the current given charge and time, find the charge given a changing current, find the power absorbed by each element using the passive sign convention and verify that the total is zero, and calculate a monthly electricity bill.

Recap: Current is charge per second (amperes), voltage is energy per charge between two points (volts), power is energy per second (watts) and p = v × i. Energy is power times time, and a bill "unit" is one kilowatt-hour. With the passive sign convention, positive absorbed power means consuming and negative means supplying, and the powers in any circuit add up to zero. Next we meet the part that controls how much current a given voltage can push: resistance.
key_points: Current is charge per second: I = Q / t, measured in amperes.
Voltage is energy per charge between two points, measured in volts (1 V = 1 J/C).
Power p = v × i, measured in watts; energy w = p × t.
mAh measures charge; Wh and kWh measure energy. One bill unit = 1 kWh.
Passive sign convention: current entering + gives absorbed power p = vi; negative absorbed power means supplying.
In any circuit, total power supplied equals total power absorbed.
A negative answer for v or i just means the real direction is opposite to the assumed one.
lessons.tip: Always write units next to every number in your working; half of all mistakes in this chapter are unit mistakes.

lessons.title: Resistance and Ohm's Law
lessons.content:
Think of the Dhaka traffic on a Friday morning compared to a weekday evening. The same number of cars want to go from Farmgate to Motijheel, but on the busy evening the road "resists" them: lanes are blocked, rickshaws crowd the edges, and fewer cars get through per minute. Electric current faces something similar inside every material. That opposition is called resistance, and the simple rule connecting resistance, voltage and current, Ohm's law, is the single most used formula in the whole of electrical engineering.

What resistance is: Resistance is the property of a material that opposes the flow of electric current. As free electrons drift through a wire, they keep bumping into vibrating atoms and lose some of their energy as heat. The more bumping, the harder it is for current to flow. Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega (Ω), named after Georg Simon Ohm. A component made specially to provide a known resistance is called a resistor.

What decides resistance: For a uniform wire, resistance depends on three things. Length: a longer wire has more resistance, because electrons must travel further through the crowd. Cross-sectional area: a thicker wire has less resistance, because there are more lanes for the electrons. Material: some materials are naturally better conductors than others. Together these give the formula R = ρL / A, where ρ (rho) is the resistivity of the material in ohm-metres, L is the length in metres and A is the area in square metres.

Resistivity examples: Copper has a resistivity of about 1.68 × 10^-8 Ω·m at room temperature. Aluminium is about 2.8 × 10^-8 Ω·m, a bit worse. Nichrome, the alloy used in heater coils and electric irons, is around 1.1 × 10^-6 Ω·m, almost a hundred times higher than copper, which is exactly why it gets hot. Rubber and glass have resistivities so huge that, for everyday purposes, no current flows at all. Resistivity is a property of the material itself, while resistance depends on the material and on the shape of the piece.

Worked example with R = ρL/A: A copper wire is 100 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm², which is 1 × 10^-6 m². R = (1.68 × 10^-8 × 100) / (1 × 10^-6) = 1.68 Ω. If you double the length to 200 m, resistance doubles to 3.36 Ω. If you instead double the area to 2 mm², resistance halves to 0.84 Ω. This is why electricians use thicker wire for the air conditioner line than for a light point: a thicker wire wastes less power as heat.

Conductance: Sometimes it is handier to talk about how easily current flows rather than how hard. That is conductance, G = 1 / R. Its unit is the siemens (S), and older books call it the mho, which is ohm spelled backwards. A 4 Ω resistor has a conductance of 0.25 S. Conductance becomes very useful in parallel circuits and in nodal analysis, because conductances in parallel simply add.

Temperature and resistance: For metals, resistance rises as temperature rises, because hotter atoms vibrate more and get in the electrons' way more often. A filament bulb has a much lower resistance when it is cold than when it is glowing hot; that is why old filament bulbs often blew out at the instant you switched them on, when a big rush of current flowed through the cold filament. Some materials, such as carbon and semiconductors, behave the other way, with resistance falling as they get hotter. Special resistors called thermistors use this effect to measure temperature, for example in a digital thermometer or a battery charger.

Ohm's law: In 1827 Georg Ohm found that for many conductors, the current through them is directly proportional to the voltage across them, as long as temperature stays the same. We write V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles. Double the resistance and the current halves. The same law can be rearranged two ways: I = V / R to find current, and R = V / I to find resistance. A simple memory trick is the VIR triangle: V on top, I and R at the bottom; cover the one you want and read the others.

Ohm's law worked examples: A 12 V battery connected to a 4 Ω resistor gives I = 12 / 4 = 3 A. A 220 V line feeding a heater coil drawing 5 A means R = 220 / 5 = 44 Ω. A 2 kΩ resistor carrying 3 mA has V = 0.003 × 2000 = 6 V. Notice how milliamps times kilo-ohms gives volts directly: 3 mA × 2 kΩ = 6 V. That shortcut saves a lot of time in electronics problems.

The I-V graph: If you plot current against voltage for a resistor that obeys Ohm's law, you get a straight line through the origin. The slope of this line is 1 / R, which is the conductance. A steep line means small resistance; a shallow line means large resistance. Elements with a straight-line graph are called linear or ohmic. Many useful devices are non-linear: a diode lets current flow easily in one direction only, and a filament lamp's line bends because its resistance changes as it heats up. Ohm's law, in the strict sense, applies only to the linear ones, but V = IR still defines the resistance at any one operating point.

Power in a resistor: Combine p = v × i with Ohm's law and you get three handy forms: P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R. All of this power turns into heat in a resistor. This is called Joule heating. Example: a 10 Ω resistor carrying 2 A dissipates 2² × 10 = 40 W. A 100 Ω resistor across 10 V dissipates 10² / 100 = 1 W. Resistors have a power rating, such as 1/4 W or 1/2 W. If you push more power through than the rating allows, the resistor overheats, changes colour and may burn.

Why power lines use high voltage: The power lost in a transmission line is I² × R_line. To deliver a fixed power P = V × I, raising the voltage lowers the current. If you raise voltage ten times, current drops ten times, and line loss drops a hundred times, because loss depends on current squared. This is why Bangladesh's national grid carries power at high voltages such as 132 kV, 230 kV and 400 kV before stepping it down near homes. We will see the transformers that do this stepping in lesson 24.

Short circuit and open circuit in terms of resistance: A short circuit is an element with R = 0, so V across it is always 0, whatever current flows. An open circuit is R = infinity, so the current through it is always 0, whatever voltage appears across it. These two extreme cases come up again and again, especially when we find Thevenin equivalents and analyse switches.

Types of resistors: Fixed resistors have one value; common kinds are carbon film and metal film resistors, the small beige or blue cylinders with coloured bands. Wire-wound resistors are used where higher power is needed. Variable resistors, such as potentiometers, let you change the resistance by turning a knob; the old volume knob on a radio was usually one. Special resistors change with the environment: thermistors with temperature and light dependent resistors (LDRs) with light. Street lights that switch on at dusk often use an LDR-based circuit.

The resistor colour code: Small resistors are too tiny to print numbers on, so they use coloured bands. The digits are: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. On a four-band resistor, the first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier (how many zeros to add), and the fourth is the tolerance: gold means ±5 percent, silver ±10 percent. Example: brown, black, red, gold means 1, 0, then two zeros, so 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ, ±5 percent. Yellow, violet, orange, gold is 47 with three zeros, 47 kΩ ±5 percent. A popular memory sentence in many classrooms is "BB ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife".

Tolerance in practice: A 1 kΩ ±5 percent resistor can really be anywhere from 950 Ω to 1050 Ω. That is why you will see measured values that are a little off in the lab, and why circuits that need precision use 1 percent resistors. Always remember that real components never match the paper values exactly; good designs work across the whole tolerance range.

A resistor that protects an LED: An LED needs only a small current, often about 10 to 20 mA, and drops roughly 2 V across itself when it is on (the exact value depends on its colour). If you connect a red LED straight to a 5 V supply, nothing limits the current and the LED can burn out in a moment. So we add a series resistor. The resistor must drop the remaining 5 - 2 = 3 V while carrying 15 mA, so R = 3 / 0.015 = 200 Ω. The nearest common value, 220 Ω, gives a slightly smaller, safe current. Its power is only 3 × 0.015 = 0.045 W, so a tiny 1/4 W resistor is plenty. This one calculation appears in almost every beginner Arduino project.

Real life example 1, the electric heater coil: A water heater or an electric iron uses a nichrome coil. Suppose an iron is rated 1000 W at 220 V. Its resistance when hot is R = V² / P = 220² / 1000 = 48400 / 1000 = 48.4 Ω, and it draws I = P / V, about 4.5 A. The coil's high resistivity turns electrical energy into heat efficiently, while the copper wires that feed it, with tiny resistance, stay cool. Same current, very different resistance, very different heating.

Real life example 2, why cheap extension boards melt: Some cheap multi-plug boards sold in local markets use thin wires. If someone plugs an AC, a rice cooker and an iron into one board, the current might reach 15 A or more. Even a small wire resistance of 0.1 Ω then wastes I²R = 15² × 0.1 = 22.5 W as heat, concentrated in a thin wire inside plastic. The plastic softens, insulation fails, and a short circuit or fire can follow. Understanding I²R is not just exam knowledge; it keeps homes safe.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to convert mm² to m² in R = ρL/A, mix up resistivity and resistance, and misread colour bands from the wrong end (the tolerance band, gold or silver, goes on the right). Another trap is using P = V²/R with the wrong V, for example the supply voltage instead of the voltage across that specific resistor. Typical exam questions: compute resistance of a wire from its dimensions, find current or voltage with Ohm's law, find power dissipated, decode colour bands, and explain how resistance changes with temperature.

Recap: Resistance opposes current and is measured in ohms; R = ρL/A shows it grows with length and shrinks with area. Conductance is G = 1/R in siemens. Ohm's law V = IR holds for linear elements, and power in a resistor is VI = I²R = V²/R, all turned into heat. Short circuit means R = 0, open circuit means R = infinity. Next, we meet the other building blocks of every circuit: the different kinds of sources and elements.
key_points: Resistance opposes current; unit ohm (Ω).
R = ρL/A: longer wire more resistance, thicker wire less.
Conductance G = 1/R, unit siemens (S).
Ohm's law: V = I × R for linear (ohmic) elements.
Power in a resistor: P = VI = I²R = V²/R, all turned into heat.
Metal resistance rises with temperature; thermistors and LDRs change with heat and light.
Colour code digits 0-9: black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white; gold ±5%, silver ±10%.
lessons.tip: Practise Ohm's law with mA and kΩ together; mA × kΩ = V saves you from powers of ten.

lessons.title: Circuit Elements and Sources
lessons.content:
A cricket team has batters, bowlers and a wicketkeeper. Each player has a clear job, and you cannot understand a match until you know who does what. A circuit is similar. Before we solve bigger circuits, we must know the players: which parts give energy, which parts take it, and how each one behaves. In this lesson we meet the cast of circuit theory: active and passive elements, ideal and practical voltage and current sources, the strange but very useful dependent sources, and the two extreme cases, the open circuit and the short circuit.

What a circuit element is: An element is the basic building block of a circuit, a part with two terminals (sometimes more) whose behaviour can be described by a relation between its voltage and its current. A resistor's relation is v = iR. A battery's ideal relation is v = constant. Later we will add capacitors and inductors, whose relations involve change over time. Circuit theory treats each element as "lumped", meaning its whole behaviour is concentrated in one point on the diagram, joined by ideal wires. This works well as long as the circuit is small compared with the wavelength of the signals, which is true for nearly everything in this course.

Active and passive elements: An active element can supply net energy to a circuit over time. Batteries, generators, solar cells and the sources we study below are active. A passive element cannot supply more energy than it has received. Resistors only absorb energy and turn it into heat. Capacitors and inductors can store energy and give it back later, but they can never give back more than they took, so they are passive too. A simple test: if an element can keep a bulb glowing on its own forever, it is active.

Ideal independent voltage source: This is an element that keeps a fixed voltage across its terminals no matter how much current flows through it. If you connect a 12 V ideal source to a 1 Ω resistor, it supplies 12 A. Connect it to a 0.01 Ω resistor and it would happily supply 1200 A, still holding exactly 12 V. It is called independent because its voltage does not depend on anything else in the circuit. Its symbol is a circle with + and - marks inside, or for DC, the familiar battery symbol of long and short lines.

Ideal independent current source: This is the twin idea: an element that forces a fixed current through its branch no matter what voltage is needed. A 2 A ideal current source connected to a 10 Ω resistor creates 20 V across it. Connected to a 1000 Ω resistor, it would create 2000 V to keep 2 A flowing. Its symbol is a circle with an arrow inside showing the current direction. Current sources feel strange at first because batteries behave like voltage sources, but many real devices, such as transistors and solar cells in some operating ranges, behave roughly like current sources.

Why ideal sources are idealisations: No real battery can supply 1200 A, and no real current source can create 2000 V without sparks. Ideal sources are mathematical models. They are extremely useful because they make equations simple, and real sources can be described by adding a resistor to them, as we see next. Two forbidden situations follow from the definitions: never short-circuit an ideal voltage source (it would demand infinite current), and never leave an ideal current source open-circuited (it would demand infinite voltage). Exam questions sometimes test whether you notice such impossible circuits.

Practical voltage source: A real battery has some internal resistance, r, inside it, caused by its chemistry and materials. We model it as an ideal voltage source E in series with r. When current I flows, part of the voltage is lost inside: terminal voltage V = E - I × r. Example: a battery with E = 12 V and r = 0.5 Ω supplying 4 A has terminal voltage 12 - 4 × 0.5 = 10 V. The 2 V difference turns into heat inside the battery. A good voltage source has small r; an ideal one has r = 0.

Measuring internal resistance: You can find r with two readings. With no load connected, a voltmeter reads nearly E, say 9.0 V. With a 10 Ω load, the voltage drops to 8.2 V. The current then is 8.2 / 10 = 0.82 A, and the lost voltage is 9.0 - 8.2 = 0.8 V, so r = 0.8 / 0.82, about 0.98 Ω. As batteries age their internal resistance grows, which is why an old battery may show a fine voltage on the meter but collapse as soon as you connect a real load.

Practical current source: A real current source is modelled as an ideal current source with a large resistance in parallel. Some of the source current leaks through that parallel resistance instead of going to the load. The larger the parallel resistance, the closer the source is to ideal. In lesson 12 we will see that a practical voltage source and a practical current source can be converted into each other; that trick is called source transformation.

Dependent (controlled) sources: A dependent source is a source whose value depends on a voltage or current somewhere else in the circuit. It is drawn as a diamond shape instead of a circle. There are four kinds. A voltage-controlled voltage source (VCVS) gives v = μ × vx, where vx is some other voltage. A current-controlled voltage source (CCVS) gives v = r × ix. A voltage-controlled current source (VCCS) gives i = g × vx. A current-controlled current source (CCCS) gives i = β × ix. The constants μ and β have no units, r is in ohms and g is in siemens.

Why dependent sources matter: Dependent sources are how circuit theory models amplifiers and transistors. In a simple transistor model, a small base current ib controls a much bigger collector current β × ib, which is exactly a CCCS. An operational amplifier, studied later in electronics, is modelled with a VCVS of huge gain. So although dependent sources look like an abstract trick now, they are the bridge between this course and the Electronic Devices course. When you solve a circuit with a dependent source, you write the controlling variable in terms of your unknowns and then solve as usual.

Worked example with a dependent source: A 10 V independent source drives a 2 Ω resistor, so the current there is ix = 5 A. Elsewhere in the circuit sits a CCVS with v = 3 × ix. Its voltage is 3 × 5 = 15 V. If ix changed to 2 A, the dependent source would automatically become 6 V. Unlike an independent source, it has no fixed value of its own; it just follows its controlling quantity.

Sources in series and parallel: Ideal voltage sources in series simply add, taking polarity into account: two 1.5 V cells in series, + to -, give 3 V, which is why a TV remote uses two cells end to end. Ideal voltage sources in parallel are allowed only if they have exactly the same voltage, otherwise the model breaks. For current sources it is the reverse: current sources in parallel add, and current sources in series are allowed only if they are equal. Real batteries of different voltages placed in parallel will push large currents into each other, so never mix old and new cells in a device.

Open circuit and short circuit as elements: An open circuit is a break where current is zero but any voltage may exist across the gap. A short circuit is a perfect wire where voltage is zero but any current may flow. You can think of an open circuit as a current source of 0 A and a short circuit as a voltage source of 0 V. This viewpoint becomes very handy when we "turn off" sources for superposition and Thevenin's theorem: a turned-off voltage source becomes a short, and a turned-off current source becomes an open.

Switches: A switch is simply an element that is a short circuit when closed and an open circuit when open. Real switches have a tiny resistance when closed and a huge one when open, but we model them as ideal. Inside a computer, transistors act as extremely fast electronic switches, flipping billions of times per second. That is the deepest link between this course and computing: a processor is, at heart, a sea of tiny controlled switches.

Sources as graphs: It helps to picture each source on a graph of terminal voltage against current. An ideal voltage source is a flat horizontal line: the voltage stays at E for every current. An ideal current source is a vertical line: the current stays fixed for every voltage. A practical voltage source is a line that slopes downward from E at zero current, losing r volts for every ampere drawn, and it hits zero volts at the short-circuit current E / r. For the 12 V, 0.5 Ω battery above, that short-circuit current would be 24 A, which is why shorting even a small battery with a wire makes the wire hot. Reading sources as lines on a graph makes the difference between ideal and practical sources very easy to remember.

Real life example 1, a car or CNG battery on a cold morning: When the starter motor of a CNG auto-rickshaw cranks, it may draw a large current, say 100 A or more, for a moment. With an internal resistance of around 0.02 Ω, the battery loses 100 × 0.02 = 2 V internally, so the terminal voltage of a 12.6 V battery drops near 10.6 V. The headlights visibly dim during cranking. An old battery with higher internal resistance drops even further, sometimes too far for the starter to turn. Mechanics test batteries "under load" for exactly this reason.

Real life example 2, a solar panel on a village roof: Under steady sunlight, a solar cell behaves roughly like a current source over much of its range: the current is set mainly by how much light falls on it, while the voltage adjusts to the load. If a cloud passes, the current drops. Solar home systems, which are common in rural Bangladesh, use a charge controller to manage this behaviour and charge a battery, which then acts like a voltage source for the lights and fans. One small system thus uses both kinds of source in one place.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse a current source with a battery, try to short an ideal voltage source on paper, forget the internal resistance in terminal voltage problems, and drop the controlling variable of a dependent source when writing equations. They also mix up which constants have units. Typical exam questions: classify elements as active or passive, find terminal voltage or internal resistance of a battery, identify the four dependent sources from their diamonds, and spot an invalid series or parallel connection of ideal sources.

Recap: Elements are the players of a circuit. Active elements supply energy, passive ones absorb or store it. An ideal voltage source fixes voltage, an ideal current source fixes current, and practical sources add internal resistance (V = E - Ir). Dependent sources, drawn as diamonds, follow another voltage or current and model transistors and amplifiers. Open circuit means zero current, short circuit means zero voltage. Next we learn the two laws that tie all these players together: Kirchhoff's laws.
key_points: Active elements supply net energy; passive elements (R, L, C) only absorb or store it.
An ideal voltage source fixes its voltage whatever the current; an ideal current source fixes its current whatever the voltage.
A practical voltage source = ideal source + series internal resistance: V = E - Ir.
A practical current source = ideal current source + parallel resistance.
Dependent sources (diamonds): VCVS, CCVS, VCCS, CCCS; they model transistors and amplifiers.
Voltage sources add in series; current sources add in parallel; unequal ideal sources cannot be paralleled (voltage) or series-connected (current).
Turned-off voltage source = short circuit; turned-off current source = open circuit.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a diamond, immediately write its controlling variable in terms of your unknowns; that one habit prevents most dependent-source mistakes.

lessons.title: Nodes, Loops and Kirchhoff's Laws
lessons.content:
Stand at a busy crossing like Shahbag at rush hour. Rickshaws, buses and cars pour in from several roads and pour out along others. However chaotic it looks, one thing is certain: every vehicle that enters the crossing must leave it, because vehicles do not vanish or appear out of thin air. Now walk once around the block and come back to where you started: whatever hills you climbed, you must have come down the same total height, because you are back at the same level. These two common-sense facts, written for electric circuits, are Kirchhoff's two laws. Together with Ohm's law, they solve every circuit in this course.

Who Kirchhoff was: Gustav Kirchhoff was a German physicist who in 1845, while still a student, published the two rules that carry his name. They are not new physics; they are simply conservation of charge and conservation of energy written in a form that suits circuits. That is why they are so reliable: they work for resistors, capacitors, inductors, diodes, transistors, AC and DC, linear and non-linear circuits alike.

Some vocabulary first: A node is a point where two or more elements connect. If several dots are joined by plain wires with no element between them, they all count as one single node, because an ideal wire has no voltage drop. A branch is a single element or path between two nodes, such as one resistor or one source. A loop is any closed path that starts at a node, passes through branches and returns to the same node without passing any node twice. A mesh is a loop that has no other loop inside it, like a single window pane in a window frame.

Counting nodes correctly: This is where many students slip. Draw the circuit and colour each wire segment that is connected without any element in between. Each colour is one node. A circuit drawing may show six dots, but if three of them are joined by bare wire, they are one node. Getting the node count right matters, because in later lessons the number of equations you write depends on it. A useful relation for a connected circuit is: number of independent loops = b - n + 1, where b is the number of branches and n the number of nodes.

Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): The algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero. Equivalently, the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. In symbols, sum of i_in = sum of i_out. Example: at a node, 5 A enters from one wire, 2 A leaves through a second wire. How much leaves through the third wire? 5 = 2 + i, so i = 3 A. If your answer for a current comes out negative, the current simply flows opposite to the arrow you drew.

Why KCL is true: Charge is conserved, and a node, being just a joint of ideal wires, cannot store charge. So whatever charge flows in per second must flow out per second. If more current entered than left, charge would pile up at the node forever, which does not happen in a real wire junction. That is why KCL is sometimes called the junction rule.

KCL for a surface: KCL works not only at a single node but for any closed boundary you draw around part of a circuit. The total current entering the boundary equals the total leaving it. This is a handy trick: if a big box of circuitry is connected to the outside world by three wires, the three wire currents must add to zero, no matter what is happening inside the box. In a house, the current in the live wire and the neutral wire should be equal; if they are not, current is leaking somewhere, perhaps through a person, and a safety device called an RCD or RCCB trips. That device is KCL in action.

Sign rule for KCL: Choose a convention and stick to it. One common rule: currents entering a node are positive and currents leaving are negative, then set the sum to zero. For the example above, +5 - 2 - i = 0, giving i = 3 A again. Either convention works as long as you use it the same way throughout one equation.

Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): The algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop is zero. As you walk around a loop, every rise in voltage is matched by drops, so they total zero. In symbols, sum of v around the loop = 0. Another way to say it: the sum of voltage rises equals the sum of voltage drops.

Why KVL is true: Voltage is energy per charge. If you carry a test charge all the way around a loop and back to where you started, it ends with the same energy it began with, just as walking around a block brings you back to the same height. So the net energy change, and therefore the sum of voltages, must be zero. KVL is conservation of energy for circuits, which is why it is also called the loop rule.

Sign rule for KVL: Pick a direction to walk around the loop, clockwise or anticlockwise. For each element, look at which terminal you meet first. If you enter at the + sign and leave at the -, write +v (a drop). If you enter at - and leave at +, write -v (a rise). Then add everything and set the sum equal to zero. The direction you choose does not matter; walking the other way just multiplies the whole equation by -1.

Worked example, single loop: A 12 V battery is in series with R1 = 2 Ω and R2 = 4 Ω. Call the loop current I, flowing clockwise out of the battery's + terminal. Walking clockwise: we pass the battery from - to +, a rise of 12 V, so we write -12. Then R1 drops 2I and R2 drops 4I. KVL: -12 + 2I + 4I = 0, so 6I = 12 and I = 2 A. The voltage across R1 is 4 V and across R2 is 8 V. Check: 4 + 8 = 12, the drops equal the rise. Power check: the battery supplies 12 × 2 = 24 W, the resistors absorb 2² × 2 + 2² × 4 = 8 + 16 = 24 W.

Worked example, two opposing sources: Now put a 20 V source and an 8 V source in the same loop, facing each other so that they push in opposite directions, with two 3 Ω resistors. Walking around: -20 + 3I + 8 + 3I = 0 (we meet the 8 V source from its + side, so it counts as a drop). That gives 6I = 12, so I = 2 A in the direction the 20 V source pushes. The bigger source wins and the smaller one is actually being charged, absorbing 8 × 2 = 16 W. This is exactly what happens when a car's alternator charges its battery.

Worked example, single node pair: A 6 A current source feeds two resistors in parallel, 3 Ω and 6 Ω. Both resistors share the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage V. KCL at the top node: 6 = V/3 + V/6. Multiply everything by 6: 36 = 2V + V, so V = 12 V. Then I1 = 12 / 3 = 4 A and I2 = 12 / 6 = 2 A. Check: 4 + 2 = 6 A, as KCL demands. Notice that the smaller resistor takes the bigger current; current prefers the easier path.

Worked example, both laws at once: A 10 V source feeds R1 = 2 Ω, which leads to a node A. From node A, two resistors R2 = 4 Ω and R3 = 4 Ω each go down to the bottom wire, which returns to the source. Call the currents I1 (through R1), I2 (through R2) and I3 (through R3). KCL at A: I1 = I2 + I3. KVL around the left loop (source, R1, R2): 10 = 2 I1 + 4 I2. KVL around the right loop (R2 and R3): 4 I2 - 4 I3 = 0, so I2 = I3. Then I1 = 2 I2, and the first loop gives 10 = 4 I2 + 4 I2, so I2 = 1.25 A, I3 = 1.25 A and I1 = 2.5 A. The voltage at node A is 4 × 1.25 = 5 V. Three unknowns, three equations, one clean answer; this is the whole method in miniature.

Kirchhoff inside a computer: The same laws govern the copper tracks of a motherboard. The voltage regulator near the processor must deliver a large current at around one volt, and KCL says all of that current must also return through the ground tracks. Designers make ground planes wide so that, by Ohm's law, the return current causes only a tiny voltage drop, and by KVL, every chip sees nearly the full supply voltage. When those drops are not controlled, computers crash in strange ways.

Using KCL and KVL together: For bigger circuits, the general recipe is: label every unknown current with an arrow, label voltages using the passive sign convention, write KCL at all but one node, write KVL around enough independent loops, use Ohm's law to link each resistor's voltage and current, then solve the equations. This recipe always works but can produce many equations. Lessons 10 and 11, nodal and mesh analysis, are smart, organised versions of exactly this method that keep the number of equations small.

Real life example 1, a laptop power strip: Suppose a power strip feeds a laptop drawing 0.4 A, a monitor drawing 0.3 A and a router drawing 0.1 A, all from the same wall cable. KCL at the strip says the wall cable carries 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.8 A. If someone adds an electric kettle drawing 8 A, the cable now carries 8.8 A. If the strip is rated 10 A, it is near its limit, and adding an iron would exceed it. Electricians use this simple addition every day to size wires and breakers.

Real life example 2, a battery pack with a weak cell: An easy-bike might use four 12 V batteries in series to make 48 V. KVL says the total voltage is the sum of the four. If one battery is weak and only gives 10 V, the pack gives 46 V instead of 48 V, and under load, because of internal resistance, the weak battery's voltage falls even more. Technicians measure across each battery separately and use KVL to spot the culprit: the four readings must add up to the pack voltage, and the odd one out is the one to replace.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common errors are wrong node counts (forgetting that wire-joined dots are one node), inconsistent sign rules within one KVL equation, writing KVL across a current source without including its unknown voltage, and writing one KCL equation too many (with n nodes, only n - 1 KCL equations are independent). Typical exam questions: state and explain KCL and KVL, count nodes, branches and loops, solve a single-loop or single-node-pair circuit, find unknown currents at a junction, and verify power balance.

Recap: KCL says current into a node equals current out, because charge is conserved. KVL says voltages around a closed loop add to zero, because energy is conserved. Count nodes carefully, choose a consistent sign rule, and use Ohm's law to connect voltages and currents in resistors. With these three laws you can, in principle, solve any circuit. In the next lesson we use them to discover the rules for series and parallel resistors.
key_points: Node: a connection point; wire-joined dots form one node. Branch: one element. Loop: closed path. Mesh: loop with no loop inside.
KCL: total current into a node equals total current out (charge conservation).
KVL: voltages around any closed loop sum to zero (energy conservation).
Pick one sign rule per equation and keep it; a negative result means the real direction is reversed.
With n nodes, n - 1 KCL equations are independent; independent loops = b - n + 1.
KCL also works for any closed boundary around part of a circuit.
Always check: total power supplied equals total power absorbed.
lessons.tip: Before writing any equation, colour the nodes and draw every current arrow; most Kirchhoff mistakes are labelling mistakes, not algebra mistakes.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Resistors
lessons.content:
Imagine two ways to get students through the gate of a school after the bell. In the first, there is one narrow gate followed by a second narrow gate, one after the other; every student must squeeze through both, so the gates add their delays. In the second, the school opens three gates side by side; students split up, and the crowd empties much faster. Resistors behave exactly like these gates. Put them one after another and they add up; put them side by side and they share the load and the total opposition falls. This lesson turns that picture into formulas you will use in nearly every problem from now on.

Equivalent resistance: When several resistors are connected between two terminals, the whole group behaves, as seen from those terminals, like one single resistor. The value of that single resistor is called the equivalent resistance, Req. Replacing a group with its equivalent is like replacing a long description with one word that means the same thing. The rest of the circuit cannot tell the difference, because the same voltage at the terminals produces the same current.

Series connection: Elements are in series when they are connected end to end, so that exactly the same current must flow through each one. The test is: two elements are in series if they share exactly one node, and nothing else is connected to that node. A classic example is a chain of old-style fairy lights, where current flows through bulb one, then bulb two, then bulb three.

Series resistance formula: Let resistors R1, R2 and R3 be in series with current I. By Ohm's law their voltages are IR1, IR2 and IR3. By KVL the total voltage across the chain is V = IR1 + IR2 + IR3 = I(R1 + R2 + R3). So the chain behaves like one resistor of Req = R1 + R2 + R3. In general, resistances in series add. Example: 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series give 10 Ω. If a 20 V source drives them, I = 20 / 10 = 2 A, and the voltages are 4 V, 6 V and 10 V, adding back to 20 V.

Properties of series circuits: The current is the same everywhere in the chain. The voltage divides among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, so the biggest resistor gets the biggest share of the voltage. The equivalent resistance is always larger than the largest single resistor. And if any one element opens, for example a bulb filament breaks, the current stops everywhere in the chain. That is why a single dead bulb could darken a whole old fairy-light string.

Parallel connection: Elements are in parallel when they are connected between the same two nodes, so that they all have exactly the same voltage across them. Each element gets its own separate path for current. The fan, the light and the socket in your room are all connected in parallel across the 220 V supply; each gets the full voltage and each can be switched on or off independently.

Parallel resistance formula: Let R1, R2 and R3 be in parallel with voltage V across all of them. Their currents are V/R1, V/R2 and V/R3. By KCL the total current is I = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3 = V(1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3). Since I = V/Req, we get 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. In words: for parallel resistors, the reciprocals add. In conductance language this is even simpler: Geq = G1 + G2 + G3, conductances in parallel just add.

The product-over-sum shortcut: For exactly two resistors in parallel, the formula simplifies to Req = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2). Example: 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel give 18 / 9 = 2 Ω. Another shortcut: n equal resistors R in parallel give R / n. Four 100 Ω resistors in parallel give 25 Ω. A handy sanity check: the equivalent of parallel resistors is always smaller than the smallest one. If 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω gave you 4 Ω, you would know immediately that something is wrong.

Properties of parallel circuits: The voltage is the same across every branch. The total current divides among the branches, and the smallest resistance carries the biggest current, because current prefers the easier path. If one branch opens, the other branches keep working, because their paths are still complete. If one branch is short-circuited, though, the whole parallel group becomes a short, since a 0 Ω path in parallel with anything gives 0 Ω.

Series-parallel combinations: Most real circuits mix both. The method is to reduce step by step. Find a group that is clearly in series or clearly in parallel, replace it with its equivalent, redraw the circuit, and repeat until only one resistor remains. Always start from the part farthest from the terminals you are looking into, and work your way back towards them. Redrawing neatly after each step is not a waste of time; it is what prevents mistakes.

Worked example 1: A 12 V source drives a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. First, 6 Ω parallel 3 Ω = 2 Ω. Then 4 Ω + 2 Ω = 6 Ω total. The source current is 12 / 6 = 2 A. The 4 Ω resistor drops 2 × 4 = 8 V, leaving 4 V across the parallel pair. So the 6 Ω carries 4/6, about 0.67 A, and the 3 Ω carries 4/3, about 1.33 A. Check by KCL: 0.67 + 1.33 = 2 A.

Worked example 2, a ladder: Find Req between terminals a and b, where a 2 Ω resistor leads from a to a node x, and from x to b there is a 6 Ω resistor in parallel with a branch containing 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series. Start at the far end: 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. That 12 Ω is in parallel with 6 Ω: (6 × 12) / 18 = 4 Ω. Then add the 2 Ω in series: Req = 6 Ω. Working from the far end towards the terminals is the key habit for ladder networks.

Worked example 3, with a power check: A 30 V source feeds a 5 Ω resistor, then a node from which two branches go back to the source: one branch is 20 Ω, the other is 10 Ω in series with 10 Ω. The second branch is 20 Ω, so the two branches are 20 Ω parallel 20 Ω = 10 Ω. Total resistance 5 + 10 = 15 Ω, source current 30 / 15 = 2 A. The 5 Ω drops 10 V, leaving 20 V across both branches, so each branch carries 20 / 20 = 1 A. Powers: 5 Ω absorbs 2² × 5 = 20 W, the 20 Ω absorbs 1² × 20 = 20 W, each 10 Ω absorbs 1² × 10 = 10 W. Total absorbed 20 + 20 + 10 + 10 = 60 W, and the source supplies 30 × 2 = 60 W. Balanced, so the answer is right.

A quick sense check with extremes: If you are unsure about a parallel result, imagine one resistor becoming huge. A 6 Ω in parallel with a 1,000,000 Ω is almost exactly 6 Ω, because nearly no current takes the huge path. Now imagine one becoming tiny: 6 Ω in parallel with 0.001 Ω is almost 0 Ω, because nearly all current takes the tiny path. Your formula must agree with these extremes. Such quick checks catch many wrong answers before the examiner does.

Which terminals matter: Equivalent resistance always depends on which two terminals you are looking into. The same network of resistors can have different equivalents between a-b, a-c and b-c. So before reducing, mark the two terminals clearly and ask, for every resistor, how it connects relative to those terminals. A resistor whose one end is not connected to anything carries no current and simply drops out, and a resistor with both ends on the same node is shorted and also drops out.

Tricky cases: Shorted resistor: if a wire connects both ends of a resistor, no current flows through the resistor and you can delete it. Floating branch: a resistor dangling with an open end carries no current. Equal-potential points: if symmetry shows two nodes are at the same voltage, the resistor between them carries no current and can be removed. Recognising these situations quickly makes many exam circuits much easier than they first look.

Power in series and parallel: A surprising result: connect a 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb (both rated for 220 V) in series across 220 V. The 60 W bulb has the larger resistance, about 807 Ω compared with 484 Ω, since R = V² / P. In series the same current, about 0.17 A, flows through both, so the bigger resistance gets more power: roughly 23 W for the "60 W" bulb and 14 W for the "100 W" bulb. The 60 W bulb glows brighter. In parallel, each gets the full 220 V and glows at its rated power, so the 100 W bulb is brighter. Many exam questions are built on this twist.

Real life example 1, wiring a room: A room in a Dhaka flat has two 10 W LED lights, one 70 W fan and a socket where a 40 W TV is plugged in, all in parallel on 220 V. The currents are about 0.045 A for each light, 0.32 A for the fan and 0.18 A for the TV. The total is about 0.59 A. The room behaves like one equivalent resistor of 220 / 0.59, about 373 Ω, which is smaller than any single appliance's resistance, just as the rule predicts. Switching off the TV removes a branch and the total current drops, but the fan and lights do not even notice.

Real life example 2, holiday lights from the market: Cheap decorative LED strings sold before Pohela Boishakh or weddings often connect LEDs in series groups, with several groups in parallel. Within a group, the LEDs share one current, so one failed LED that goes open darkens its group. The other groups keep shining because they are in parallel. Designers choose this mix to get a sensible total voltage per group while still keeping some protection against one failure darkening the entire string.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students add parallel resistances directly, forget to take the reciprocal at the end of 1/Req, call two resistors in series when a third wire also connects at their shared node, and lose track of which two terminals they are reducing between. Typical exam questions: find Req of a ladder or a series-parallel network, find all branch currents and voltages, compare brightness of bulbs in series and parallel, and explain why houses are wired in parallel.

Recap: Series means same current; resistances add and voltage divides. Parallel means same voltage; reciprocals (or conductances) add and current divides. Two in parallel: product over sum. n equal in parallel: R/n. Reduce step by step from the far end, redrawing as you go, and always keep the two terminals in mind. The next lesson turns the "divides" part into two neat formulas: the voltage divider and the current divider.
key_points: Series: same current; Req = R1 + R2 + ...; Req is bigger than the largest resistor.
Parallel: same voltage; 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...; Req is smaller than the smallest resistor.
Two in parallel: Req = R1R2 / (R1 + R2); n equal in parallel: R/n.
Conductances in parallel add: Geq = G1 + G2 + ...
Reduce series-parallel networks step by step from the far end toward the terminals.
A shorted resistor or a dangling resistor carries no current and drops out.
Houses are wired in parallel so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently.
lessons.tip: Redraw the circuit after every single reduction step; it feels slow but it is the fastest way to a correct answer.
lessons.task: Draw your own room's electrical points as a parallel circuit, estimate each appliance's current from its wattage (I = P/220), and find the total current and the equivalent resistance.

quiz.explain: Product over sum: 48 / 16 = 3 Ω.

quiz.q: Five 50 Ω resistors in parallel give:
quiz.explain: n equal resistors in parallel: R / n = 50 / 5 = 10 Ω.

quiz.q: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same for every resistor?
quiz.explain: Series elements share one path, so the same current flows through each.

quiz.q: A 60 W and a 100 W bulb (both 220 V rated) are in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
quiz.explain: The 60 W bulb has higher resistance; with the same current, P = I²R is larger for it.

quiz.q: A resistor has a plain wire connected across both its ends. Its current is:
quiz.explain: The wire shorts it; all current takes the 0 Ω wire, so the resistor carries none.

lessons.title: Voltage and Current Dividers
lessons.content:
When your family orders a large pizza for four people, nobody calculates each slice from scratch. You know the rule: each person gets a share in proportion to how much they are allowed. Circuits have two such sharing rules. In a series chain, the total voltage is shared out among the resistors. In a parallel group, the total current is shared out among the branches. The voltage divider rule and the current divider rule let you write each share directly, in one line, without solving the whole circuit. They save a huge amount of time in exams and they are used in real electronics every single day.

Where dividers come from: In the last lesson we saw that in series, voltage divides, and in parallel, current divides. The divider rules are simply those facts written as ready-made formulas. They are not new laws; they come straight from Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws. Still, they are so common that it is worth learning them as tools of their own.

The voltage divider: Take a source V connected across two resistors R1 and R2 in series. The current is I = V / (R1 + R2). The voltage across R2 is V2 = I × R2 = V × R2 / (R1 + R2). Similarly V1 = V × R1 / (R1 + R2). In words: each resistor gets the fraction of the total voltage equal to its share of the total resistance. If R2 is three quarters of the total resistance, it gets three quarters of the voltage.

Voltage divider examples: A 12 V source across 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ: the 4 kΩ resistor gets 12 × 4 / 6 = 8 V and the 2 kΩ gets 12 × 2 / 6 = 4 V. Equal resistors split the voltage equally: 10 V across 5 kΩ and 5 kΩ gives 5 V each. To get a small fraction, make the lower resistor small: 9 V across 8 kΩ and 1 kΩ gives 9 × 1 / 9 = 1 V across the 1 kΩ.

Voltage divider with many resistors: The rule extends to any number of series resistors. The voltage across resistor Rk is Vk = V × Rk / (R1 + R2 + ... + Rn). Example: 24 V across 1 Ω, 2 Ω and 3 Ω (total 6 Ω) gives 4 V, 8 V and 12 V. You can also find the voltage across a group: the voltage across the 2 Ω and 3 Ω together is 24 × 5 / 6 = 20 V. This is often the quickest way to find the voltage at a point in a resistor chain.

Important condition for the voltage divider: The formula is only valid when the resistors truly carry the same current, meaning nothing else draws current from the middle point. If some other element is connected at the middle node and draws current, the plain divider formula gives the wrong answer. This leads directly to one of the most important practical ideas in this lesson: loading.

The loading effect: Suppose a divider of 10 kΩ and 10 kΩ across 10 V gives 5 V at the middle, unloaded. Now connect a 10 kΩ load across the lower resistor. The lower part becomes 10 kΩ parallel 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ, and the output becomes 10 × 5 / 15, about 3.33 V instead of 5 V. The load "pulled down" the output. If instead the load is 100 kΩ, the lower part becomes 10 parallel 100, about 9.09 kΩ, and the output is 10 × 9.09 / 19.09, about 4.76 V, close to 5 V. The rule of thumb: the load resistance should be much larger, at least about ten times larger, than the divider resistors if you want the output to stay near its unloaded value.

Choosing divider values: The ratio of the resistors sets the output, but their size sets the current wasted. A 1 kΩ and 1 kΩ divider across 10 V wastes 10 / 2000 = 5 mA, which is 50 mW, all the time. A 100 kΩ and 100 kΩ divider gives the same 5 V but wastes only 50 µA, which is 0.5 mW. For a battery-powered gadget that must last months, the larger values are much better. But larger values make the divider more sensitive to loading. So designers pick resistor sizes that are as large as possible while still being at least about ten times smaller than whatever load will be connected.

Node voltages in a chain: A divider chain can also give several voltages at once. Put 1 kΩ, 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series across 12 V, with the bottom end at ground. The total is 4 kΩ and the current is 3 mA. Measuring from ground upwards, the node above the 2 kΩ is at 6 V, the next node is at 9 V and the top is at 12 V. Each node voltage is the source voltage times the resistance below that node divided by the total. This is how simple reference ladders inside some analog-to-digital converters create many evenly spaced voltages from one supply.

Why dividers are not power supplies: Because of loading, a simple voltage divider is a poor way to power a device that draws a lot or a changing amount of current. A divider wastes power continuously in its resistors, and its output changes whenever the load changes. To power something properly, engineers use voltage regulators, which you meet in electronics courses. Dividers are perfect, however, for creating reference voltages and for reading sensors, where the load draws almost no current.

The potentiometer as an adjustable divider: A potentiometer has three terminals: two ends of a resistive track and a sliding contact called the wiper. Connect the two ends across a voltage and the wiper picks off any voltage from zero to the full value, depending on its position. If a 10 kΩ potentiometer is across 5 V and the wiper sits at the 30 percent position, the output is 5 × 0.3 = 1.5 V. This is how an analog volume knob or a joystick axis turns a mechanical position into a voltage.

Sensors in a divider: Many sensors are variable resistors, such as a light dependent resistor (LDR) whose resistance falls as light increases, or a thermistor whose resistance changes with temperature. Put the sensor in a divider with a fixed resistor and its changing resistance becomes a changing voltage, which a microcontroller can read. Example: an LDR of 20 kΩ in the dark and 2 kΩ in bright light, in a divider with a fixed 10 kΩ on the bottom across 5 V. In the dark the output is 5 × 10 / 30, about 1.67 V. In bright light it is 5 × 10 / 12, about 4.17 V. A program can switch a light on when the voltage drops below a threshold.

The current divider: Now take a current I entering two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel. Both share voltage V = I × (R1 R2) / (R1 + R2). Then I1 = V / R1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2) and I2 = I × R1 / (R1 + R2). Notice the twist: the current through R1 uses the other resistor, R2, in the numerator. That makes sense: if R2 is large, more current goes through R1. The bigger the other path's resistance, the more current you get.

Current divider examples: 12 mA enters 4 kΩ parallel 2 kΩ. Through the 4 kΩ: 12 × 2 / 6 = 4 mA. Through the 2 kΩ: 12 × 4 / 6 = 8 mA. The smaller resistor takes twice as much current, because it has half the resistance. Check: 4 + 8 = 12 mA. Another example: 3 A into 10 Ω parallel 20 Ω gives 2 A through the 10 Ω and 1 A through the 20 Ω.

Current divider with many branches: For more than two branches, conductances make it clean. The current in branch k is Ik = I × Gk / (G1 + G2 + ... + Gn), where G = 1/R. Example: 10 A enters 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel. The conductances are 0.5, 0.333 and 0.167 S, adding to 1 S. So the currents are 10 × 0.5 = 5 A, 10 × 0.333, about 3.33 A, and 10 × 0.167, about 1.67 A. This form looks exactly like the voltage divider, with conductance in place of resistance; that symmetry is worth remembering.

Divider rules in the lab, the ammeter shunt: An ammeter can be built from a sensitive meter that measures only a tiny current, say 1 mA, by putting a small "shunt" resistor in parallel with it. Most of the current goes through the shunt and only a known small fraction goes through the meter. By the current divider rule, choosing the right shunt lets a 1 mA meter read up to 1 A or 10 A. Similarly, a voltmeter uses a large series resistor so that the meter's small voltage is a known fraction of the total, which is the voltage divider idea. We return to this in lesson 9.

Real life example 1, reading a 12 V battery with a 5 V microcontroller: A student building a solar project in a village wants an Arduino to monitor a 12 V battery. The Arduino's analog input accepts at most 5 V, so connecting 12 V directly could damage it. Use a divider: R1 = 20 kΩ on top and R2 = 10 kΩ on the bottom. The input sees 12 × 10 / 30 = 4 V. Even if the battery reaches 14.4 V while charging, the input sees 4.8 V, still safe. The program multiplies the reading by 3 to get the battery voltage back. The Arduino input draws almost no current, so loading is negligible.

Real life example 2, connecting 5 V and 3.3 V chips: Many modern chips, such as the ESP32 used in IoT projects, run at 3.3 V and can be damaged by 5 V signals. A common trick for a slow signal is a divider of 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ: 5 × 2 / 3, about 3.33 V. With 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ you get the same ratio and waste less current, but the larger resistors make fast signals sluggish. Engineers pick values by balancing power waste, loading and speed, and that balance is exactly what these simple formulas let you think about.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In the voltage divider, students sometimes put the other resistor in the numerator, which is the current divider form, and vice versa. They also apply the divider when a load or another branch draws current from the middle node, ignoring loading. In the current divider with three branches, using resistances instead of conductances gives wrong answers. Typical exam questions: find a voltage at a point in a resistor chain, find branch currents in a parallel group, compute the output of a loaded divider, and design a divider for a given ratio.

Recap: Voltage divider: Vx = V × Rx / Rtotal for series resistors carrying the same current. Current divider: for two resistors, I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2); for many, Ik = I × Gk / Gtotal. A load on a divider lowers its output unless the load is much larger than the divider resistors. Potentiometers and sensors use dividers to turn position, light or temperature into voltage. Next we tackle networks that are neither series nor parallel, with the wye-delta transformation and bridge circuits.
key_points: Voltage divider: Vx = V × Rx / (sum of series R), valid only if no current leaves the middle node.
Current divider (two resistors): I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2); the other resistor goes on top.
Many branches: Ik = I × Gk / Gtotal using conductances.
Loading: a load across a divider lowers its output; keep the load at least ~10× the divider resistance.
Dividers are good for references and sensors, not for powering loads.
A potentiometer is an adjustable voltage divider; LDRs and thermistors in dividers make sensor voltages.
Ammeter shunts use the current divider; voltmeter series resistors use the voltage divider.
lessons.tip: Say the rule out loud while writing it: 'voltage: my own resistor on top; current: the other resistor on top'. It stops the most common swap.
lessons.task: Design a divider that turns 9 V into about 3 V using standard resistor values, then calculate what happens to the output if a 10 kΩ load is connected.

quiz.explain: I(3Ω) = 6 × 6 / 9 = 4 A; the smaller resistor takes more.
