lessons.title: Wye-Delta Transformation and Bridge Circuits
lessons.content:
Sometimes a puzzle looks impossible because you are staring at it from the wrong angle. Turn the page sideways and suddenly the answer is obvious. Some resistor networks are exactly like that. You look for resistors in series, you look for resistors in parallel, and you find neither. Every resistor seems to be tangled with three others. The classic example is the bridge circuit, shaped like a diamond with a resistor across the middle. In this lesson we learn a clever re-drawing trick, the wye-delta transformation, that untangles such networks, and we study the famous Wheatstone bridge, a circuit that has been used for over 150 years to measure resistance precisely.

When series-parallel fails: Draw a diamond with corners a (top), b (bottom), c (left) and d (right). Put resistors on the four sides a-c, a-d, c-b and d-b, and one more across the middle, c-d. Look from terminals a and b. Is a-c in series with c-b? No, because node c also connects to the middle resistor. Is a-c in parallel with a-d? No, because their other ends go to different nodes. The middle resistor spoils every simple pattern. We need a new tool.

Delta and wye shapes: Three resistors connected in a triangle between three terminals form a delta (Δ) network, also called a pi (π) network when drawn differently. Three resistors that each go from one terminal to a shared centre point form a wye (Y) network, also called a tee (T) network. Both shapes connect the same three terminals. The key insight is that for any delta there is a wye that behaves identically at the three terminals, and the other way round. Swapping one for the other often turns a tangled network into a simple series-parallel one.

Naming: Call the three terminals a, b and c. In the delta, the resistors sit between pairs of terminals: Rab, Rbc and Rca. In the wye, each resistor runs from a terminal to the centre: Ra, Rb and Rc. To convert correctly you must keep track of which resistor touches which terminals, so always label carefully before using any formula.

Delta to wye: Each wye resistor equals the product of the two delta resistors that touch the same terminal, divided by the sum of all three delta resistors. Ra = (Rab × Rca) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca). Rb = (Rab × Rbc) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca). Rc = (Rbc × Rca) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca). A memory trick: for Ra, use the two delta resistors that have "a" in their name.

Wye to delta: Each delta resistor equals the sum of the pairwise products of the wye resistors, divided by the wye resistor opposite to it, meaning the one connected to the terminal not touched by that delta resistor. Let P = RaRb + RbRc + RcRa. Then Rab = P / Rc, Rbc = P / Ra and Rca = P / Rb. A memory trick: for Rab, divide by the wye resistor whose terminal is missing from "ab", which is Rc.

Where the formulas come from: The idea behind the derivation is simple even if the algebra is a little long. For the two networks to be equivalent, the resistance measured between any pair of terminals, with the third terminal left open, must be the same. In the wye, between a and b with c open, you see Ra + Rb. In the delta, between a and b you see Rab in parallel with (Rbc + Rca). Writing this equality for all three pairs gives three equations, and solving them gives the formulas above. You are rarely asked to derive them in full, but knowing this idea helps you trust them and rebuild them if you forget.

The balanced case: When all three resistors are equal, the formulas become beautifully simple: R_Y = R_Δ / 3, or R_Δ = 3 × R_Y. A delta of three 30 Ω resistors equals a wye of three 10 Ω resistors. This balanced case is the most common in exams and in three-phase power systems, which we will meet in the final lesson. Check with the formula: Ra = (30 × 30) / 90 = 10 Ω.

A non-balanced conversion example: A delta has Rab = 10 Ω, Rbc = 20 Ω and Rca = 20 Ω. The sum is 50 Ω. Then Ra = (10 × 20) / 50 = 4 Ω, Rb = (10 × 20) / 50 = 4 Ω and Rc = (20 × 20) / 50 = 8 Ω. Now go back: P = 4 × 4 + 4 × 8 + 8 × 4 = 16 + 32 + 32 = 80. Rab = 80 / 8 = 10 Ω, Rbc = 80 / 4 = 20 Ω, Rca = 80 / 4 = 20 Ω. We are back where we started, which confirms the arithmetic.

Using the transformation on a bridge: Take the diamond with Rac = 30 Ω, Rad = 30 Ω and the middle Rcd = 30 Ω, so the top triangle a-c-d is a delta of three 30 Ω resistors. The lower sides are Rcb = 20 Ω and Rdb = 40 Ω. Convert the top delta to a wye of three 10 Ω resistors with centre n. Now the circuit is easy: from a, a 10 Ω goes to n. From n, one path goes 10 Ω to c and then 20 Ω to b, a total of 30 Ω. The other path goes 10 Ω to d and then 40 Ω to b, a total of 50 Ω. These two paths are in parallel: (30 × 50) / 80 = 18.75 Ω. Add the first 10 Ω: Req = 28.75 Ω. A network that had no series or parallel pairs is now solved in four lines.

Which way to convert: In a bridge, you can convert either the upper triangle or the lower triangle from delta to wye, or convert a wye formed around one of the middle nodes into a delta. All choices give the same final answer, but some give friendlier numbers. A good habit is to pick the triangle or star whose resistors are equal or simple multiples of each other, since the balanced formula then does the work in your head. After converting, redraw the circuit completely, mark the new centre node, and only then look for series and parallel pairs.

The Wheatstone bridge: The Wheatstone bridge, popularised by Charles Wheatstone in 1843, is a diamond of four resistors with a source across one diagonal and a sensitive meter, traditionally a galvanometer, across the other diagonal. Think of it as two voltage dividers side by side, both fed by the same source. The left divider is R1 on top and R2 at the bottom; the right divider is R3 on top and Rx at the bottom. The meter compares the middle voltages of the two dividers.

Balance condition: The bridge is balanced when the meter reads zero, meaning both middle points are at the same voltage. That happens when the two dividers have the same ratio: R2 / (R1 + R2) = Rx / (R3 + Rx), which simplifies to R1 / R2 = R3 / Rx, or Rx = R3 × R2 / R1. Example: R1 = 100 Ω, R2 = 200 Ω and R3 = 150 Ω. At balance Rx = 150 × 200 / 100 = 300 Ω. Notice that the source voltage does not appear in the answer at all, which is one reason the method is accurate: a slightly weak battery does not spoil the measurement.

A balanced bridge simplifies analysis: When a bridge is balanced, no current flows through the middle branch, so you can remove that branch completely, or equally replace it with a short, without changing anything. Then the circuit becomes two simple series-parallel paths. In exams, always check the ratio first. If R1/R2 equals R3/Rx, the middle resistor is irrelevant and the problem collapses. For example, with sides 2 Ω, 4 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω arranged so that 2/4 = 3/6, the equivalent resistance between the source corners is (2 + 4) parallel (3 + 6) = 6 parallel 9 = 3.6 Ω, whatever the middle resistor is.

How the bridge measures an unknown resistance: In a classic laboratory bridge, R1 and R2 are fixed precision resistors and R3 is a calibrated variable resistor. You connect the unknown Rx, then adjust R3 until the galvanometer shows zero. Then read R3 and compute Rx. Because the method detects zero current rather than measuring a large value, even a very sensitive meter does not disturb the result. The slide-wire metre bridge used in many college physics labs in Bangladesh is a version of this idea, where a uniform wire replaces R1 and R2 and the sliding jockey position sets their ratio.

Slightly unbalanced bridges and sensors: Many modern sensors use bridges that are deliberately nearly balanced. A strain gauge glued to a beam changes its resistance very slightly when the beam bends. Placed in a bridge, this tiny change creates a small voltage across the middle, which an amplifier boosts and measures. Electronic weighing scales in shops and the load cells that weigh trucks on highway weigh stations commonly work this way. Temperature sensors using platinum resistors are also read with bridge circuits.

Real life example 1, a digital weighing scale at a shop: When a shopkeeper in Karwan Bazar puts a bag of rice on a digital scale, the platform presses on a metal block with strain gauges arranged as a full bridge. With no weight, the bridge is balanced and the output is close to zero. The rice bends the block by a microscopic amount, a few gauges get slightly longer and others slightly shorter, and the bridge becomes unbalanced by a few millivolts. The scale's electronics amplify this and convert it to kilograms. Every reading on that display starts with the balance condition you just learned.

Real life example 2, finding a fault in a long cable: Telephone and power engineers once used bridge methods, such as the Murray loop test, to locate where a long underground cable had a fault to ground. Because the resistance of a uniform cable is proportional to its length, the bridge balance tells them the ratio of the distances to the fault. Knowing the total length, they can dig at the right spot instead of opening the whole road. Modern methods also use pulses and reflections, but the bridge idea shows how resistance ratios can turn into distances.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up which delta resistors touch which terminal, use the wrong denominator in the wye-to-delta formula, and forget that after converting, the new wye centre is a brand new node. Another mistake is solving a balanced bridge the long way, never noticing that the middle branch carries no current. Typical exam questions: convert a given delta to wye or vice versa, find Req of a bridge network using a transformation, state and derive the Wheatstone bridge balance condition, and find an unknown resistance from balance values.

Recap: Delta and wye are two ways of connecting three terminals, and each can be replaced by the other. Delta to wye: product of the two adjacent delta resistors over the sum of all three. Wye to delta: sum of pairwise products over the opposite wye resistor. Balanced: R_Y = R_Δ / 3. A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when R1/R2 = R3/Rx; then the middle branch carries no current and can be removed. Next we move from paper to the lab bench and learn how voltage, current and resistance are actually measured.
key_points: Some networks have no series or parallel pairs; bridges are the classic case.
Delta (Δ, π) and wye (Y, T) both connect three terminals and can replace each other.
Δ to Y: Ra = Rab·Rca / (Rab + Rbc + Rca), and similarly for Rb, Rc.
Y to Δ: Rab = (RaRb + RbRc + RcRa) / Rc, dividing by the opposite wye resistor.
Balanced: R_Y = R_Δ / 3.
Wheatstone bridge balance: R1/R2 = R3/Rx; no current in the middle branch, which can then be removed.
Bridges measure unknown resistances and read strain gauges in weighing scales.
lessons.tip: Before any transformation, check whether the bridge is balanced; if the ratios match, the middle resistor can be ignored and you save ten minutes.

quiz.q: A balanced delta has 45 Ω in each arm. The equivalent wye resistors are:
quiz.explain: Balanced: R_Y = R_Δ / 3 = 15 Ω.

quiz.q: Delta to wye: Ra equals:
quiz.explain: Ra uses the two delta resistors touching terminal a, over the sum of all three.

quiz.q: A Wheatstone bridge has R1 = 50 Ω, R2 = 100 Ω, R3 = 80 Ω. At balance (R1/R2 = R3/Rx), Rx is:
In a balanced bridge, the current through the middle (galvanometer) branch is:
quiz.explain: Both middle points are at the same voltage, so no current flows across.

quiz.q: Why does a bridge's balance result not depend on the battery voltage?
options: Because the batteries are always ideal
Because the balance condition is a ratio of resistances only
quiz.explain: Balance needs R1/R2 = R3/Rx; the source voltage cancels out.

lessons.title: Measuring Instruments and the Circuits Lab
lessons.content:
A doctor does not guess your temperature; she uses a thermometer. A tailor does not guess your waist; he uses a measuring tape. An electrical engineer, likewise, does not guess voltages and currents; she measures them. But measuring electricity has a twist that a tape measure does not have: the instrument becomes part of the circuit, and if you connect it the wrong way it can give a wrong answer, blow a fuse, or even damage the circuit. This lesson is about the tools of the circuits lab, how they work inside using the ideas you already know, how to connect them correctly, and how to stay safe.

Why measurement matters in this course: Every theory lesson so far ends with numbers: a current of 2 A, a voltage of 8 V. In the lab you check those numbers against reality. When they agree, you trust your analysis. When they disagree, either your calculation, your circuit or your measurement is wrong, and finding out which one is a real engineering skill. Most university circuits courses in Bangladesh have a lab part, called a sessional, that runs alongside the theory, and it uses exactly the instruments described here.

The voltmeter: A voltmeter measures the voltage between two points, so it is always connected in parallel with, or across, the element you are measuring. You touch the red probe to one end and the black probe to the other. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so it draws no current and does not disturb the circuit. Real voltmeters have a large but finite resistance. A typical digital multimeter has an input resistance of around 10 MΩ on its voltage ranges, which is large enough for most circuits.

The ammeter: An ammeter measures the current flowing through a branch, so it must be connected in series: you break the circuit and let the current flow through the meter. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, so it causes no voltage drop. Real ammeters have a small resistance. The golden rule is easy to state and important to remember: voltmeter across, ammeter in series. An ammeter connected across a voltage source is effectively a short circuit, which is why multimeters have a fuse in the current input, and why that fuse is the part that most often blows in student labs.

The ohmmeter: An ohmmeter measures resistance by passing a small known current from its own internal battery through the component and measuring the resulting voltage, then applying R = V / I. Because it uses its own battery, you must never use an ohmmeter on a powered circuit; switch the power off first. Also, if the component is still connected in a circuit, other parallel paths will change the reading, so for an accurate value you should disconnect at least one end of the component.

The multimeter: A multimeter combines a voltmeter, an ammeter and an ohmmeter in one box, with a rotary switch to select the function and range. Digital multimeters (DMMs) show a number on a display. Older analog multimeters use a needle moving over a scale. Most DMMs also include a continuity test, which beeps when the resistance between the probes is very low, and a diode test. Many also measure capacitance, frequency and temperature. A basic DMM is cheap and widely available in electronics markets such as those around Elephant Road and Stadium Market in Dhaka.

Ranges and how to choose them: On a manual-range meter, you choose a range like 2 V, 20 V or 200 V. Pick the smallest range that is still larger than the value you expect, because that gives the most digits of precision. If you have no idea what to expect, start on the highest range and step down. Many modern meters are auto-ranging and do this for you. If the display shows "OL" or "1" on the left, the value is over the selected range.

Inside an analog meter, the galvanometer: The heart of a classic analog meter is a moving-coil galvanometer, a coil of wire in a magnetic field that turns a needle in proportion to the current through it. A typical movement might need only 1 mA for full-scale deflection and have an internal resistance of, say, 100 Ω. On its own it can measure only up to 1 mA, or up to 1 mA × 100 Ω = 0.1 V. The clever part is that with a single extra resistor, the same movement becomes an ammeter or voltmeter of any range you like, using the divider rules from lesson 7.

Building an ammeter with a shunt: To measure up to 1 A with the 1 mA, 100 Ω movement, put a shunt resistor in parallel. At full scale, 1 mA goes through the meter and the remaining 999 mA through the shunt. Both have the same voltage: 0.001 × 100 = 0.1 V. So the shunt is R_sh = 0.1 / 0.999, about 0.1001 Ω. The general formula is R_sh = Im × Rm / (I - Im). Notice how tiny the shunt is; that is why real ammeters have such low resistance.

Building a voltmeter with a multiplier: To measure up to 10 V with the same movement, put a large resistor in series. At full scale, 1 mA must flow when 10 V is applied, so the total resistance must be 10 / 0.001 = 10,000 Ω. The meter already provides 100 Ω, so the series multiplier is 9,900 Ω. The general formula is R_s = V / Im - Rm. A voltmeter's quality is often given as its sensitivity in ohms per volt, equal to 1 / Im. Our 1 mA movement gives 1000 Ω per volt; a good analog meter might give 20,000 Ω per volt, which disturbs circuits much less.

The loading effect of meters: Since real voltmeters draw some current, they slightly change the circuit they measure, just like the loaded divider in lesson 7. Example: a 10 V source across two 1 MΩ resistors should give 5 V at the middle. Measure across the bottom resistor with a 10 MΩ voltmeter. The bottom part becomes 1 MΩ parallel 10 MΩ, about 0.909 MΩ, so the meter reads 10 × 0.909 / 1.909, about 4.76 V. The reading is about 5 percent low, not because the meter is broken, but because it joined the circuit. With 1 kΩ resistors instead, the effect would be negligible. Similarly, an ammeter's small resistance slightly reduces the current in low-resistance circuits.

Accuracy, precision and error: Accuracy is how close a reading is to the true value. Precision is how consistent repeated readings are and how finely the instrument can resolve differences. A meter can be precise but inaccurate if it is badly calibrated. Errors are often grouped as systematic errors, which push every reading the same way, such as loading or a calibration offset, and random errors, which scatter readings around, such as a shaky probe contact. Lab reports usually ask you to compare measured and calculated values and to compute the percentage error: (measured - theoretical) / theoretical × 100.

The clamp meter: Breaking a circuit to insert an ammeter is inconvenient for a heavy household line. A clamp meter solves this for AC: you open its jaws around one single wire, and it measures the current from the magnetic field around the wire, without any electrical contact. Electricians in Bangladesh commonly use clamp meters to check how much current an air conditioner or a motor pump is drawing. Clamping both the live and neutral wires together reads nearly zero, because their currents are equal and opposite, which is KCL again.

The oscilloscope: A multimeter shows a single number, but many signals change quickly, such as AC waves or digital clock pulses. An oscilloscope draws voltage against time on a screen, so you can see the shape, the peak value, the period and any noise. Modern digital oscilloscopes also compute values like frequency and RMS automatically. You will use one more in the AC part of this course and heavily in later digital electronics courses.

The breadboard: A solderless breadboard lets you build circuits by pushing component legs into holes. Inside, metal strips connect the holes in short groups, typically five holes in a row on each side of the centre gap, and the long strips along the edges, the power rails, run the length of the board. The most common beginner mistake is placing both legs of a resistor in the same connected group, which shorts it out. Another is assuming the power rails are continuous across the whole board when some boards split them in the middle.

Lab safety: Low-voltage breadboard circuits powered by a bench supply or batteries are safe for your body, but they can still burn components and fingers if a short makes something hot. Mains voltage is different and dangerous; student labs handle it only with proper equipment and supervision. A few habits keep you safe: switch off power before changing connections, check the meter's function and probe sockets before touching a circuit, never measure resistance on a powered circuit, start on the highest range, keep one hand away from mains-level circuits, and never work with wet hands.

Real life example 1, a hostel room socket: A student in a university hall wants to know why her phone charges slowly. With a multimeter on the AC voltage range, she measures the wall socket and reads about 205 V in the evening and about 228 V late at night. Voltage dips at peak hours are common because many loads share the same supply lines. Her charger's label says it accepts 100 to 240 V, so the dip is not the cause. Next she sets the meter to continuity, checks the USB cable from end to end and finds one wire broken inside the cable. One quick measurement saved her from buying a new charger.

Real life example 2, an electrician checking a water pump: In a building in Chattogram, a water pump keeps tripping its breaker. The electrician clamps the pump's live wire and reads 14 A while the pump's nameplate says it should draw about 6 A. That points to a mechanical problem, such as a jammed impeller, or a winding problem. With power off, he uses the ohmmeter to compare the motor winding resistances with each other. A much lower reading on one winding suggests shorted turns. Measurements, not guesses, lead to the right repair.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The classic mistakes are measuring current with the meter in parallel, leaving the red probe in the current socket and then trying to measure voltage, measuring resistance with the power on, and choosing a range that is too small. In exams, typical questions ask you to design a shunt or multiplier for a given meter movement, compute the loading error of a voltmeter, explain why an ammeter must have low resistance and a voltmeter high resistance, and compute percentage error from measured and theoretical values.

Recap: Voltmeters go across and should have very high resistance; ammeters go in series and should have very low resistance. Ohmmeters use their own battery, so power must be off. A galvanometer becomes an ammeter with a parallel shunt, R_sh = Im Rm / (I - Im), and a voltmeter with a series multiplier, R_s = V / Im - Rm. Every real meter loads the circuit a little. With these lab skills in hand, we return to theory for the first systematic analysis method: nodal analysis.
key_points: Voltmeter: across the element, ideally infinite resistance (DMMs ~10 MΩ).
Ammeter: in series, ideally zero resistance; never connect it across a source.
Ohmmeter: uses its own battery; power off and isolate the component.
Shunt for an ammeter: R_sh = Im·Rm / (I - Im).
Multiplier for a voltmeter: R_s = V/Im - Rm; sensitivity = 1/Im ohms per volt.
Every real meter loads the circuit; high-resistance circuits suffer most.
Clamp meters measure AC current without contact; oscilloscopes show voltage versus time.
Breadboard: five-hole row groups and power rails; avoid putting both legs of a part in one group.
lessons.tip: Before touching probes to a circuit, say three things aloud: the function, the range, and which socket the red probe is in.
lessons.task: If you can borrow a multimeter, measure a fresh and an old AA cell, the resistance of your own body between two fingers (dry, then slightly damp), and the continuity of a charging cable.

quiz.explain: Voltage exists between two points, so the voltmeter goes across the element.

quiz.explain: An ammeter is in series, so it should cause no voltage drop: zero resistance.

Why must you never measure resistance on a powered circuit?
options: The ohmmeter uses its own small current, and external voltage corrupts the reading and can damage the meter

quiz.explain: 1 MΩ ∥ 10 MΩ ≈ 0.909 MΩ; 10 × 0.909 / 1.909 ≈ 4.76 V: the loading effect.

lessons.title: Nodal Analysis
lessons.content:
Imagine you are asked to describe the height of every rooftop in your neighbourhood. You could measure the difference between every pair of roofs, but that would be a huge, messy list. Much smarter: pick the road as "height zero" and write one number per roof, its height above the road. From those numbers you can get any difference you want by simple subtraction. Nodal analysis does exactly this for circuits. Pick one node as zero volts, give every other node a single voltage, and write KCL at each node. It is the most widely used systematic method in circuit analysis, and it is essentially what circuit simulators like SPICE do inside.

Why we need a systematic method: In lesson 5 we solved circuits by labelling every branch current and writing KCL, KVL and Ohm's law everywhere. That works, but a circuit with ten branches might need ten or more equations, and it is easy to lose track. Nodal analysis cuts the number of unknowns to the number of nodes minus one, and it gives a step-by-step recipe that never changes. Once you learn the recipe, even big circuits become routine.

The reference node: First choose one node as the reference, also called ground or datum, and assign it 0 V. It is marked with the ground symbol, a few horizontal lines getting shorter. Any node can be chosen, but a good choice is the node with the most connections, often the bottom wire, or the node connected to the most voltage sources. All other node voltages, v1, v2 and so on, are measured relative to this reference.

Node voltages determine everything: Once all node voltages are known, every element voltage follows by subtraction. A resistor between node 1 and node 2 has voltage v1 - v2 across it, and by Ohm's law the current from node 1 to node 2 through it is (v1 - v2) / R. A resistor from node 1 to ground carries v1 / R. So node voltages are the only unknowns we need. With n nodes there are n - 1 unknown node voltages.

The basic recipe: Step 1, select the reference node. Step 2, label the remaining node voltages v1, v2, ..., v(n-1). Step 3, apply KCL at each non-reference node, writing every resistor current in terms of node voltages with Ohm's law. Step 4, solve the resulting simultaneous equations. Step 5, compute any currents or powers you need from the node voltages. That is the whole method for circuits with resistors and current sources.

A consistent convention for KCL: A common and safe convention is to write, at each node, "sum of currents leaving through resistors = sum of currents entering from sources". For a resistor from node k to node j, the current leaving node k is (vk - vj) / R. Always write "this node minus the other node". If you use this rule at every node, the signs take care of themselves, even if some currents actually flow the other way; those will simply come out negative.

Worked example 1: Node 1 has a 5 A current source feeding into it from ground, a 4 Ω resistor to ground and a 2 Ω resistor to node 2. Node 2 has a 10 Ω resistor to ground and a 2 A current source drawing current out of it to ground. KCL at node 1: v1/4 + (v1 - v2)/2 = 5. Multiply by 4: v1 + 2v1 - 2v2 = 20, so 3v1 - 2v2 = 20. KCL at node 2: (v2 - v1)/2 + v2/10 + 2 = 0. Multiply by 10: 5v2 - 5v1 + v2 + 20 = 0, so -5v1 + 6v2 = -20.

Solving example 1: Multiply the first equation by 3: 9v1 - 6v2 = 60. Add it to the second: 4v1 = 40, so v1 = 10 V. Then 3(10) - 2v2 = 20 gives v2 = 5 V. Now the currents: the 4 Ω carries 10/4 = 2.5 A down to ground, the 2 Ω carries (10 - 5)/2 = 2.5 A from node 1 to node 2, and the 10 Ω carries 5/10 = 0.5 A. Check at node 2: 2.5 A arrives, 0.5 A goes down the 10 Ω and 2 A leaves through the source. It balances.

Power check for example 1: The 5 A source pushes current up into node 1, which sits at 10 V, so it supplies 5 × 10 = 50 W. The 2 A source pulls current out of node 2 at 5 V down to ground, so current enters its + end and it absorbs 2 × 5 = 10 W. The resistors absorb 2.5² × 4 = 25 W, 2.5² × 2 = 12.5 W and 0.5² × 10 = 2.5 W. Total absorbed: 25 + 12.5 + 2.5 + 10 = 50 W, exactly what was supplied. Doing this check takes a minute and catches almost every sign error, so it is worth doing in exams whenever time allows.

The matrix form: For circuits with only resistors and independent current sources, the nodal equations have a beautiful pattern, G v = i. The diagonal entry Gkk is the sum of all conductances connected to node k. The off-diagonal entry Gkj is minus the sum of conductances directly between nodes k and j. The right side ik is the total source current flowing into node k. For example 1: G11 = 1/4 + 1/2 = 0.75, G22 = 1/2 + 1/10 = 0.6, G12 = G21 = -0.5, i1 = 5 and i2 = -2. You can write this matrix just by looking at the circuit, without writing KCL term by term. The matrix is symmetric, which is a useful check.

Solving the equations: Two equations can be solved by substitution or elimination. Three or more are easier with Cramer's rule, matrix inversion or Gaussian elimination. Many scientific calculators allowed in Bangladeshi university exams can solve simultaneous equations directly, and in practice engineers use software such as MATLAB, Python or a SPICE simulator. Still, you should be able to solve a 2 by 2 or 3 by 3 system by hand, because exams test it.

Voltage source connected to the reference: If a voltage source connects a node directly to ground, that node voltage is simply known. Example: a 12 V source from ground to node 1 makes v1 = 12 V, with no equation needed. If node 1 then connects through 4 Ω to node 2, which has a 12 Ω resistor to ground and a 2 A source feeding into it, KCL at node 2 gives (v2 - 12)/4 + v2/12 = 2. Multiply by 12: 3v2 - 36 + v2 = 24, so v2 = 15 V. Voltage sources to ground actually make nodal analysis easier, because they remove unknowns.

Voltage source between two non-reference nodes, the supernode: Now suppose a voltage source sits between node 1 and node 2, with neither node grounded. We cannot write the current through a voltage source with Ohm's law, because it can be anything. The trick is to treat the source and its two nodes together as one "supernode". Write KCL for the whole supernode as if it were one big node, and add one extra equation from the source itself: v1 - v2 = Vs. You still get as many equations as unknowns.

Supernode example: A 7 A source feeds node 1. Node 1 has a 2 Ω resistor to ground. Node 2 has a 4 Ω resistor to ground. A 2 V source sits between them with its + side at node 1, so v1 - v2 = 2. KCL for the supernode (currents leaving through resistors equal current entering from the source): v1/2 + v2/4 = 7. Substitute v2 = v1 - 2: v1/2 + (v1 - 2)/4 = 7. Multiply by 4: 2v1 + v1 - 2 = 28, so v1 = 10 V and v2 = 8 V. Check: the 2 Ω carries 5 A and the 4 Ω carries 2 A, total 7 A. Correct.

Dependent sources in nodal analysis: A dependent source is handled exactly like an independent one while writing the equations, and then you add one more equation expressing its controlling variable in terms of the node voltages. Example: node 1 gets 2 A from a source and has 4 Ω to ground and 2 Ω to node 2. Node 2 has 4 Ω to ground and receives a dependent current of v1/8 amperes. KCL: v1/4 + (v1 - v2)/2 = 2 and (v2 - v1)/2 + v2/4 = v1/8. The second gives 6v2 = 5v1. Substituting into the first gives v1 = 6 V and v2 = 5 V. One important consequence: with dependent sources the G matrix is usually no longer symmetric, so do not use symmetry as a check in that case.

When nodal analysis shines: Nodal analysis is usually the best choice when the circuit has many parallel elements, many current sources, or voltage sources connected to ground, and when you need node voltages directly. It works for planar and non-planar circuits alike, which is one reason computer programs prefer it. In the next lesson we learn mesh analysis, which is the mirror-image method based on KVL, and we will compare when each is easier.

Real life example 1, circuit simulators: When an engineer at a Dhaka electronics design company draws a circuit in a simulator and presses "run", the program numbers every node, picks ground as the reference, builds a large conductance matrix using exactly the stamp pattern you saw above, and solves it. A modern chip simulation may have millions of nodes, but the basic idea is the same as the 2 by 2 example. Learning nodal analysis by hand is learning what the software is really doing.

Real life example 2, a sensor network on a breadboard: A student builds a temperature monitor with two thermistors and fixed resistors feeding two microcontroller inputs, all sharing the same 5 V supply and ground. The inputs are nodes, and nodal analysis gives their voltages at each temperature. Writing the equations once tells the student exactly what voltage to expect at 25 °C and at 40 °C, which values of fixed resistor give the biggest change, and whether the two sensors interfere with each other through shared paths.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget a branch at a node, mix up signs by writing "other node minus this node" in some terms, write KCL at the reference node too, apply Ohm's law to a voltage source, and forget the constraint equation of a supernode. Typical exam questions: find all node voltages in a two or three node circuit, find a particular current or power using nodal analysis, solve a circuit with a supernode, and solve a circuit with a dependent source.

Recap: Choose a reference node, label n - 1 node voltages, write KCL at each non-reference node using (this node minus other node) / R for every resistor, and solve. Voltage sources to ground give known node voltages. A voltage source between two non-reference nodes forms a supernode: one KCL equation for the combined node plus the source constraint. Dependent sources add an equation for their controlling variable. Next we meet nodal analysis's twin: mesh analysis.
key_points: Choose a reference (ground) node at 0 V; unknowns are the other n - 1 node voltages.
At each non-reference node write KCL, with each resistor current as (this node - other node)/R.
For R and independent current sources only: G v = i, with a symmetric conductance matrix.
A voltage source to ground fixes that node voltage directly.
A voltage source between two non-reference nodes forms a supernode: KCL around both + the source constraint.
Dependent sources: write their controlling variable in node voltages; the matrix may become non-symmetric.
Circuit simulators like SPICE are built on nodal analysis.
lessons.tip: Always write 'this node minus the other node' for every term at a node; consistent signs are worth more than speed.
lessons.task: Draw a three-node circuit of your own with two current sources and four resistors, write its conductance matrix just by inspection, and solve it with a calculator.

quiz.q: A circuit has 5 nodes. How many unknown node voltages does nodal analysis need?
quiz.explain: One node is the reference, so n - 1 = 4 unknowns.

quiz.q: The current leaving node 1 through a 5 Ω resistor to node 2 is:
quiz.explain: Ohm's law with 'this node minus other node': (v1 - v2)/R.

quiz.q: A voltage source sits between two non-reference nodes. You should:
options: Form a supernode and add the source's constraint equation
Apply Ohm's law to the source
Make one of them the reference and delete the other
quiz.explain: Treat both nodes plus the source as one supernode for KCL, and use v1 - v2 = Vs.

quiz.q: In the conductance matrix (no dependent sources), the diagonal term G11 is:
options: Minus the conductance between nodes 1 and 2
The sum of all conductances connected to node 1
quiz.explain: Diagonal entries collect all conductances touching that node.

quiz.q: A 12 V source connects ground to node 1; node 1 connects through 4 Ω to node 2, which has 12 Ω to ground and nothing else. v2 is:
quiz.explain: (v2 - 12)/4 + v2/12 = 0 gives 4v2 = 36, so v2 = 9 V (a voltage divider).

lessons.title: Mesh Analysis
lessons.content:
Think of a window with several panes of glass, each surrounded by its own wooden frame. Neighbouring panes share one strip of wood between them. Now imagine an ant walking around the edge of each pane, always clockwise. Where two panes share a strip, two ants walk along the same strip in opposite directions. Mesh analysis pictures current like these ants: one imaginary current circulating around each pane, or mesh, of a circuit. Where two meshes share a branch, the real current in that branch is the difference between the two circulating currents. Writing KVL around each pane gives just enough equations to find everything.

Mesh analysis in one sentence: Assign a circulating mesh current to each mesh, write KVL around each mesh in terms of those currents, solve, and then find any branch current as one mesh current or the difference of two. It is the twin of nodal analysis: nodal uses node voltages and KCL, mesh uses mesh currents and KVL.

Where mesh analysis applies: Mesh analysis works for planar circuits, meaning circuits that can be drawn on a flat sheet of paper without any wires crossing. Most textbook circuits are planar. For a non-planar circuit, where crossings are unavoidable, the panes are not well defined and mesh analysis in its basic form does not apply; nodal analysis still works there. Recall from lesson 5 that the number of meshes in a connected planar circuit is b - n + 1, and that is the number of unknown mesh currents.

Mesh currents versus branch currents: A mesh current is a mathematical helper, not something you can always measure directly. In a branch that belongs to only one mesh, the branch current equals that mesh current. In a branch shared by two meshes, the branch current equals the difference of the two mesh currents. If both mesh currents are drawn clockwise, then in a shared branch they flow in opposite directions, so the shared branch current is i1 - i2 in the direction of i1.

The basic recipe: Step 1, check the circuit is planar and identify the meshes. Step 2, assign mesh currents i1, i2, ..., usually all clockwise for consistency. Step 3, write KVL around each mesh, using Ohm's law for every resistor; for a resistor shared with another mesh, the voltage is R times the difference of the mesh currents, (this mesh current minus the neighbour's mesh current). Step 4, solve the equations. Step 5, find branch currents, voltages and powers.

Writing KVL for a mesh: Walk around the mesh in the direction of its mesh current. A resistor that belongs only to this mesh contributes R × i_this. A resistor shared with a neighbouring mesh contributes R × (i_this - i_neighbour). A voltage source contributes its voltage with a sign: if you meet its - terminal first, it is a rise in the walking direction; if you meet its + terminal first, it is a drop. A clean way to write each mesh equation is "sum of resistor drops = sum of source rises".

Worked example 1: A 20 V source sits on the left edge of mesh 1, with its + terminal at the top, so it pushes current clockwise around mesh 1. Mesh 1 also has a 2 Ω resistor of its own. A 4 Ω resistor sits in the middle branch shared by both meshes. Mesh 2 has a 6 Ω resistor of its own and a 6 V source on its right edge, placed so that walking clockwise around mesh 2 you meet its + terminal first, a drop of 6 V. Mesh 1: 2i1 + 4(i1 - i2) = 20, so 6i1 - 4i2 = 20. Mesh 2: 4(i2 - i1) + 6i2 = -6, so -4i1 + 10i2 = -6.

Solving example 1: From the first equation, multiply by 5: 30i1 - 20i2 = 100. Multiply the second by 2: -8i1 + 20i2 = -12. Add them: 22i1 = 88, so i1 = 4 A. Then -16 + 10i2 = -6 gives i2 = 1 A. The 2 Ω carries 4 A, the 6 Ω carries 1 A, and the shared 4 Ω carries i1 - i2 = 3 A downward, in the direction of i1. Check with power: the 20 V source supplies 20 × 4 = 80 W; the 6 V source absorbs 6 × 1 = 6 W (it is being charged); resistors absorb 4² × 2 + 3² × 4 + 1² × 6 = 32 + 36 + 6 = 74 W. Total absorbed 80 W. Balanced.

The matrix form: With only resistors and independent voltage sources, and all mesh currents clockwise, the mesh equations take the pattern R i = v. The diagonal entry Rkk is the total resistance around mesh k. The off-diagonal entry Rkj is minus the total resistance shared by meshes k and j. The right side vk is the sum of source voltage rises around mesh k in the clockwise direction. For example 1: R11 = 2 + 4 = 6, R22 = 4 + 6 = 10, R12 = R21 = -4, v1 = 20 and v2 = -6. Exactly the same equations, written by inspection. Like the conductance matrix, it is symmetric.

Three meshes by inspection: For a circuit with three meshes in a row, the matrix pattern saves real time. Suppose mesh 1 contains 1 Ω and 2 Ω of its own, mesh 2 contains 3 Ω of its own, mesh 3 contains 4 Ω of its own, mesh 1 and mesh 2 share 5 Ω, mesh 2 and mesh 3 share 6 Ω, and mesh 1 and mesh 3 share nothing. Then R11 = 1 + 2 + 5 = 8, R22 = 5 + 3 + 6 = 14, R33 = 6 + 4 = 10, R12 = -5, R23 = -6 and R13 = 0. You can write the whole left side of the three equations in under a minute, and only the source column needs care with signs.

Current source on an outer branch: If a current source sits on a branch that belongs to only one mesh, that mesh current is simply known. Example: mesh 1 has a 12 V source and a 2 Ω resistor, and shares a 4 Ω resistor with mesh 2, whose outer branch holds a 3 A current source pointing clockwise. Then i2 = 3 A immediately. Mesh 1: 2i1 + 4(i1 - 3) = 12, so 6i1 = 24 and i1 = 4 A. The shared resistor carries 4 - 3 = 1 A. Current sources on outer branches make mesh analysis easier, just as voltage sources to ground make nodal analysis easier.

Current source on a shared branch, the supermesh: When a current source sits in the branch shared by two meshes, we cannot write its voltage with Ohm's law. So we avoid that branch: we combine the two meshes into a supermesh, the outer loop that goes around both meshes while skipping the shared branch, and write KVL around that. Then we add the constraint from the current source: the difference of the two mesh currents equals the source current.

Supermesh example: Mesh 1 has a 10 V source and a 2 Ω resistor; mesh 2 has a 4 Ω resistor. The shared branch holds a 2 A current source oriented so that i1 - i2 = 2. KVL around the supermesh, the outer loop: 2i1 + 4i2 = 10. Substitute i2 = i1 - 2: 2i1 + 4i1 - 8 = 10, so 6i1 = 18 and i1 = 3 A, then i2 = 1 A. Check: the current source branch carries i1 - i2 = 2 A, as it must.

Dependent sources in mesh analysis: Treat a dependent source like an independent one when writing KVL, then express its controlling variable in mesh currents. Example: mesh 1 has a 10 V source and 2 Ω, the shared branch has 3 Ω, and mesh 2 has 1 Ω plus a current-controlled voltage source of 2ix volts, where ix is the current in the 2 Ω resistor, so ix = i1. Suppose the dependent source is a rise of 2i1 when walking clockwise around mesh 2. Mesh 1: 2i1 + 3(i1 - i2) = 10. Mesh 2: 3(i2 - i1) + 1 × i2 = 2i1, which gives 4i2 = 5i1. Substituting: 5i1 - 3.75i1 = 10, so i1 = 8 A and i2 = 10 A. As with nodal analysis, the matrix is generally not symmetric when dependent sources are present.

Nodal or mesh: which to choose: Count the equations each method would need. Nodal needs (number of nodes - 1) minus the number of voltage sources that fix node voltages. Mesh needs (number of meshes) minus the number of current sources on outer branches. Choose the method with fewer equations. As a rough guide, circuits with many parallel elements and current sources favour nodal; circuits with many series elements and voltage sources favour mesh. Also consider what is asked: if the question wants a voltage, nodal often gets there faster; if it wants a current, mesh may. For non-planar circuits, only nodal works.

Real life example 1, a two-battery solar and grid charger: Imagine a small shop in a market in Rajshahi with a solar panel charger and a grid charger both connected, through their own wiring resistances, to the same battery and a load. Each source with its wire forms one mesh, and the battery with the load sits in shared branches. Mesh analysis tells the shop owner how much current each charger contributes and whether one of them is actually pushing current backwards into the other. Engineers use exactly this kind of analysis to decide where to place diodes or controllers.

Real life example 2, a multi-loop LED panel: An LED advertising panel at a bus stand is built from several loops of LED strings with current-limiting resistors, powered from one supply. If the resistors are a little mismatched, some strings glow brighter than others. A designer writes mesh equations for the loops, sees how much current each string actually gets, and adjusts resistor values so that the brightness is even. The same idea scales up inside computer power distribution networks, where many loops share copper paths.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget the shared resistor term, write (neighbour minus this) in some terms, mix up the sign of voltage sources, and include the current source branch in a supermesh KVL. Another frequent slip is forgetting that a branch current in a shared branch is the difference of mesh currents, not either one alone. Typical exam questions: solve a two or three mesh circuit, find a branch current or power, handle a current source on an outer or shared branch, solve with a dependent source, and choose between nodal and mesh with reasons.

Recap: Assign clockwise mesh currents, write KVL around each mesh as resistor drops equal source rises, using (this mesh - neighbour) for shared resistors, and solve. A current source in an outer branch fixes that mesh current; one in a shared branch calls for a supermesh plus a constraint equation. Dependent sources add an equation for the controlling variable. Choose nodal or mesh by counting equations. Next we learn principles that let us break circuits into simpler pieces: linearity, superposition and source transformation.
key_points: Assign a circulating mesh current to each mesh (usually clockwise) of a planar circuit.
Write KVL per mesh: resistor drops = source rises; shared resistor uses R(i_this - i_neighbour).
Branch current in a shared branch = difference of the two mesh currents.
R and independent voltage sources only: R i = v with a symmetric matrix written by inspection.
Current source on an outer branch fixes that mesh current.
Current source on a shared branch: supermesh KVL around both meshes + constraint equation.
Choose nodal or mesh by counting equations; non-planar circuits need nodal.
lessons.tip: Draw all mesh currents clockwise every single time; one fixed habit removes a whole family of sign errors.
lessons.task: Take the circuit from nodal example 1 in lesson 10, convert it so it has voltage sources, and solve it both ways. Compare how many equations each method needed.

quiz.explain: Meshes are the 'window panes' of a circuit drawn without crossings, so the circuit must be planar.

quiz.q: Two clockwise mesh currents i1 = 5 A and i2 = 2 A share a 3 Ω resistor. The voltage across it is:
quiz.explain: Branch current = i1 - i2 = 3 A; V = 3 × 3 = 9 V.

quiz.q: A current source sits in the branch shared by meshes 1 and 2. You should:
options: Write KVL through the source using Ohm's law
Form a supermesh around both meshes and add i1 - i2 = Is (with suitable sign)

options: Minus the resistance shared by meshes 1 and 2
quiz.explain: Off-diagonal entries are minus the shared resistance.

quiz.q: A circuit has 6 nodes and 3 meshes, with 2 current sources on outer branches and no voltage sources. The fewest equations come from:
quiz.explain: Mesh: 3 meshes minus 2 known mesh currents = 1 equation, versus 5 for nodal.

lessons.title: Linearity, Superposition and Source Transformation
lessons.content:
Think about the sound in a classroom. When one student talks, you hear a certain sound. When the fan is running alone, you hear its hum. When both happen together, what you hear is simply the student plus the hum, added together. Each source of sound contributes its own part, independently of the others. Many circuits behave exactly like this. If a circuit has two batteries, the current anywhere is the current due to the first battery alone plus the current due to the second battery alone. This idea, called superposition, comes from a deeper property called linearity, and it sits beside a handy redrawing trick called source transformation. Together they let you take a circuit apart, solve simple pieces, and put the answers back together.

What linearity means: A circuit is linear if its outputs depend on its inputs in a straight-line way, with two properties. Homogeneity, or scaling: if you multiply every independent source by a factor k, every voltage and current in the circuit is multiplied by k. Additivity: the response to two sources acting together equals the sum of the responses to each one acting alone. A circuit made only of resistors, linear dependent sources, independent sources, and later capacitors and inductors, is linear. Diodes and transistors used as switches are not, and these methods do not apply directly to them.

Homogeneity in action: In a resistor circuit driven by one 10 V source, suppose some current is 2 A. If you change the source to 30 V, that current becomes 6 A, and every other current and voltage triples too. This is just Ohm's law spread across the whole circuit. A nice consequence: the ratio of output to input, called the gain or transfer ratio, is a fixed number for a given linear circuit, regardless of the input size.

The ladder trick using linearity: For a ladder network driven by one source, there is a clever backwards method. Instead of starting from the source, assume the output is 1 V and work back to find what source voltage would produce it. Then scale. Example: a source Vs feeds a 2 Ω series resistor to node x, which has a 2 Ω resistor to ground; from x another 2 Ω series resistor goes to node y, which has a final 2 Ω resistor to ground, and the output vo is across that last resistor. Assume vo = 1 V. The last resistor carries 0.5 A, and so does the series 2 Ω before it, so vx = 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 2 V. The shunt 2 Ω at x carries 2 / 2 = 1 A, so the first series resistor carries 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 A, and Vs = 2 + 1.5 × 2 = 5 V. So vo is one fifth of Vs. If the real source is 20 V, then vo = 4 V.

Why resistor circuits are linear: Look back at nodal analysis. Every equation had the form "sum of conductances times node voltages = source currents". No squares, no products of unknowns, no square roots. Equations of that kind are called linear equations, and their solutions always scale and add in exactly the way homogeneity and additivity describe. So linearity is not a lucky accident; it follows directly from Ohm's law being a straight line and from Kirchhoff's laws being simple sums. As soon as an element breaks that straight line, like a diode whose current grows exponentially with voltage, the equations stop being linear and superposition stops working.

The superposition principle: In a linear circuit with several independent sources, the voltage across (or current through) any element is the algebraic sum of the voltages (or currents) caused by each independent source acting alone, with all the other independent sources turned off. The method has three steps: turn off all independent sources except one and find the response; repeat for each source; add all the partial responses, paying attention to directions.

How to turn a source off: Turning off a source means setting its value to zero. A voltage source set to 0 V is a plain wire, so you replace it with a short circuit. A current source set to 0 A carries no current, so you replace it with an open circuit. Any internal resistance of a practical source stays in place. Dependent sources are never turned off, because their values depend on the circuit; they stay active in every sub-circuit.

Superposition worked example: A 12 V source in series with 6 Ω feeds node A. From A, a 3 Ω resistor goes to ground, and a 3 A current source also pushes current into A from ground. Find vA. Step 1, voltage source alone, current source opened: 12 V across 6 Ω and 3 Ω in series, so vA1 = 12 × 3 / 9 = 4 V. Step 2, current source alone, voltage source shorted: the 6 Ω and 3 Ω are now in parallel between A and ground, 2 Ω, so vA2 = 3 × 2 = 6 V. Step 3, add: vA = 4 + 6 = 10 V. Checking by nodal analysis: (vA - 12)/6 + vA/3 = 3 gives 3vA = 30, so vA = 10 V. Same answer.

Superposition does not work for power: Power is not linear, because it depends on the square of current or voltage. In the example above, the 3 Ω resistor really absorbs vA² / 3 = 100 / 3, about 33.3 W. Adding the powers of the two separate cases gives 4² / 3 + 6² / 3 = 16 / 3 + 36 / 3, about 17.3 W, which is wrong. The correct procedure is: add the voltages or currents first, then compute power from the total. This is one of the most frequent exam traps.

When superposition is worth it: Superposition often takes more work than nodal or mesh analysis, because you solve several circuits instead of one. It shines in three situations: when sources are of different kinds, such as a DC source and an AC source together (used in transistor amplifier analysis, where a DC bias and a small AC signal coexist); when you want to know how much each source contributes; and when each partial circuit is a simple series-parallel network that can be solved in your head. It is also the theoretical basis for Thevenin's theorem in the next lesson.

Superposition with a dependent source: With dependent sources, keep them in every partial circuit and solve each partial circuit normally, with the controlling variable re-computed in each case. The partial controlling variables add up to the real controlling variable, which keeps everything consistent. The arithmetic is longer, so in exams superposition with dependent sources usually appears only when explicitly requested.

Source transformation: A practical voltage source, a voltage Vs in series with a resistance R, and a practical current source, a current Is in parallel with the same resistance R, behave identically at their two terminals when Is = Vs / R. They give the same open-circuit voltage (Vs, or Is × R) and the same short-circuit current (Vs / R, or Is). So you may swap one for the other anywhere in a circuit, as long as you keep R the same and point the current source's arrow toward the voltage source's + terminal.

Source transformation example 1: A 12 V source in series with 3 Ω can be replaced by a 4 A current source in parallel with 3 Ω. A 2 A current source in parallel with 5 Ω can be replaced by a 10 V source in series with 5 Ω. Remember the direction: the current source's arrow points toward the end where the voltage source's + terminal was.

Source transformation example 2, simplifying a circuit: A 12 V source with 3 Ω in series, and a 2 A source with 6 Ω in parallel, both feed the same pair of nodes, across which sits a 2 Ω load. Find the load current. Transform the 12 V and 3 Ω into 4 A parallel 3 Ω. Now both current sources are in parallel and point the same way: 4 + 2 = 6 A, and their resistors are in parallel: 3 parallel 6 = 2 Ω. Transform back: 6 A parallel 2 Ω becomes 12 V in series with 2 Ω. Now the load sees 12 V through 2 Ω, so I = 12 / (2 + 2) = 3 A. A quick nodal check: (V - 12)/3 + V/6 + V/2 = 2 gives V = 6 V, and 6 / 2 = 3 A. Correct.

Limits of source transformation: Transformation needs a resistor: an ideal voltage source with no series resistance, or an ideal current source with no parallel resistance, cannot be transformed. Also, the element being transformed must not itself be the element you want to find, because after transformation that resistor's current or voltage is no longer the same as in the original circuit, only the behaviour at the terminals is. Dependent sources can be transformed too, provided the controlling variable is not hidden inside the part you transform.

Real life example 1, a phone on a charger and a power bank: Suppose a phone receives current from both a wall charger and a power bank through a special dual-input board. Superposition, applied to a simple linear model of the board, tells the designer how much of the phone's current comes from each source. If the wall charger alone would deliver 1.5 A and the power bank alone 0.5 A into the same load path, then in a linear model together they deliver 2 A. Real chargers include control electronics that are not linear, but the linear model is where design begins.

Real life example 2, audio mixing: When you plug two microphones into a simple passive mixer made of resistors, the output voltage is the sum of each microphone's contribution, scaled by resistor ratios. That is superposition in sound form. Each microphone's voice reaches the speaker without changing the other's, and turning one microphone off simply removes its part. Simple resistor mixers are a real application, and the same principle explains why a song recording is the sum of its tracks.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students short a current source instead of opening it (or open a voltage source instead of shorting it), turn off dependent sources, add powers, forget directions when adding partial currents, and transform a source while keeping the wrong resistor or pointing the current arrow the wrong way. Typical exam questions: use superposition to find a current or voltage and verify by another method, show that superposition fails for power, use repeated source transformations to simplify a circuit, and use linearity to scale a ladder network's output.

Recap: A linear circuit obeys scaling and additivity. Superposition: find the response to each independent source alone, with other voltage sources shorted and current sources opened, then add the responses; never add powers. Source transformation: Vs in series with R equals Is = Vs / R in parallel with R, with the arrow pointing toward the + end. These tools break circuits into easy pieces. Next, they combine into one of the most powerful results of circuit theory: Thevenin's and Norton's theorems.
key_points: Linear circuits obey homogeneity (scaling) and additivity.
Ladder trick: assume output = 1 V, work back to the source, then scale.
Superposition: response = sum of responses to each independent source alone.
Turn off sources: voltage source → short, current source → open; dependent sources stay on.
Never add powers; add voltages or currents first, then compute power.
Source transformation: Vs in series with R ⇔ Is = Vs/R in parallel with R (arrow toward +).
Ideal sources without a resistor cannot be transformed; don't transform the element you are solving for.
lessons.tip: In superposition problems, redraw each sub-circuit completely with the turned-off sources visibly replaced; half the errors come from 'imagining' the change.
lessons.task: Build the superposition example of this lesson on paper with your own numbers, solve it by superposition and by nodal analysis, and show that adding partial powers gives the wrong total.
