quiz.explain: A 0 A source carries no current, which is an open circuit.

quiz.q: Two sources alone give 2 A and 3 A through a 4 Ω resistor (same direction). The true power in that resistor is:
quiz.explain: Add currents first: 5 A; P = 5² × 4 = 100 W. Adding powers (16 + 36) would be wrong.

quiz.q: A 20 V source in series with 4 Ω is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: Is = Vs / R = 20 / 4 = 5 A, with the same 4 Ω in parallel.

quiz.q: During superposition, dependent sources are:
quiz.explain: Their values depend on circuit variables, so they always stay in the circuit.

quiz.q: In a linear circuit, doubling every independent source will:
quiz.explain: Homogeneity: all responses scale by the same factor as the sources.

lessons.title: Thevenin's and Norton's Theorems
lessons.content:
When you plug a phone charger into a socket, you do not care about the power station in Rooppur or Payra, the hundreds of kilometres of grid lines, the transformers on the poles, or the wiring inside your walls. From the socket's two holes, that whole enormous system looks like one simple thing: a voltage with a little bit of internal resistance behind it. Thevenin's theorem says this is not just a convenient feeling but a mathematical fact. Any linear circuit, however complicated, can be replaced, as seen from two terminals, by one voltage source in series with one resistor. Norton's theorem says the same thing with a current source and a parallel resistor. These two theorems are probably the most useful results in this whole course.

Why we need them: Very often we care about one particular part of a circuit, called the load. It might be a speaker, a sensor, an LED or a motor, and we may want to try several different loads. Solving the whole circuit again for each load would be tiring. With Thevenin's theorem, we simplify everything except the load into two numbers once, and then each new load becomes a one-line calculation with Ohm's law.

Thevenin's theorem: A linear two-terminal circuit can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of a voltage source V_Th in series with a resistor R_Th. V_Th is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals, measured with the load removed. R_Th is the resistance seen looking into the terminals when all independent sources are turned off. The theorem is named after Léon Charles Thévenin, a French telegraph engineer who published it in 1883; Hermann von Helmholtz had stated a similar result earlier.

Norton's theorem: A linear two-terminal circuit can also be replaced by a current source I_N in parallel with a resistor R_N. I_N is the short-circuit current that flows when the terminals are joined by a wire, and R_N equals R_Th. It is named after Edward Lawry Norton of Bell Labs, who described it in 1926. Thevenin and Norton equivalents are related by source transformation from lesson 12: V_Th = I_N × R_Th. So once you know any two of V_Th, I_N and R_Th, you know the third.

Finding V_Th: Remove the load, leaving the two terminals a and b open. Then find the voltage between a and b using any method you like: voltage divider, nodal, mesh or superposition. Since no current flows out of the open terminals, any resistor in series with a terminal carries no current and has no voltage across it, which often simplifies things.

Finding R_Th when there are only independent sources: Turn off every independent source, voltage sources replaced by shorts and current sources by opens, and find the equivalent resistance between a and b using series-parallel reduction. This is usually the quickest route. Remember to look into the circuit from the load terminals, not from the source.

Worked example 1: A 12 V source in series with R1 = 4 Ω connects to terminal a. A resistor R2 = 12 Ω connects a to terminal b, which is the bottom wire. Find the Thevenin equivalent at a-b. V_Th: with terminals open, R1 and R2 form a voltage divider: V_Th = 12 × 12 / 16 = 9 V. R_Th: short the 12 V source; then from a-b, R1 and R2 are in parallel: 4 × 12 / 16 = 3 Ω. So the circuit is equivalent to 9 V in series with 3 Ω. Now any load is easy: a 6 Ω load gets I = 9 / (3 + 6) = 1 A; a 3 Ω load gets 1.5 A; a 0 Ω short gets 3 A, which is I_N.

Checking with Norton: For the same circuit, short a to b. Then R2 is shorted out and the short-circuit current is 12 / 4 = 3 A. So I_N = 3 A, and V_Th / I_N = 9 / 3 = 3 Ω, the same R_Th. This gives a powerful alternative formula: R_Th = V_oc / I_sc, open-circuit voltage divided by short-circuit current, which works even when dependent sources are present.

Worked example 2, with a current source: A 2 A current source in parallel with 6 Ω, followed by a 4 Ω resistor in series to terminal a, with b at the bottom. V_Th: with a-b open, no current flows through the 4 Ω, so the whole 2 A flows through the 6 Ω and V_Th = 2 × 6 = 12 V. R_Th: open the current source; looking in from a-b we see 4 Ω in series with 6 Ω, so R_Th = 10 Ω. I_N = 12 / 10 = 1.2 A. Check directly: shorting a-b, the 2 A splits between the 6 Ω and the 4 Ω path; by the current divider, the short gets 2 × 6 / 10 = 1.2 A. It agrees.

Worked example 3, an unbalanced bridge: Thevenin's theorem is the neatest way to find the current through the middle meter of an unbalanced Wheatstone bridge from lesson 8. A 12 V source feeds two dividers: on the left, 3 Ω on top and 6 Ω below; on the right, 6 Ω on top and 6 Ω below. A 5 Ω meter joins the two middle points. Remove the meter. The left middle point sits at 12 × 6 / 9 = 8 V and the right at 12 × 6 / 12 = 6 V, so V_Th = 8 - 6 = 2 V. With the source shorted, looking in from the meter's terminals we see (3 parallel 6) in series with (6 parallel 6), which is 2 + 3 = 5 Ω. So the meter current is 2 / (5 + 5) = 0.2 A, flowing from the left middle point to the right. Without Thevenin this would need three mesh equations.

A recipe to follow every time: Step 1, mark the two terminals and remove the load. Step 2, find V_oc between them, noting which terminal is positive. Step 3, find R_Th: by reduction if there are only independent sources, or by I_sc or a test source if there are dependent sources. Step 4, draw the equivalent circuit with the correct polarity. Step 5, reconnect the load and use Ohm's law. Writing these five steps as headings in your exam answer also makes it easy for the examiner to give you part marks.

Circuits with dependent sources: When a circuit contains dependent sources, you cannot simply turn everything off and reduce resistors, because the dependent sources must stay active. There are two good methods. Method one: find V_oc and I_sc separately and use R_Th = V_oc / I_sc. Method two: turn off only the independent sources, apply a test source at the terminals, say 1 A, compute the resulting voltage v_test, and then R_Th = v_test / 1 A. Method two is necessary when the circuit has no independent sources at all, in which case V_Th = 0 and only R_Th exists.

Dependent source example: A 10 V source, a 2 Ω resistor carrying current i towards terminal a, and a current-controlled voltage source of 3i volts in series in the same path, oriented to oppose the current. With a-b open, i = 0, so the dependent source is 0 V and V_oc = 10 V. With a-b shorted, KVL around the loop gives 10 - 2i - 3i = 0, so i = 2 A, which is I_sc. So R_Th = 10 / 2 = 5 Ω. Notice the dependent source acts just like an extra 3 Ω resistor here, which the test-source method would also show. Even negative values of R_Th are possible in circuits with dependent sources, which is how some oscillator circuits work.

Measuring a Thevenin equivalent in the lab: You can find V_Th and R_Th of a real device without opening it. Measure the open-circuit voltage with a voltmeter; that is V_Th. Then connect a known load resistor and measure the new voltage V_L. The current is V_L / R_L and the lost voltage is V_Th - V_L, so R_Th = (V_Th - V_L) / (V_L / R_L). Example: a USB charger reads 5.1 V with no load and 4.9 V while supplying 1 A to a test load. Then R_Th = (5.1 - 4.9) / 1 = 0.2 Ω. This is the same idea as finding a battery's internal resistance in lesson 4, now with a theoretical name.

Why the theorems are true: The proof uses linearity and superposition. Imagine driving the terminals with a current source i. By superposition, the terminal voltage is the part due to the internal sources, which is V_oc when i = 0, plus the part due to i alone with internal sources off, which is R_Th times i in the appropriate direction. So the terminal voltage is a straight-line function of the terminal current, and a straight line is fully described by two numbers. A voltage source in series with a resistor has exactly such a straight line. That is the whole reason a giant linear circuit can collapse into two numbers.

Real life example 1, the national grid at your socket: Seen from your socket, the grid behaves roughly like a Thevenin source of about 220 to 230 V with a small series resistance (for AC, an impedance, which we meet later). When a heavy load such as an electric water heater switches on, current through that small internal resistance increases, and the socket voltage drops a little. That is why the lights may dim briefly when a pump motor starts in your building. A building with long, thin supply wires has a larger R_Th, so the dips are bigger.

Real life example 2, choosing a speaker for an amplifier: A small audio amplifier in a school's public address system can be modelled at its output as a Thevenin source with a small internal resistance. Engineers use that model to predict how loud different speakers will be and how much the output voltage will sag when two speakers are connected in parallel. With the Thevenin model, each choice is one line of arithmetic instead of a new circuit analysis.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to remove the load before finding V_Th, turn off dependent sources when finding R_Th, look into the circuit from the wrong pair of terminals, and use a wrong polarity for V_Th. Another mistake is computing R_Th by reduction when dependent sources are present. Typical exam questions: find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents at given terminals, then find the load current for several loads; find R_Th of a circuit with a dependent source using V_oc / I_sc or a test source; and draw the equivalent circuits with correct polarities.

Recap: Any linear two-terminal circuit equals V_Th in series with R_Th, or I_N in parallel with R_N = R_Th. V_Th is the open-circuit voltage, I_N is the short-circuit current, and R_Th = V_oc / I_sc, or the resistance looking in with independent sources off. With dependent sources, use V_oc / I_sc or a test source. Next we use the Thevenin model to answer a very practical question: what load gets the most power from a source?
key_points: Thevenin: any linear two-terminal circuit = V_Th in series with R_Th.
Norton: the same circuit = I_N in parallel with R_N, where R_N = R_Th.
V_Th = open-circuit voltage; I_N = short-circuit current; R_Th = V_oc / I_sc.
Only independent sources: turn them off (V→short, I→open) and reduce to get R_Th.
With dependent sources: use V_oc / I_sc or a test source; never turn dependent sources off.
V_Th = I_N × R_Th links the two forms (source transformation).
R_Th can be measured: open-circuit voltage, then voltage under a known load.
lessons.tip: Always draw the final Thevenin circuit with its polarity marked before attaching the load; it turns the last step into simple Ohm's law.
lessons.task: Measure (or ask someone with a multimeter to measure) a power bank's USB output with no load and with a phone charging, estimate the current from the phone, and compute its Thevenin resistance.

quiz.q: V_Th of a circuit is:
options: The short-circuit current times the load
The open-circuit voltage at the terminals
The voltage across the internal resistor
quiz.explain: V_Th is measured with the load removed: the open-circuit voltage.

quiz.q: A circuit has V_oc = 15 V and I_sc = 3 A. R_Th is:
quiz.explain: R_Th = V_oc / I_sc = 15 / 3 = 5 Ω.

quiz.q: A 9 V source with 3 Ω (Thevenin) drives a 6 Ω load. Load current:
When a circuit has dependent sources, R_Th should be found by:
options: Turning off all sources and reducing resistors
V_oc / I_sc or a test source with only independent sources off
quiz.explain: Dependent sources must stay active, so simple reduction fails.

quiz.q: A Thevenin equivalent of 12 V and 4 Ω has Norton equivalent:
quiz.explain: I_N = V_Th / R_Th = 3 A, with R_N = 4 Ω in parallel.

lessons.title: Maximum Power Transfer
lessons.content:
Imagine you are pushing a friend on a swing. If you push too gently, the swing barely moves. If you try to push hard but at the wrong moment, you fight the swing and waste effort. There is a "just right" way to push that gives the swing the most energy. Circuits have a similar sweet spot. A source with some internal resistance can feed loads of different sizes. A tiny load resistance draws lots of current but has almost no voltage across it. A huge load resistance has nearly the full voltage but almost no current. Somewhere in between, the power delivered to the load is the greatest. The maximum power transfer theorem tells you exactly where.

Setting up the problem: Thanks to Thevenin's theorem, any linear source circuit, seen from the load, is just V_Th in series with R_Th. Connect a load resistor R_L. The current is I = V_Th / (R_Th + R_L), and the power absorbed by the load is P_L = I² × R_L = V_Th² × R_L / (R_Th + R_L)². The question is: for fixed V_Th and R_Th, which R_L makes P_L as large as possible?

Exploring with numbers first: Take V_Th = 12 V and R_Th = 4 Ω. With R_L = 1 Ω, I = 12 / 5 = 2.4 A and P_L = 2.4² × 1 = 5.76 W. With R_L = 2 Ω, I = 2 A and P_L = 8 W. With R_L = 4 Ω, I = 1.5 A and P_L = 9 W. With R_L = 8 Ω, I = 1 A and P_L = 8 W. With R_L = 16 Ω, I = 0.6 A and P_L = 5.76 W. The power rises, peaks at R_L = 4 Ω, then falls again. Notice the peak is at the load that equals R_Th, and that the curve is symmetric in a ratio sense: 1 Ω and 16 Ω give the same power, as do 2 Ω and 8 Ω, each pair multiplying to 16, which is R_Th squared.

The maximum power transfer theorem: Maximum power is delivered from a source to a load when the load resistance equals the Thevenin resistance of the source as seen from the load: R_L = R_Th. This condition is called matching, and a load that satisfies it is a matched load. The theorem is often credited to Moritz von Jacobi, who discussed it around 1840, so it is sometimes called Jacobi's law.

The maximum power itself: Substitute R_L = R_Th into the power formula: P_max = V_Th² × R_Th / (2R_Th)² = V_Th² / (4 R_Th). For our example: 12² / (4 × 4) = 144 / 16 = 9 W, which matches the table. In Norton terms, with I_N = V_Th / R_Th, the same result is P_max = I_N² × R_N / 4.

Deriving it with calculus: For students comfortable with derivatives, set dP_L / dR_L = 0. Using the quotient rule on V_Th² R_L / (R_Th + R_L)², the derivative is V_Th² [(R_Th + R_L)² - 2R_L(R_Th + R_L)] / (R_Th + R_L)^4. This is zero when (R_Th + R_L) - 2R_L = 0, that is R_L = R_Th. Checking the second derivative, or just the table above, confirms it is a maximum. Exams often ask for this short derivation.

Efficiency at maximum power is only 50 percent: At matching, the same current flows through R_Th and R_L, and they are equal, so they absorb equal power. The source therefore delivers half its power to the load and burns the other half inside its own internal resistance. In our example, the source supplies V_Th × I = 12 × 1.5 = 18 W: 9 W reaches the load and 9 W is lost in R_Th. Efficiency, defined as load power divided by total power, is R_L / (R_Th + R_L). At R_L = 16 Ω it is 16 / 20 = 80 percent, even though the load gets less power. Maximum power and maximum efficiency are different goals.

When to match and when not to: If the source is weak and the signal is precious, such as the tiny signal from a radio antenna, a microphone, or a sensor, we care about getting as much power as possible, and matching is the goal. If the source is huge and energy costs money, such as a power station feeding a city, wasting half the energy is unacceptable. Power systems are designed with R_Th far smaller than the load, so efficiency is high and the voltage stays steady. Your house never "matches" the grid, and that is a good thing.

A common trap, when R_L is fixed: The theorem answers the question "which load gets the most power from a given source?" It does not answer "which source resistance gives the most power to a given load?" If the load is fixed and you can change R_Th, the best choice is R_Th as small as possible, ideally zero, because a smaller internal resistance always lets more current flow. Many exam questions test whether you can tell these two situations apart.

Worked example 1, using a Thevenin equivalent: In lesson 13 we found that a circuit with a 12 V source, 4 Ω and 12 Ω has V_Th = 9 V and R_Th = 3 Ω at its terminals. For maximum power, choose R_L = 3 Ω. Then P_max = 9² / (4 × 3) = 81 / 12 = 6.75 W. The load current is 9 / 6 = 1.5 A and the load voltage is 4.5 V, exactly half of V_Th, which is another way to recognise a matched load: the load voltage is half the open-circuit voltage.

Worked example 2, a circuit with a current source: A 2 A current source is in parallel with 6 Ω, followed by 4 Ω in series to the terminals. From lesson 13, V_Th = 12 V and R_Th = 10 Ω. So the best load is 10 Ω and P_max = 144 / 40 = 3.6 W. If someone connects a 5 Ω load instead, I = 12 / 15 = 0.8 A and P = 0.8² × 5 = 3.2 W, a bit less. If they connect 20 Ω, I = 0.4 A and P = 3.2 W again, matching the ratio symmetry we saw earlier.

Worked example 3, with a dependent source: In lesson 13 we met a circuit of a 10 V source, a 2 Ω resistor and a current-controlled voltage source of 3i, and found V_Th = 10 V and R_Th = 5 Ω using V_oc / I_sc. The load for maximum power is therefore 5 Ω, and P_max = 10² / (4 × 5) = 100 / 20 = 5 W. The method does not change at all when dependent sources are present: find the Thevenin equivalent by whichever method is valid, then apply R_L = R_Th. The only extra care is in step one, never in step two.

What the power curve looks like: If you plot P_L on the vertical axis against R_L on the horizontal axis, the curve starts at zero (a short circuit load gets current but no voltage), rises steeply, flattens into a rounded peak at R_L = R_Th, and then falls slowly towards zero as R_L grows very large (an open circuit gets voltage but no current). The peak is broad: any load from about two thirds of R_Th up to one and a half times R_Th still receives at least 96 percent of the maximum power. That is useful in practice, because it means a rough match is almost as good as a perfect one, and engineers need not chase exact values.

A note on solar panels: Solar panels are not linear sources, so the simple R_L = R_Th rule does not apply to them directly. But the same idea, finding the operating point where the product of voltage and current is largest, is exactly what a solar charge controller with maximum power point tracking (MPPT) does. It keeps adjusting how heavily it loads the panel, watching the power, and settles near the peak as sunlight changes during the day. Solar home systems and rooftop solar installations in Bangladesh increasingly use MPPT controllers for this reason.

Practical matching with fixed resistor values: In real designs the load is often fixed, like an 8 Ω speaker, while the source resistance is not exactly 8 Ω. Engineers then use matching networks. For DC that is rarely needed, but for AC signals transformers and special networks of inductors and capacitors can make a load appear to have a different resistance. We will see in lesson 24 how a transformer with a turns ratio changes the apparent resistance by the square of that ratio. For AC, the matching condition becomes the load impedance equal to the complex conjugate of the source impedance, which you will understand after the phasor lessons.

Real life example 1, the antenna and your phone: The radio parts inside a mobile phone are designed around a standard impedance, commonly 50 Ω. The antenna, the cables and the amplifier input are all designed to look like 50 Ω to each other. A weak signal arriving from a Grameenphone or Banglalink tower might be only billionths of a watt, so losing half of it to mismatch, or worse, reflecting it back, would hurt reception. Matching is why phone engineers carefully tune the antenna area. The same 50 Ω standard appears on Wi-Fi routers and lab signal generators.

Real life example 2, why the power grid is deliberately not matched: The Thevenin resistance of the grid seen at your socket is tiny compared with any appliance. A 1000 W heater on 220 V has about 48 Ω, while the supply's effective internal resistance is a small fraction of an ohm. If the grid were matched to your heater, half the energy would turn into heat inside cables and transformers, the voltage at your socket would collapse to half, and electricity bills would double for the same work. Power engineers aim for efficiency, communication engineers aim for maximum signal power, and the same theorem helps both understand their trade-off.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to find the Thevenin equivalent first and instead set R_L equal to some random resistor in the circuit. They also apply the theorem when the load is fixed and R_Th is the variable, and they forget that the efficiency at maximum power is only 50 percent. Typical exam questions: find R_L for maximum power and the value of that power, derive the condition using calculus, sketch P_L versus R_L, compute efficiency for different loads, and find maximum power in a circuit with a dependent source after finding its Thevenin equivalent.

Recap: For a source with Thevenin values V_Th and R_Th, the load power is maximum when R_L = R_Th, and the maximum power is V_Th² / (4R_Th). At that point the load voltage is V_Th / 2 and the efficiency is just 50 percent. Matching suits weak signals like antennas and sensors; power systems avoid it to stay efficient. If the load is fixed, make R_Th as small as possible instead. With resistive circuits now fully covered, we turn to the two energy-storing elements: capacitors and inductors.

lessons.title: Capacitors
lessons.content:
Think of the water tank on the roof of a building in Dhaka. When the pump runs, the tank fills up. When the pump stops, the taps downstairs keep working for a while, because the tank stores water and releases it when needed. A capacitor is an electrical tank. It stores electric charge, and with it energy, and it can release that energy later. Until now every element we studied, the resistor, simply turned energy into heat at the moment it received it. Capacitors, and the inductors of the next lesson, are different: they remember. That memory makes circuits behave in time, and it is behind camera flashes, power supply smoothing, touchscreens and even the memory chips inside your computer.

What a capacitor is: A capacitor is made of two conducting plates separated by an insulating material called the dielectric. The dielectric might be air, paper, plastic film, ceramic or a thin oxide layer. When a voltage is applied, positive charge collects on one plate and an equal amount of negative charge on the other. No charge actually crosses the insulator. Instead, charge flows in the outside circuit, piling up on one plate and leaving the other, which is why the capacitor seems to "pass" current while it is charging.

Capacitance: The amount of charge stored for each volt applied is called capacitance, C. The basic equation is q = C × v. The unit is the farad (F), named after Michael Faraday; one farad means one coulomb per volt. A farad is a very large unit, so practical capacitors are usually measured in microfarads (µF, 10^-6 F), nanofarads (nF, 10^-9 F) and picofarads (pF, 10^-12 F). Example: a 100 µF capacitor charged to 12 V stores q = 100 × 10^-6 × 12 = 1.2 × 10^-3 C, or 1.2 millicoulombs.

What decides capacitance: For a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε × A / d, where A is the plate area, d is the distance between the plates, and ε is the permittivity of the dielectric. Larger plates hold more charge, closer plates hold more charge, and a better dielectric holds more charge. Permittivity is often written ε = εr × ε0, where ε0 is about 8.854 × 10^-12 F/m (the permittivity of empty space) and εr is the relative permittivity, also called the dielectric constant, of the material. Air has εr very close to 1, while many ceramics have values in the hundreds or thousands.

Parallel-plate example: Two square plates, each 10 cm by 10 cm, so A = 0.01 m², separated by 1 mm of air. C = 8.854 × 10^-12 × 0.01 / 0.001, which is about 8.85 × 10^-11 F, or 88.5 pF. That is tiny. To make microfarads in a small package, manufacturers roll long thin foils with a very thin dielectric, or use special ceramic materials with a high dielectric constant, or electrolytic designs with an extremely thin oxide layer.

The current-voltage relation: Since q = C v and current is the rate of change of charge, i = dq/dt = C × dv/dt. This is the defining equation of a capacitor in circuits. It says that current flows only while the voltage is changing. If the voltage is constant, dv/dt = 0 and the current is zero. Example: if the voltage across a 10 µF capacitor rises steadily by 5 V every millisecond, dv/dt = 5000 V/s and i = 10 × 10^-6 × 5000 = 0.05 A, or 50 mA. If the voltage stays flat, the current is zero.

Worked example, a piecewise voltage: The voltage across a 2 µF capacitor rises from 0 to 10 V in the first 2 ms, stays at 10 V from 2 ms to 5 ms, then falls back to 0 V between 5 ms and 6 ms. Find the current in each interval. From 0 to 2 ms the slope is 10 / 0.002 = 5000 V/s, so i = 2 × 10^-6 × 5000 = 10 mA. From 2 to 5 ms the voltage is flat, so i = 0. From 5 to 6 ms the slope is -10 / 0.001 = -10,000 V/s, so i = -20 mA, flowing out of the capacitor as it discharges. Notice the current is a set of flat steps, because the current follows the slope of the voltage, not its height. Exams love this kind of graph question.

Capacitors at DC: open circuits: In a DC circuit that has been switched on for a long time, all voltages are constant, so every capacitor carries zero current. A capacitor at DC steady state therefore behaves like an open circuit. This rule makes many problems easy: to find capacitor voltages after a long time, simply remove the capacitors, solve the resistor circuit, and read the voltages where the capacitors were.

Voltage cannot jump: Because i = C dv/dt, an instant jump in capacitor voltage would need an infinite current, which is impossible. So the voltage across a capacitor is continuous: its value just after a switch operates equals its value just before. This is the single most important rule for switching problems in lesson 17. Current, on the other hand, can jump suddenly in a capacitor; a discharged capacitor connected through a resistor to a battery draws a sudden current at the moment of connection.

Energy stored: The energy stored in a capacitor charged to voltage V is W = ½ C V². It is stored in the electric field between the plates. Example: the 100 µF capacitor at 12 V stores ½ × 100 × 10^-6 × 144 = 7.2 × 10^-3 J, or 7.2 millijoules. Doubling the voltage quadruples the energy, which is why high-voltage capacitors can store dangerous amounts of energy even when they are small. An ideal capacitor does not lose energy; it gives it all back when it discharges.

Capacitors in parallel: Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage, and their charges add: q = C1 v + C2 v + ... So the equivalent capacitance is the sum: Ceq = C1 + C2 + C3. This is like putting more tanks side by side. Example: 4 µF and 6 µF in parallel give 10 µF. Note that this is the opposite of resistors, where series resistances add.

Capacitors in series: Capacitors in series carry the same charge, and their voltages add. Since v = q / C, we get 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ..., the same form as resistors in parallel. Two in series: Ceq = C1 C2 / (C1 + C2). Example: 6 µF and 3 µF in series give 18 / 9 = 2 µF, smaller than either. In series, the voltage divides inversely to capacitance: with 12 V across the pair, the 6 µF gets 12 × 3 / 9 = 4 V and the 3 µF gets 12 × 6 / 9 = 8 V. The smaller capacitor gets the bigger voltage, because the same charge on a smaller capacitor needs more voltage.

A DC steady-state example: A 12 V source feeds 2 kΩ in series with 4 kΩ to ground, and a 10 µF capacitor sits across the 4 kΩ. After a long time, the capacitor is an open circuit, so it carries no current and the resistors form a plain divider: the capacitor voltage is 12 × 4 / 6 = 8 V. Its charge is 10 × 10^-6 × 8 = 80 µC and its energy is ½ × 10 × 10^-6 × 64 = 0.32 mJ. Notice we never needed to know how the capacitor charged up; the steady-state rule skips straight to the end.

Smoothing in power supplies: A phone charger first turns AC into a bumpy DC that rises and falls 100 times a second (twice per mains cycle). A large capacitor placed across this bumpy output fills up at each peak and supplies current in the gaps between peaks, so the voltage dips only a little before the next peak arrives. This "reservoir" or "smoothing" capacitor is exactly the water tank picture: it absorbs the bumps and releases charge when supply is low. A bigger capacitor gives smaller ripple. You will analyse this precisely in electronics, but the idea is all here.

Types of capacitors: Ceramic capacitors are small, cheap and good for high frequencies, usually from picofarads to a few microfarads. Electrolytic capacitors offer large values, from about 1 µF to many thousands of µF, but they are polarised: they have a + and a - lead, and connecting them backwards can make them fail, sometimes by bulging or bursting. Film capacitors are stable and used in audio and AC motor circuits. Supercapacitors reach whole farads and are used for short-term backup power. Every capacitor also has a voltage rating; exceeding it can break down the dielectric.

Real capacitors are not perfect: A real capacitor has a little leakage, so charge slowly drains through the dielectric. It also has a small series resistance and inductance in its leads. Electrolytic capacitors age, especially in heat, and their capacitance falls. Many cheap power supplies and TV boards fail because an electrolytic capacitor near a hot component has dried out, which repair technicians in local electronics markets know very well.

Safety note: A large capacitor can stay charged after the device is unplugged. Inside microwave ovens, old TVs and some power supplies, capacitors can hold enough energy to give a painful or dangerous shock. Technicians discharge them safely with a suitable resistor before working. As a student, never open mains-powered equipment just because it is unplugged.

Real life example 1, the ceiling fan capacitor: Most ceiling fans in Bangladeshi homes contain a small capacitor, usually a few microfarads, connected to the motor. A single-phase AC motor needs a little help to start turning in the right direction, and the capacitor creates a shifted current in a second winding that gives that push. When this capacitor weakens, a common symptom is a fan that hums but turns slowly, or that starts only if you spin the blades by hand. Electricians often fix the fan simply by replacing this cheap part.

Real life example 2, memory and touchscreens: Each bit in the DRAM memory of your laptop is stored as charge on a tiny capacitor, so tiny that it slowly leaks. That is why DRAM must be refreshed, rewritten, many times every second. Your phone's touchscreen also uses capacitance: your finger, being conductive, changes the capacitance at the point you touch, and the screen controller measures that change to find your finger's position. So capacitors are not just about power; they are at the heart of computing hardware.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up the series and parallel formulas because they are opposite to resistors, forget that capacitors are open circuits at DC steady state, and think voltage can jump across a capacitor. They also forget the half in ½CV² and the units of µF. Typical exam questions: find charge and energy stored, compute current from a given voltage waveform using i = C dv/dt, find equivalent capacitance of a network, find the voltage on each capacitor in series, and find capacitor voltages in a DC circuit at steady state.

Recap: A capacitor stores charge q = Cv on two plates separated by a dielectric, with C = εA/d. Its current is i = C dv/dt, so it is an open circuit at DC steady state and its voltage cannot change instantly. It stores energy ½CV². Parallel capacitances add; series capacitances combine like parallel resistors. Next we meet the capacitor's magnetic twin, the inductor.
key_points: A capacitor is two plates separated by a dielectric; it stores charge q = Cv.
Capacitance C = εA/d, unit farad; practical values in µF, nF, pF.
i = C dv/dt: current flows only while voltage changes.
At DC steady state a capacitor is an open circuit.
Capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously; current can.
Energy stored W = ½CV², in the electric field.
Parallel: Ceq = C1 + C2; series: 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 (opposite of resistors).
Electrolytics are polarised; every capacitor has a voltage rating.

lessons.title: Inductors
lessons.content:
Have you ever pushed a heavy loaded van that had broken down on the road? Getting it to start moving is hard, but once it rolls, it wants to keep rolling, and stopping it suddenly is just as hard. The van has inertia: it resists changes in its motion. An inductor gives electric current exactly this kind of inertia. It resists any change in the current through it. It is easy to keep a steady current flowing through an inductor, but any attempt to start, stop or change that current is met with an opposing voltage. Where the capacitor stores energy in an electric field, the inductor stores it in a magnetic field. Together, they give circuits their behaviour in time.

What an inductor is: An inductor is usually a coil of insulated wire, sometimes wound around a core of iron or ferrite. When current flows through the coil, it creates a magnetic field around and inside it. The more turns, the stronger the field for the same current. Inductors are found in chargers, laptop power supplies, motors, transformers, radios, old fluorescent tube light fittings and many other places.

Electricity and magnetism, a quick reminder: In the 1820s Hans Christian Ørsted discovered that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, showing that current creates a magnetic field. In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered the reverse: a changing magnetic field passing through a coil creates a voltage in it. This is Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction. Heinrich Lenz added the direction rule: the induced voltage always acts to oppose the change that caused it. That opposition is the source of the inductor's inertia.

Inductance: The inductance L of a coil measures how much magnetic flux linkage it produces per ampere of current. Its unit is the henry (H), named after the American scientist Joseph Henry. Practical inductors range from nanohenries (nH) in radio circuits, through microhenries (µH) in switching power supplies, to millihenries (mH) and whole henries in filters and motors.

What decides inductance: For a long air-cored coil, called a solenoid, L = µ N² A / l, where N is the number of turns, A is the cross-sectional area, l is the length, and µ is the permeability of the core. In air, µ is about µ0 = 4π × 10^-7 H/m. Notice N is squared: doubling the turns quadruples the inductance. Example: 1000 turns on a 10 cm long air core with 1 cm² cross-section gives L = 4π × 10^-7 × 1000² × 10^-4 / 0.1, which is about 1.26 mH. Putting an iron or ferrite core inside, whose permeability is hundreds or thousands of times larger, raises the inductance hugely.

The voltage-current relation: The defining equation of an inductor is v = L × di/dt. The voltage across an inductor is proportional to how fast its current is changing. If the current is steady, di/dt = 0 and the voltage is zero. Example: in a 50 mH inductor, if the current rises steadily by 2 A in 10 ms, di/dt = 200 A/s and v = 0.05 × 200 = 10 V. Compare this with the capacitor's i = C dv/dt: the roles of voltage and current are simply swapped. This symmetry is called duality, and it makes the two elements easy to learn together.

Worked example, a piecewise current: The current in a 10 mH inductor rises from 0 to 4 A in the first 2 ms, stays at 4 A until 5 ms, then falls to 0 between 5 ms and 6 ms. From 0 to 2 ms, di/dt = 4 / 0.002 = 2000 A/s, so v = 0.01 × 2000 = 20 V. From 2 to 5 ms the current is flat, so v = 0. From 5 to 6 ms, di/dt = -4 / 0.001 = -4000 A/s, so v = -40 V. The faster the current falls, the bigger the reverse voltage. Imagine making that fall almost instant; the voltage would become enormous.

Inductors at DC: short circuits: In a DC circuit that has been on for a long time, all currents are constant, so every inductor has zero voltage across it. An ideal inductor at DC steady state therefore behaves like a short circuit, a plain wire. Real inductors have some wire resistance, so they act like a small resistor at DC. To find inductor currents after a long time, replace each inductor with a short and solve the resistor circuit.

Current cannot jump: Because v = L di/dt, an instant change in inductor current would require an infinite voltage. So the current through an inductor is continuous: its value just after a switch operates equals its value just before. The voltage across an inductor, however, can jump suddenly. This is the twin of the capacitor rule, and together they are the key to all switching problems in lesson 17: capacitor voltage and inductor current hold their values across a switching instant.

The inductive kick: What happens if you suddenly open a switch in series with an inductor carrying current? The inductor insists on keeping its current flowing, and the only way it can try is by producing a very large voltage, often big enough to make a spark jump across the opening switch contacts. This is called an inductive kick. It can damage transistors that switch relay coils or motors, so designers place a diode, called a flyback or freewheeling diode, across the coil to give the current a safe path when the switch opens. The same effect is used on purpose in petrol engine ignition coils to create the high-voltage spark.

Energy stored: The energy stored in an inductor carrying current I is W = ½ L I². It lives in the magnetic field. Example: a 0.2 H inductor carrying 3 A stores ½ × 0.2 × 9 = 0.9 J. The energy depends on current, not voltage: an inductor with a steady current and zero voltage still holds energy, just as a capacitor with a steady voltage and zero current does. An ideal inductor returns all of its stored energy; real ones lose a bit in the wire resistance and in the core.

DC steady-state example: A 12 V source feeds a 2 Ω resistor, followed by a 0.5 H inductor connected in parallel with a 4 Ω resistor, all returning to the source. After a long time, the inductor is a short circuit, which shorts out the 4 Ω, so all the current flows through the inductor: I = 12 / 2 = 6 A. The 4 Ω carries nothing. The stored energy is ½ × 0.5 × 36 = 9 J. Spotting that the short removes the parallel resistor is the whole trick.

Inductors in series and parallel: Inductors in series carry the same current, and their voltages add, so Leq = L1 + L2 + L3, just like resistors. Inductors in parallel share the same voltage, and 1/Leq = 1/L1 + 1/L2 + ..., again like resistors. Examples: 2 mH and 3 mH in series give 5 mH; 6 mH and 3 mH in parallel give 18 / 9 = 2 mH. These formulas assume the coils do not share magnetic fields; coupled coils are the topic of lesson 24.

A preview of inductors with AC: Because an inductor reacts to how fast current changes, it treats slow and fast signals very differently. A steady DC current passes freely, but a rapidly alternating current faces a strong opposing voltage. So inductors block high frequencies and pass low ones, the opposite of capacitors, which block DC and pass high frequencies. The small cylindrical lump you often see near the end of a laptop charger cable is a ferrite bead, a tiny inductor-like part that lets the DC power through while choking off high-frequency electrical noise. We will put numbers on this behaviour with reactance in lesson 20.

Comparing the three passive elements: A resistor has v = Ri, stores no energy and dissipates power. A capacitor has i = C dv/dt, stores ½CV² in an electric field, is open at DC, and has continuous voltage. An inductor has v = L di/dt, stores ½LI² in a magnetic field, is short at DC, and has continuous current. Writing these facts in a table and learning them as a set is one of the best investments you can make in this course.

Real inductors and their imperfections: Real inductors have winding resistance, so they waste some power as heat. Iron cores lose energy through hysteresis and eddy currents, which is why transformer and motor cores are made of thin insulated sheets. Cores can also saturate: above a certain current, the core cannot magnetise any further and the inductance drops sharply. Inductors are bulkier and more expensive than capacitors for similar energy, which is one reason modern circuits avoid them where they can.

Real life example 1, the old tube light ballast: Many older fluorescent tube light fittings in Bangladeshi homes and offices use a heavy magnetic ballast, which is essentially an inductor, together with a small starter. When the starter opens, the current through the ballast is interrupted and the inductive kick produces a high voltage that strikes the gas in the tube. After that, the ballast limits the current while the tube glows. The faint hum and the warmth you may notice from these fittings come from the ballast's core and winding. Newer fittings and LED tubes use electronic drivers instead.

Real life example 2, laptop and phone chargers: Modern chargers are switching power supplies. A transistor switches on and off tens of thousands of times per second or more, and inductors and capacitors smooth the result into steady DC. During each on-phase, energy is stored in the inductor's magnetic field; during the off-phase, it is released to the output. Because inductors store energy without wasting much, these supplies reach high efficiencies, which is why a modern charger is small and only slightly warm compared with the heavy transformer chargers of the past.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget that an inductor is a short at DC steady state, assume inductor current can jump at a switching instant, and mix up the inductor and capacitor equations. They also miss the square on N in the solenoid formula and on I in the energy formula. Typical exam questions: find the voltage across an inductor for a given current waveform, compute stored energy, find equivalent inductance, find inductor currents at DC steady state, and explain why a flyback diode is needed across a relay coil.

Recap: An inductor is a coil that stores energy ½LI² in its magnetic field. Its voltage is v = L di/dt, so it is a short circuit at DC steady state, its current cannot change instantly, and suddenly interrupting its current produces a large voltage kick. Inductances add in series and combine like resistors in parallel. With R, C and L understood, we are ready to see what happens in time when circuits containing them are switched: first-order RC and RL circuits.

lessons.title: First-Order Circuits: RC and RL Transients
lessons.content:
Pour hot tea into a cup and leave it on the table. At first it cools quickly, then more and more slowly, and after a while it simply sits at room temperature. The bigger the difference from room temperature, the faster it cools. This pattern, fast at first and then gently settling, is called exponential decay, and it appears everywhere: in cooling tea, in a draining water tank, and in circuits with one capacitor or one inductor. When such a circuit is switched, its voltages and currents do not jump to their new values. They glide there along an exponential curve, and one number, the time constant, tells you how fast. This lesson teaches you to predict those curves.

What a first-order circuit is: A first-order circuit contains resistors and sources plus exactly one energy-storing element, either one capacitor (an RC circuit) or one inductor (an RL circuit), or several that can be combined into one. It is called first-order because its behaviour is described by a first-order differential equation, an equation involving only the first derivative of the unknown. Such circuits are the simplest circuits with memory, and they are everywhere in electronics: timers, filters, delays and the charging of every capacitor in your phone.

Transient and steady state: After a switch is thrown, a circuit goes through a transient period, during which voltages and currents are changing, and then reaches a new steady state, where everything is constant again (for DC sources). In lessons 15 and 16 we learned to find steady states quickly: capacitors become open circuits and inductors become short circuits. The new skill in this lesson is describing the transient in between.

The source-free RC circuit: Charge a capacitor C to an initial voltage V0, then at t = 0 connect it across a resistor R with no source. The capacitor current flows through the resistor. KCL at the top node gives C dv/dt + v/R = 0. The solution is v(t) = V0 × e^(-t/RC). The voltage starts at V0 and decays towards zero. The quantity τ = RC is called the time constant, measured in seconds. Ohms times farads indeed gives seconds.

What the time constant means: After one time constant, t = τ, the voltage has fallen to e^-1 of its starting value, about 36.8 percent. After 2τ it is about 13.5 percent, after 3τ about 5 percent, and after 5τ about 0.7 percent. Engineers treat 5τ as "practically finished". Example: R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF give τ = 10,000 × 0.0001 = 1 s. A capacitor starting at 10 V would read about 3.68 V after 1 s and be essentially empty after 5 s.

The source-free RL circuit: Now let an inductor carry an initial current I0 and at t = 0 connect it across a resistor R. KVL gives L di/dt + R i = 0, with solution i(t) = I0 × e^(-t/τ), where τ = L / R. Notice the difference: in RC, τ grows with R; in RL, τ shrinks with R. A big resistor drains a capacitor slowly but stops an inductor's current quickly. Example: L = 2 H and R = 4 Ω give τ = 0.5 s.

Which R to use: In a real circuit there may be several resistors. The R in τ = RC or τ = L/R is the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor or inductor, found with all independent sources turned off and the energy-storing element removed. So the Thevenin skill from lesson 13 is exactly what you need here. Note that the R may be different before and after the switch, because the switch changes the circuit; always use the circuit that exists after the switching.

The step response: Now suppose a DC source is switched into the circuit, so the capacitor charges or the inductor current builds up. The general solution for any first-order circuit with DC sources has one universal form: x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0+) - x(∞)] × e^(-t/τ), where x is the capacitor voltage or inductor current, x(0+) is its value just after switching, and x(∞) is its final steady-state value. This one formula solves almost every first-order exam problem.

The three-number recipe: Step 1, find the initial value x(0+). For a capacitor voltage or inductor current, this equals the value just before switching, x(0-), found from the old steady state. Step 2, find the final value x(∞) from the new steady state, with capacitors open and inductors shorted. Step 3, find τ from the Thevenin resistance seen by the element after switching. Then plug into the universal formula. Every first-order problem becomes three small DC problems and one exponential.

Charging example, RC: A discharged 100 µF capacitor is connected at t = 0 through 10 kΩ to a 10 V source. Initial value 0 V, final value 10 V, τ = 1 s. So v(t) = 10 + (0 - 10) e^(-t) = 10 (1 - e^(-t)) volts. At 1 s, v is about 6.32 V, which is 63.2 percent of the way. At 2 s, about 8.65 V. At 5 s, about 9.93 V. The current is i = C dv/dt = (10 / 10,000) e^(-t) = 1 mA × e^(-t): it starts at 1 mA, as if the capacitor were a short circuit at first, and decays to zero.

Build-up example, RL: A 24 V source is switched at t = 0 onto a 4 Ω resistor in series with a 2 H inductor that carried no current. Initial current 0, final current 24 / 4 = 6 A, τ = 2 / 4 = 0.5 s. So i(t) = 6 (1 - e^(-2t)) A. After 0.5 s the current is about 3.79 A, and after 2.5 s it is practically 6 A. The inductor voltage is v = L di/dt = 24 e^(-2t): at the very first instant the inductor takes the whole 24 V, behaving like an open circuit, and its voltage then fades to zero as it becomes a short.

A switching example with initial conditions: A 12 V source feeds 2 kΩ in series with 4 kΩ to ground, with a 10 µF capacitor across the 4 kΩ. The switch has been closed for a long time, so the capacitor sits at the divider voltage 12 × 4 / 6 = 8 V. At t = 0 the switch opens and disconnects the source. Now the capacitor discharges through the 4 kΩ alone. Initial value 8 V (it cannot jump), final value 0 V, τ = 4000 × 10^-5 = 40 ms. So v(t) = 8 e^(-t/0.04) V. After 40 ms the voltage is about 2.94 V, and the initial current through the 4 kΩ is 8 / 4000 = 2 mA.

What can and cannot jump: At a switching instant, capacitor voltage and inductor current keep their values. Everything else may jump: capacitor current, inductor voltage, resistor voltages and currents. So when a problem asks for the current just after switching, first find the continuous quantity, then use it like a temporary source: a capacitor at t = 0+ acts like a voltage source of value v(0), and an inductor acts like a current source of value i(0). A discharged capacitor acts like a short at t = 0+, and an inductor with zero current acts like an open.

Sketching the curve quickly: To sketch any first-order response, mark the initial value at t = 0 and draw a dashed horizontal line at the final value. Then use a neat property of exponentials: if the curve kept its starting slope, it would reach the final value in exactly one time constant. So draw a straight line from the starting point to the final level at t = τ; the real curve starts along that line and bends away, passing 63.2 percent of the way at t = τ and hugging the final line by about 5τ. This sketch method also works in reverse: in the lab you can estimate τ from an oscilloscope trace by finding when the curve covers 63 percent of its total change.

Finding the time to reach a value: Sometimes you need the time when the response reaches a certain level. Rearranging the universal formula gives t = τ × ln[(x(0) - x(∞)) / (x(t) - x(∞))]. Example: how long does a capacitor charging from 0 to a final 10 V take to reach 9 V? t = τ × ln(10 / 1) = τ × ln 10, about 2.3τ. With τ = 1 s, that is about 2.3 seconds. A calculator with a natural log key is all you need.

Energy during switching: When a charged capacitor discharges through a resistor, all its stored energy ½CV0² ends up as heat in the resistor, no matter what the resistance is. A bigger resistor just spreads that heat over a longer time. The same holds for an inductor's ½LI0². This is a nice check: integrating the resistor's power over time gives exactly the stored energy.

Real life example 1, the camera flash and the blinking LED: A camera flash charges a capacitor through a resistance from a battery, which is why there is a short wait before the next flash. The charging follows the RC curve: the flash is "ready" at around 3τ to 5τ. Many simple timer circuits, such as the blinking LEDs in toys or the delay before a staircase light switches off in some buildings, use an RC time constant to set the timing. Choosing R and C sets the delay: double either one and the delay doubles.

Real life example 2, button debouncing in computers: When you press a mechanical button, the metal contacts bounce several times in a few milliseconds, which a fast microcontroller could read as many presses. A simple fix is an RC circuit across the button with a time constant of a few milliseconds, which smooths the bounces into one clean rise or fall. Another example: when a relay coil, an RL circuit, is switched on, its current takes about a few time constants to build up, which is why relays have a small pull-in delay. Embedded systems engineers think about these τ values daily.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students assume capacitor voltage jumps, use the wrong R for τ (not the Thevenin resistance seen after switching), mix up τ = RC with τ = L/R by writing R/L, and forget that the final value must be found with capacitors open and inductors shorted. Typical exam questions: find v(t) or i(t) for t > 0 after a switch operates, find the value at a given time or the time to reach a value, find the initial current just after switching, sketch the response, and find the energy dissipated.

Recap: First-order circuits have one capacitor or one inductor and respond exponentially. The time constant is τ = RC or τ = L/R, with R the Thevenin resistance seen by the element. Every response follows x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0+) - x(∞)] e^(-t/τ): find the initial value, the final value and τ. Capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump. After 5τ the transient is practically over. Next, with one capacitor and one inductor together, we get second-order circuits that can even oscillate.
key_points: First-order circuits have one capacitor or one inductor and respond exponentially.
RC time constant τ = RC; RL time constant τ = L/R, with R the Thevenin resistance seen by the element after switching.
After 1τ: 63.2% of the change done; after 5τ: practically finished.
Universal formula: x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0+) - x(∞)] e^(-t/τ).
Recipe: initial value (from old steady state), final value (C open, L short), time constant.
Capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump; other quantities can.
Time to reach a value: t = τ ln[(x(0) - x(∞)) / (x(t) - x(∞))].
lessons.tip: Write 'x(0+), x(∞), τ' as three headings for every transient problem and fill them in before touching the exponential.
lessons.task: With your phone's stopwatch, time how long a phone camera's flash or a torch with a capacitor takes to be ready again, then estimate what RC value would give that delay if 'ready' means 5τ.

lessons.title: Second-Order Circuits: RLC Responses
lessons.content:
Hang a weight from a spring and pull it down a little, then let go. It bounces up and down, each bounce a bit smaller, until it settles. Now imagine the same spring and weight inside a jar of thick honey: let go, and the weight creeps slowly back to rest without bouncing at all. A car's suspension is designed to be in between, so it settles quickly after a speed breaker without bouncing for long. A circuit with both an inductor and a capacitor behaves exactly like this spring and weight. Energy sloshes between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field, and the resistor plays the role of the honey. This lesson explains when such a circuit bounces, when it creeps, and how to write its response.

What a second-order circuit is: A second-order circuit contains two energy-storing elements that cannot be combined into one, typically one inductor and one capacitor along with resistors. Its behaviour is described by a second-order differential equation, which involves the second derivative of the unknown. The classic examples are the series RLC circuit, where R, L and C sit in one loop, and the parallel RLC circuit, where they sit across one pair of nodes.

Why energy can oscillate: A capacitor stores energy in its voltage, an inductor in its current. Suppose a charged capacitor is connected to an inductor. The capacitor pushes current into the inductor, and its voltage falls while the inductor's current grows. When the capacitor is empty, the inductor's current is at its maximum and, because inductor current cannot stop suddenly, it keeps flowing and charges the capacitor the other way. Then the process reverses. Without resistance this back-and-forth would continue forever, like a frictionless swing. The resistor removes a little energy each cycle as heat, so the swings die down.

The series RLC equation: In a source-free series RLC circuit, KVL around the loop, written for the loop current i, gives L d²i/dt² + R di/dt + i/C = 0. Dividing by L: d²i/dt² + (R/L) di/dt + i/(LC) = 0. We try solutions of the form e^(st), which turns the differential equation into an ordinary quadratic: s² + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0. This is called the characteristic equation.

Two key numbers, α and ω0: It is neat to write the characteristic equation as s² + 2α s + ω0² = 0. For the series circuit, the damping factor is α = R / (2L) and the resonant frequency (also called the undamped natural frequency) is ω0 = 1 / √(LC), both in units of per second (radians per second for ω0). The roots are s = -α ± √(α² - ω0²). Everything about the response depends on comparing α with ω0.

The parallel RLC circuit: For R, L and C in parallel with no source, KCL at the top node gives the same kind of equation for the voltage v: C d²v/dt² + (1/R) dv/dt + v/L = 0. Here ω0 = 1 / √(LC) again, but the damping factor is α = 1 / (2RC). Notice the twist: in series, a larger R means more damping; in parallel, a larger R means less damping, because a large parallel resistor draws little current and wastes little energy.

Case 1, overdamped: When α > ω0, the square root is real and the two roots s1 and s2 are real, negative and different. The response is x(t) = A1 e^(s1 t) + A2 e^(s2 t). It returns to zero slowly without oscillating, like the weight in honey. Example: series L = 1 H, C = 0.25 F, so ω0 = 1 / √0.25 = 2 rad/s. With R = 5 Ω, α = 5 / 2 = 2.5, which is greater than 2. The roots are -2.5 ± √(6.25 - 4) = -2.5 ± 1.5, so s1 = -1 and s2 = -4.

Case 2, critically damped: When α = ω0, the two roots are equal: s = -α. The response becomes x(t) = (A1 + A2 t) e^(-αt). This is the fastest possible return to zero without overshooting, the ideal that car suspensions and measuring instruments often aim for. In our example, critical damping happens at α = 2, that is R = 4 Ω. In general, for a series RLC, the critical resistance is R = 2√(L/C); here 2√(1/0.25) = 2 × 2 = 4 Ω.

Case 3, underdamped: When α < ω0, the square root is of a negative number, so the roots are complex: s = -α ± jωd, where ωd = √(ω0² - α²) is the damped natural frequency and j is the square root of -1 (engineers use j because i is already taken by current). The response is x(t) = e^(-αt) (B1 cos ωd t + B2 sin ωd t): a sine-like oscillation inside a shrinking exponential envelope, like the bouncing spring. In our example with R = 2 Ω, α = 1 and ωd = √(4 - 1) = √3, about 1.73 rad/s. With R = 0, α = 0 and the circuit oscillates forever at ω0; that ideal is called the lossless LC circuit.

A parallel RLC classification example: Use the same L = 1 H and C = 0.25 F, now connected in parallel with a resistor R, so ω0 = 2 rad/s again and α = 1 / (2R × 0.25) = 2 / R. With R = 0.5 Ω, α = 4, greater than 2: overdamped. With R = 1 Ω, α = 2: critically damped. With R = 5 Ω, α = 0.4, much less than 2: underdamped, ringing at ωd = √(4 - 0.16), about 1.96 rad/s. Compare with the series case, where a small R gave ringing and a large R gave overdamping. In parallel it is the other way round. Writing both cases side by side in your notes makes this flip easy to remember.

Why the roots decide the shape: Each root s contributes a term e^(st). A negative real root gives a smooth exponential decay; two such terms added give the slow, non-oscillating overdamped shape. A complex pair -α ± jωd gives e^(-αt) times a cosine and sine at ωd, using Euler's formula e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, which is the decaying oscillation. If α were negative, the terms would grow instead of shrink, which happens only in circuits with active elements that feed in energy, such as oscillators.

Initial conditions for second-order circuits: A second-order equation needs two initial conditions to find the two constants. One is the value of the unknown at t = 0+, say i(0) for series RLC; it equals the inductor current just before switching. The other is its initial rate of change, di/dt at 0+, which comes from the inductor voltage: L di/dt(0+) = vL(0+), and vL(0+) is found with KVL using the known capacitor voltage and inductor current at that instant. For a parallel RLC, the capacitor voltage and dv/dt(0+) = iC(0+) / C play the same roles.

A full worked example: A capacitor of 0.25 F charged to 6 V is connected at t = 0 into a series loop with R = 5 Ω and L = 1 H, with no initial inductor current. From above, the circuit is overdamped with s1 = -1 and s2 = -4, so i(t) = A1 e^(-t) + A2 e^(-4t). At t = 0+, i = 0 (inductor current cannot jump), so A1 + A2 = 0. Also at t = 0+ there is no current, so the resistor has no voltage and the whole 6 V of the capacitor appears across the inductor: di/dt(0+) = 6 / 1 = 6 A/s. Differentiating, -A1 - 4A2 = 6. With A2 = -A1, this gives 3A1 = 6, so A1 = 2 and A2 = -2. Therefore i(t) = 2(e^(-t) - e^(-4t)) A. The current rises from zero, peaks at about 0.94 A near t = 0.46 s, then decays without oscillating.

The step response: When a DC source is switched in, the response is the final steady-state value plus a natural response of the same three types: x(t) = x(∞) + (natural part). The final value comes from the usual DC steady state, with capacitors open and inductors shorted. The constants in the natural part are found from the initial value and initial derivative, exactly as above. In an underdamped step response, the output overshoots its final value and rings around it before settling; in an overdamped one, it rises slowly without overshoot.

Seeing it on an oscilloscope: Underdamped responses are easy to recognise: you see ringing, decaying wiggles. The spacing between peaks gives the period 2π / ωd, and how fast the peaks shrink gives α. Engineers often measure these two quantities from a screen to find unknown component values in a real circuit. Sharp edges in digital circuits sometimes ring because the wiring's small inductance and capacitance form an accidental underdamped RLC circuit, which is a real problem for high-speed computer boards.

Real life example 1, a car or motorbike suspension and the same maths: The equation for a mass on a spring with a damper has exactly the same form as the RLC equation: mass plays the role of inductance, the spring's softness the role of capacitance, and the damper the role of resistance. A motorbike on a broken road in a Bangladeshi village with worn-out shock absorbers is underdamped: after each bump it bounces several times. New, well-tuned shocks are close to critically damped. Engineers sometimes even simulate mechanical systems with electric circuits because the maths is identical.

Real life example 2, radios and clocks: An LC circuit with little resistance rings at ω0 = 1 / √(LC), and radios use this to pick one station out of many, which we study in lesson 23. Example: L = 1 mH and C = 1 µF give ω0 = 1 / √(10^-9), about 31,600 rad/s, which is about 5 kHz. Changing C with a tuning capacitor shifts that frequency. Electronic oscillators that generate clock signals also build on circuits that ring, with an amplifier added to replace the energy lost in the resistance so that the oscillation does not die.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up the α formulas for series (R/2L) and parallel (1/2RC), forget the second initial condition, take the wrong sign of di/dt(0+), and misclassify the damping by comparing α with ωd instead of ω0. Typical exam questions: find α, ω0 and the type of damping; find the value of R for critical damping; find i(t) or v(t) for a source-free series or parallel RLC; find the step response; and sketch the three response types.

Recap: Second-order circuits have an L and a C, giving the characteristic equation s² + 2αs + ω0² = 0 with ω0 = 1/√(LC); α = R/2L for series and 1/2RC for parallel. α > ω0 is overdamped (two real roots), α = ω0 is critically damped (repeated root, fastest without overshoot), and α < ω0 is underdamped (oscillation at ωd = √(ω0² - α²) inside a decaying envelope). Two initial conditions fix the constants. Now we leave switching transients behind and study circuits driven continuously by sinusoids: AC.
key_points: Second-order circuits contain an L and a C; energy can slosh between them.
Characteristic equation: s² + 2αs + ω0² = 0, with ω0 = 1/√(LC).
Series RLC: α = R/(2L); parallel RLC: α = 1/(2RC).
α > ω0: overdamped (two real roots); α = ω0: critically damped; α < ω0: underdamped.
Underdamped response oscillates at ωd = √(ω0² - α²) inside an e^(-αt) envelope.
Series critical resistance: R = 2√(L/C).
Two initial conditions are needed: the value and the first derivative at t = 0+.
Step response = final value + natural response.
lessons.tip: Always compute α and ω0 first and write the damping type in words before solving; it tells you which form of solution to use.

lessons.title: AC Fundamentals: Sinusoids, RMS and Phase
lessons.content:
Watch a fisherman on the Padma rowing a small boat. His oar goes forward and back, forward and back, in a smooth steady rhythm. The water does not flow in one direction because of the oar; it is pushed one way and then the other, again and again, yet the boat moves and real work gets done. The electricity in your wall socket behaves like that oar. It does not flow steadily in one direction like a battery's current. It swings forward and back, fifty times every second in Bangladesh, in a smooth wave called a sinusoid. This is alternating current, AC, and from this lesson on, it is our main subject.

Why AC is used for power: In the late 1800s there was a famous contest, sometimes called the "war of the currents", between Thomas Edison's DC system and the AC system championed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla. AC won for power distribution mainly because of the transformer, which can step AC voltages up and down efficiently, while DC could not be transformed easily with the technology of that time. As we saw in lesson 3, high voltage means low current and small I²R losses on long lines. Also, the rotating generators in power stations naturally produce sinusoidal voltages. Today, high-voltage DC links are also used for some very long connections, thanks to modern electronics, but homes still receive AC.

How a generator makes a sinusoid: Inside a power station generator, a magnet and a set of coils turn relative to each other. As a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the magnetic flux through it changes, and by Faraday's law a voltage is induced. Because the flux changes like the cosine of the rotation angle, the induced voltage follows a sine wave. One full rotation of a simple two-pole generator produces one full cycle of the wave, so a two-pole generator must spin at 3000 revolutions per minute to produce 50 hertz.

Describing a sinusoid: A sinusoidal voltage is written v(t) = Vm sin(ωt + φ). Vm is the amplitude or peak value, the highest point of the wave. ω is the angular frequency in radians per second. φ is the phase angle, which tells where the wave is at t = 0. The same description works with cosine instead of sine; many textbooks prefer cosine, and the two are related by cos x = sin(x + 90°).

Frequency and period: The period T is the time for one complete cycle, measured in seconds. The frequency f is the number of cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz), named after Heinrich Hertz. They are related by f = 1 / T and ω = 2πf. In Bangladesh the mains frequency is 50 Hz, so T = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms, and ω = 2π × 50, about 314 rad/s. Countries such as the USA use 60 Hz, and Japan famously uses 50 Hz in its eastern half and 60 Hz in its western half.

Worked example, reading an expression: Take v(t) = 311 sin(314t - 60°) volts. The peak is 311 V, so the RMS is 311 / √2, about 220 V. The angular frequency is 314 rad/s, so f = 314 / 2π, about 50 Hz, and T = 20 ms. At t = 0, v = 311 × sin(-60°) = 311 × (-0.866), about -269 V. When does it first reach its positive peak? The angle must reach 90°, so the wave must advance by 150° from its starting angle of -60°. That is 150 / 360 of a period: 20 ms × 150 / 360, about 8.33 ms. Notice how we turned an angle into a time; be careful never to plug degrees directly into ωt, which is in radians.

Peak and peak-to-peak: The peak value Vm is measured from zero to the top of the wave. The peak-to-peak value, from the lowest point to the highest, is 2Vm. An oscilloscope makes these easy to read directly from the screen. For a household supply around 230 V (as we will see, that is an RMS value), the peak is about 325 V and the peak-to-peak about 650 V, which is one reason mains must be treated with great respect.

Phase and phase difference: Two sinusoids of the same frequency can be shifted in time relative to each other. If v = 10 sin(314t + 30°) and i = 2 sin(314t - 15°), the voltage reaches its peak earlier than the current, and we say v leads i by 30 - (-15) = 45 degrees, or equivalently i lags v by 45 degrees. To compare phases, both waves must be written in the same form, both sines or both cosines with positive amplitudes. A phase difference can also be expressed as a time delay: 45 degrees is one eighth of a cycle, so at 50 Hz it is 20 ms / 8 = 2.5 ms.

Useful conversions: Several identities help put waves in the same form. -sin x = sin(x ± 180°), so a negative amplitude is just a 180-degree phase shift. cos x = sin(x + 90°), so a cosine leads the sine of the same angle by 90 degrees. sin x = cos(x - 90°). Example: compare v1 = 5 cos(ωt) and v2 = -3 sin(ωt). Write v1 = 5 sin(ωt + 90°) and v2 = 3 sin(ωt + 180°). Then v2 leads v1 by 90 degrees.

Average value: The average of a full sine wave over a complete cycle is zero, because the positive half and negative half cancel. That is not very useful, so for sinusoids we often quote the average over a half cycle, called the half-cycle average: Vavg = 2Vm / π, about 0.637 Vm. Average values matter for rectified waveforms in power supplies, and they are what a DC voltmeter would read on a rectified signal.

The RMS value: The most important AC quantity is the root mean square, or RMS, value, also called the effective value. It is defined as the square root of the average of the square of the waveform over one period. The physical meaning is beautiful: the RMS value of an AC voltage is the DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. A 230 V RMS supply heats a kettle exactly as much as a 230 V DC supply would. For a sinusoid, Vrms = Vm / √2, about 0.707 Vm.

Why RMS is Vm / √2: The power in a resistor is v² / R. For v = Vm sin ωt, v² = Vm² sin² ωt, and sin² averages to exactly one half over a full cycle, because sin² x = (1 - cos 2x) / 2 and the cos 2x part averages to zero. So the average power is Vm² / (2R), which equals Vrms² / R if Vrms² = Vm² / 2. Taking the square root gives Vrms = Vm / √2. Currents work the same way: Irms = Im / √2.

Mains voltages are RMS: When we say the supply in Bangladesh is about 220 to 230 V, we mean the RMS value. So the peak of a 220 V supply is 220 × √2, about 311 V, and for 230 V it is about 325 V. All appliance ratings, meter readings on AC ranges and power formulas such as P = Vrms × Irms for resistive loads use RMS values unless stated otherwise. Insulation and component voltage ratings, however, must handle the peak value.

Form factor and peak factor: Two ratios describe the shape of a waveform. The form factor is RMS divided by average, which for a sine is (Vm / √2) / (2Vm / π), about 1.11. The peak or crest factor is peak divided by RMS, which for a sine is √2, about 1.414. Other waveforms have different values. A square wave of amplitude Vm has RMS equal to Vm, so its peak factor is 1. Exams often ask you to compute RMS and average for square, triangular and half-wave rectified waveforms.

RMS of other waveforms: For a square wave that switches between +Vm and -Vm, v² is always Vm², so Vrms = Vm. For a triangle or sawtooth wave of peak Vm, Vrms = Vm / √3, about 0.577 Vm. For a half-wave rectified sine (only the positive halves kept), Vrms = Vm / 2 and Vavg = Vm / π. These come from the same definition: square, average over a period, square root.

True RMS meters: Many inexpensive multimeters do not really compute RMS. They measure an average and multiply by 1.11, the sine wave's form factor. That gives correct RMS readings for clean sine waves but wrong readings for distorted waveforms, such as the current drawn by computers and LED drivers. Meters labelled "True RMS" compute the real value and are preferred for modern loads with distorted currents.

Real life example 1, the voltage in your room: Measure a socket in a Dhaka flat with an AC voltmeter and you might read 225 V. That is RMS. The actual voltage swings between about +318 V and -318 V, fifty times a second, completing each full swing in 20 ms. Your ceiling fan's motor, your LED bulb's driver and your phone charger are all designed around this rhythm. The LED bulb's driver converts the AC to steady DC so you do not see flicker; a poor-quality bulb may show a slight 100 Hz flicker, which some phone cameras can reveal as dark bands.

Real life example 2, the IPS and inverter output: An IPS or inverter in a Bangladeshi home creates AC from a 12 V or 24 V battery during load-shedding. Cheaper models produce a "modified sine wave" that looks like a stepped square wave, while better ones produce a "pure sine wave". Both may be set to about 220 V RMS at 50 Hz, but their peak values and shapes differ. Motors such as fans and refrigerator compressors run cooler and quieter on a pure sine wave, which is why the waveform type is printed in inverter specifications.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse peak and RMS, use degrees and radians together inside one expression, compare phases of waves written in different forms, and forget that the full-cycle average of a sine is zero. Typical exam questions: find amplitude, frequency, period and phase from an expression; find which wave leads and by how much; compute RMS and average values of standard waveforms from the definition; and convert between peak, RMS and peak-to-peak values.

Recap: AC voltage in Bangladesh is a 50 Hz sinusoid, v = Vm sin(ωt + φ), with T = 20 ms and ω about 314 rad/s. Phase tells which wave leads. RMS, Vm/√2 for a sine, is the DC-equivalent heating value, and mains ratings like 220 to 230 V are RMS, so the peak is about 311 to 325 V. Form factor 1.11 and peak factor 1.414 describe the sine's shape. Next we learn the clever tool that makes AC circuit analysis almost as easy as DC: phasors and impedance.
key_points: AC follows v(t) = Vm sin(ωt + φ); ω = 2πf, T = 1/f.
Bangladesh mains: 50 Hz, T = 20 ms, ω ≈ 314 rad/s; voltage ratings (about 220-230 V) are RMS.
Phase difference tells which wave leads; compare only after writing both in the same form.
Full-cycle average of a sine is 0; half-cycle average = 2Vm/π ≈ 0.637Vm.
RMS = √(mean of v²): the DC value giving the same heating; for a sine Vrms = Vm/√2.
Form factor (sine) = 1.11; peak factor (sine) = √2 ≈ 1.414.
Square wave: Vrms = Vm; triangle: Vm/√3; half-wave rectified sine: Vm/2.
AC won for power because transformers change its voltage easily.
lessons.tip: Before comparing two sinusoids, rewrite both as positive-amplitude sines (or cosines); most phase errors come from skipping this step.
