lessons.title: Complex Numbers, Phasors and Impedance
lessons.content:
Imagine giving directions in a crowded market: "walk 30 steps east, then 40 steps north". A friend who knows geometry says, "or just walk 50 steps in a direction 53 degrees north of east". Both describe the same journey: one splits it into two perpendicular parts, the other gives one length and one angle. AC circuit analysis uses exactly this trick. Every sinusoidal voltage or current in a circuit has the same frequency, so the only things that differ are size and timing, that is, amplitude and phase. If we represent each sinusoid as an arrow with a length and an angle, called a phasor, then calculus turns into simple algebra, and all the DC methods we learned come back to life for AC.

Why we need a new tool: In an AC circuit with capacitors and inductors, the element equations involve derivatives: v = L di/dt and i = C dv/dt. Solving circuits by writing differential equations every time would be painful. But in steady state, with a sinusoidal source of one frequency, every voltage and current is a sinusoid of that same frequency. Only amplitudes and phases differ. Phasors exploit this to convert the differential equations into algebraic equations with complex numbers.

Complex numbers in rectangular form: A complex number is written z = a + jb, where a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, and j = √-1. Electrical engineers use j instead of i, since i is reserved for current. You can picture z as a point, or an arrow from the origin, on a plane with a horizontal real axis and a vertical imaginary axis. Example: z = 3 + j4 is the point 3 to the right and 4 up.

Complex numbers in polar form: The same arrow can be described by its length r, called the magnitude, and its angle θ from the positive real axis: z = r∠θ. Converting: r = √(a² + b²) and θ = arctan(b / a), adjusting the angle for the correct quadrant. Back again: a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ. Example: 3 + j4 has r = √(9 + 16) = 5 and θ = arctan(4/3), about 53.13°, so 3 + j4 = 5∠53.13°. Euler's formula, e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, connects the two: r∠θ is shorthand for r e^(jθ).

Doing arithmetic: Add and subtract in rectangular form: (3 + j4) + (1 - j2) = 4 + j2. Multiply and divide in polar form: multiply magnitudes and add angles; divide magnitudes and subtract angles. Example: (5∠53.13°) × (2∠-30°) = 10∠23.13°, and (5∠53.13°) / (2∠-30°) = 2.5∠83.13°. Two more useful facts: j = 1∠90°, so multiplying by j rotates an arrow by 90° anticlockwise; and 1/j = -j = 1∠-90°. The complex conjugate of a + jb is a - jb, which in polar form keeps r and flips the sign of θ.

The quadrant trap: A calculator's arctan only returns angles between -90° and +90°, so it cannot tell -3 + j4 from 3 - j4, since both have b/a = -4/3. Always sketch the point. -3 + j4 lies in the second quadrant, up and to the left, so its angle is 180° - 53.13° = 126.87°, giving 5∠126.87°. And -3 - j4 lies in the third quadrant, at -126.87° (or 233.13°). Many scientific calculators have a built-in rectangular-to-polar function that handles quadrants correctly; learn to use yours.

The phasor idea: A sinusoid v(t) = Vm cos(ωt + φ) is completely described, once ω is known, by its amplitude Vm and phase φ. So we represent it by the phasor V = Vm∠φ, a complex number. To go back, multiply by e^(jωt) and take the real part. Example: v(t) = 10 cos(314t + 30°) has phasor V = 10∠30°; i(t) = 2 cos(314t - 20°) has phasor I = 2∠-20°. If a sinusoid is given as a sine, convert first: sin(ωt + φ) = cos(ωt + φ - 90°). Some books use RMS values as phasor magnitudes instead of peak values; both work as long as you are consistent.

Picturing a phasor: Think of the phasor as an arrow that rotates anticlockwise at ω radians per second. Its shadow on the real axis traces out the cosine wave over time. All phasors in a circuit rotate together at the same speed, so their relative angles stay fixed. That is why we can freeze the picture at t = 0 and work with the arrows as if they were still. A drawing of several phasors on one plane is called a phasor diagram.

Calculus becomes algebra: The derivative of Vm cos(ωt + φ) is -ωVm sin(ωt + φ) = ωVm cos(ωt + φ + 90°). In phasor terms, differentiating multiplies the phasor by ω and rotates it by 90°, which is exactly multiplication by jω. So d/dt becomes jω, and integration becomes division by jω. This single fact turns the inductor and capacitor equations into Ohm's-law-like statements.

Impedance: Impedance Z is the ratio of the voltage phasor to the current phasor for an element: Z = V / I, measured in ohms. It is the AC generalisation of resistance and obeys Ohm's law in phasor form: V = I Z. For a resistor, Z_R = R, real and frequency-independent. For an inductor, v = L di/dt becomes V = jωL I, so Z_L = jωL. For a capacitor, i = C dv/dt becomes I = jωC V, so Z_C = 1 / (jωC) = -j / (ωC).

Reactance: The imaginary part of an impedance is called reactance, X. Inductive reactance is X_L = ωL, positive and growing with frequency. Capacitive reactance is usually written as a magnitude X_C = 1 / (ωC), shrinking with frequency, and the capacitor's impedance is then -jX_C. A general impedance is Z = R + jX, with resistance R as its real part and reactance X as its imaginary part. Example at 50 Hz (ω ≈ 314 rad/s): a 0.1 H inductor has X_L = 31.4 Ω; a 100 µF capacitor has X_C = 1 / (314 × 10^-4), about 31.8 Ω.

Frequency behaviour and DC: At DC, ω = 0. Then Z_L = 0, a short circuit, and Z_C is infinite, an open circuit, exactly the steady-state rules from lessons 15 and 16. At very high frequency, an inductor approaches an open circuit and a capacitor approaches a short circuit. This is why capacitors pass high-frequency signals and block DC, while inductors pass DC and block high frequencies, the basis of all filters.

Phase relationships, ELI the ICE man: In a resistor, voltage and current are in phase. In an inductor, Z_L = ωL∠90°, so the voltage leads the current by 90°. In a capacitor, Z_C = (1/ωC)∠-90°, so the current leads the voltage by 90°. A popular memory aid: "ELI the ICE man". In L, E (voltage) comes before I (current); in C, I comes before E. A phasor diagram shows these as arrows at right angles.

Admittance: The reciprocal of impedance is admittance, Y = 1 / Z, measured in siemens. Written Y = G + jB, its real part G is conductance and its imaginary part B is susceptance. For a resistor Y = 1/R, for an inductor Y = 1/(jωL) = -j/(ωL), and for a capacitor Y = jωC. Admittances in parallel add, just as conductances did, which makes parallel AC circuits easier.

Worked example, from time domain and back: A voltage v(t) = 20 cos(100t) V is applied across a 0.05 H inductor. Here ω = 100 rad/s, so Z_L = j × 100 × 0.05 = j5 Ω = 5∠90°. The voltage phasor is 20∠0°, so I = 20∠0° / 5∠90° = 4∠-90° A, and back in time i(t) = 4 cos(100t - 90°) = 4 sin(100t) A. If instead a 1 mF capacitor is used, Z_C = 1 / (j × 100 × 0.001) = -j10 Ω = 10∠-90°, so I = 2∠90° A and i(t) = 2 cos(100t + 90°) A. No derivatives were taken anywhere; the phasor method did the calculus for us.

Worked example, a series RL circuit: A 30 Ω resistor in series with an inductor of reactance 40 Ω at the source frequency. Z = 30 + j40 = 50∠53.13° Ω. Apply a source V = 100∠0° V. Then I = V / Z = (100∠0°) / (50∠53.13°) = 2∠-53.13° A. The current has magnitude 2 A and lags the voltage by 53.13°. The resistor voltage is 30 × 2 = 60 V in phase with I, and the inductor voltage is 40 × 2 = 80 V leading I by 90°. As phasors they add to 100 V, but as plain numbers 60 + 80 = 140, not 100. AC voltages add as arrows, not as numbers.

Worked example, a series RC circuit: A 6 Ω resistor in series with a capacitor of reactance 8 Ω. Z = 6 - j8 = 10∠-53.13° Ω. With V = 50∠0° V, I = 5∠53.13° A: the current leads the voltage, as expected for a capacitive circuit. The resistor's voltage is 30 V and the capacitor's 40 V, combining as perpendicular arrows into 50 V, a 3-4-5 triangle once again.

Real life example 1, why the fan capacitor works: In a ceiling fan, the auxiliary winding is placed in series with the capacitor, while the main winding is not. Because a capacitor's current leads its voltage, the auxiliary winding's current is shifted in time relative to the main winding's current. Two coils at different positions carrying currents shifted in phase create a rotating magnetic field, which gives the motor a direction to start turning. Phasors are the natural way to see and design this phase shift.

Real life example 2, a computer speaker crossover: Many two-way speakers have a small woofer for bass and a tweeter for treble. A capacitor in series with the tweeter has high reactance at low frequencies, blocking the bass that could damage it, and low reactance at high frequencies, letting treble through. An inductor in series with the woofer does the opposite. Using X_C = 1/(ωC) and X_L = ωL, designers choose values so the crossover happens at the right frequency.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students add magnitudes of phasors as if they were plain numbers, forget to convert sines to cosines before writing phasors, use degrees and radians inconsistently, mix up the signs of inductive and capacitive reactance, and forget to adjust arctan for the quadrant. Typical exam questions: convert between rectangular and polar forms, multiply and divide complex numbers, write the phasor of a sinusoid and back, compute the impedance of an element or series combination at a given frequency, and find current phasors with Ohm's law.

Recap: A complex number can be written a + jb or r∠θ; add in rectangular, multiply and divide in polar. A sinusoid Vm cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the phasor Vm∠φ, and d/dt becomes jω. Impedances: Z_R = R, Z_L = jωL, Z_C = 1/(jωC); V = IZ. Inductor voltage leads current by 90°, capacitor current leads voltage by 90°. Admittance Y = 1/Z. Next we use these tools to bring every DC method, from KVL to Thevenin, into AC.
key_points: Complex numbers: rectangular a + jb or polar r∠θ; add in rectangular, multiply/divide in polar.
A sinusoid Vm cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the phasor Vm∠φ; d/dt becomes jω.
Impedance Z = V/I: Z_R = R, Z_L = jωL, Z_C = 1/(jωC) = -j/(ωC).
Reactance: X_L = ωL grows with frequency; X_C = 1/(ωC) falls with frequency.
At DC an inductor is a short and a capacitor an open; at high frequency the reverse.
ELI the ICE man: inductor voltage leads current by 90°, capacitor current leads voltage by 90°.
Admittance Y = 1/Z = G + jB; admittances in parallel add.
AC voltages add as phasors (arrows), not as plain magnitudes.
lessons.tip: Practise complex arithmetic on your calculator until converting rectangular to polar takes seconds; every AC problem depends on it.

lessons.title: Sinusoidal Steady-State Analysis
lessons.content:
Learning a second language is hard at first, but once you know it, you can read all the same kinds of stories you already enjoy. Phasors are like a translation into a new language. Once a sinusoidal circuit is translated into phasors and impedances, every method you learned for DC circuits works again: Ohm's law, KCL and KVL, series and parallel combinations, voltage and current dividers, nodal and mesh analysis, superposition, source transformation, and Thevenin and Norton. The only difference is that the numbers are now complex. This lesson shows how to carry out that translation and apply each familiar tool in its new AC form.

What sinusoidal steady state means: When a linear circuit is driven by a sinusoidal source and has been running for a long time, any transients from switching have died out, as we saw in lessons 17 and 18. What remains is the steady-state response: every voltage and current is a sinusoid at the same frequency as the source. This condition is called sinusoidal steady state, and it describes almost all of the AC power you use: your fan, your fridge and your phone charger spend nearly all their time in it.

The translation recipe: Step 1, convert every source to a phasor, writing all sinusoids as cosines (or all as sines) first. Step 2, replace every element by its impedance at the source frequency: R stays R, L becomes jωL, C becomes 1/(jωC). Step 3, solve the circuit using any DC method, but with complex arithmetic. Step 4, convert the answer phasors back to time-domain sinusoids if needed. The circuit drawn with phasors and impedances is called the frequency-domain circuit.

Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws in phasor form: Ohm's law becomes V = I Z. KCL becomes "the phasor sum of currents entering a node is zero", and KVL becomes "the phasor sum of voltages around a loop is zero". These hold because adding sinusoids of the same frequency is equivalent to adding their phasors. Note that it is the phasors that add, not the magnitudes: the magnitudes of two element voltages in a loop may add up to much more than the source magnitude.

Series and parallel impedances: Impedances in series add, exactly like resistors: Z = Z1 + Z2 + ... Impedances in parallel combine by reciprocals: 1/Z = 1/Z1 + 1/Z2 + ..., or for two, Z = Z1 Z2 / (Z1 + Z2). Equivalently, admittances in parallel add. Voltage and current divider rules also carry over unchanged, with impedances in place of resistances.

Worked example 1, a series RLC circuit: R = 8 Ω, X_L = 10 Ω and X_C = 4 Ω in series, driven by V = 100∠0° V. Total Z = 8 + j10 - j4 = 8 + j6 = 10∠36.87° Ω. Current I = 100∠0° / 10∠36.87° = 10∠-36.87° A, lagging the voltage, so the circuit is inductive overall. Element voltages: V_R = 80∠-36.87° V, V_L = j10 × I = 100∠53.13° V, V_C = -j4 × I = 40∠-126.87° V. Notice V_L alone is 100 V, as large as the whole source, because V_L and V_C partly cancel. Adding the three phasors gives back exactly 100∠0°, which you can check on a calculator.

Inductive or capacitive overall: The sign of the total reactance tells you the character of a circuit. If the imaginary part of Z is positive, the circuit is inductive and current lags voltage. If it is negative, the circuit is capacitive and current leads voltage. If it is zero, the circuit is purely resistive at that frequency and current is in phase with voltage, a special condition called resonance, the subject of lesson 23.

Worked example 2, a parallel circuit: A 10 Ω resistor in parallel with a capacitor of reactance 10 Ω, across V = 100∠0° V. I_R = 100 / 10 = 10∠0° A. I_C = 100∠0° / 10∠-90° = 10∠90° A. Total current, by KCL with phasors: 10 + j10 = 14.14∠45° A. The magnitudes 10 and 10 do not add to 20; they add as perpendicular arrows to 14.14. The equivalent impedance is 100∠0° / 14.14∠45° = 7.07∠-45° Ω, which matches the product-over-sum formula: (10 × -j10) / (10 - j10).

Worked example 3, series-parallel: A 60∠0° V source feeds Z1 = 1 + j5 Ω in series with a parallel pair of 10 Ω and -j10 Ω. The parallel pair is (10 × -j10) / (10 - j10) = 5 - j5 Ω. Total Z = 1 + j5 + 5 - j5 = 6 Ω, purely resistive, so the source current is 10∠0° A, in phase with the source. The voltage across the parallel pair is 10 × (5 - j5) = 70.7∠-45° V. Then the resistor carries 7.07∠-45° A and the capacitor 7.07∠45° A; their phasor sum is 10∠0° A, as KCL requires. A circuit full of reactive parts can still look purely resistive from the source.

Nodal and mesh analysis with phasors: Both methods work exactly as in lessons 10 and 11. In nodal analysis, write KCL at each node with currents (Vk - Vj) / Z for each branch, or use admittances in the matrix. In mesh analysis, write KVL around each mesh with impedances. Supernodes, supermeshes and dependent sources are handled the same way. The equations simply have complex coefficients, and solving a 2 by 2 complex system by hand takes care; this is where a calculator with complex-number mode is a great help.

Worked example 4, AC nodal analysis: A 10∠0° V source in series with 2 Ω feeds node 1. Node 1 has a capacitor of -j2 Ω to ground and an inductor of j2 Ω to node 2. Node 2 has a 2 Ω resistor to ground. KCL at node 1: (V1 - 10)/2 + V1/(-j2) + (V1 - V2)/(j2) = 0. Since 1/(-j2) = j0.5 and 1/(j2) = -j0.5, this simplifies to 0.5V1 + j0.5V2 = 5; the capacitor and inductor terms on V1 cancel. KCL at node 2: (V2 - V1)/(j2) + V2/2 = 0, which becomes j0.5V1 + (0.5 - j0.5)V2 = 0. Solving gives V1 = 6 - j2 V, about 6.32∠-18.4° V, and V2 = 2 - j4 V, about 4.47∠-63.4° V. Substituting back into both equations confirms the result. The steps are exactly those of lesson 10; only the arithmetic is complex.

Thevenin and Norton in AC: Any linear AC circuit seen from two terminals can be replaced by a Thevenin voltage phasor V_Th in series with a Thevenin impedance Z_Th, or by a Norton current phasor I_N in parallel with Z_N = Z_Th. Example: a 20∠0° V source in series with 4 Ω feeds node a, which connects to ground through an inductor of j4 Ω. V_Th is the divider voltage: 20 × j4 / (4 + j4) = 14.14∠45° V. Z_Th is 4 in parallel with j4: (4 × j4) / (4 + j4) = 2 + j2 Ω.

Maximum power transfer for AC: For AC, the load that receives maximum average power is the complex conjugate of the Thevenin impedance: Z_L = Z_Th*, so its reactance cancels the source's reactance, and its resistance matches the source's resistance. The maximum average power is |V_Th|² / (8 R_Th) with peak phasors, or |V_Th|² / (4 R_Th) with RMS phasors. For the example above, if the 20 V is an RMS value, the best load is 2 - j2 Ω and P_max = 14.14² / (4 × 2) = 200 / 8 = 25 W.

Superposition and source transformation in AC: Source transformation works with impedances: a voltage source V_s in series with Z equals a current source V_s / Z in parallel with Z. Superposition also works, and it becomes essential when sources have different frequencies, because then a single frequency-domain circuit is impossible: each frequency gives different impedances. You must solve one frequency-domain circuit per frequency, convert each answer back to the time domain, and only then add the time-domain sinusoids. Adding phasors of different frequencies is a classic serious mistake.

Phasor diagrams as a check: Sketching the phasors for a solved circuit is a powerful sanity check. In a series circuit, start with the current as the reference arrow; draw V_R along it, V_L at +90° and V_C at -90°, and check that they add tip to tail to the source voltage. In a parallel circuit, take the voltage as reference and draw the branch currents. A diagram that does not close shows immediately that a sign or angle is wrong.

Real life example 1, a fan regulator and a capacitor in a dimmer box: Some older fan regulators in Bangladeshi homes worked by adding series reactance, using a choke (an inductor) or capacitors with a selector switch, to reduce the voltage reaching the fan. Each switch position changes the total series impedance, and so the current and the fan speed. A capacitor-based regulator wastes little energy compared with a resistor-based one, because an ideal reactance stores and returns energy instead of burning it. Analysing such a regulator is a direct application of series impedance and voltage division.

Real life example 2, a computer power supply's input filter: Inside desktop power supplies there is an input filter made of inductors and capacitors, designed to stop high-frequency noise from the computer from flowing back into the house wiring and to block noise from the mains. Engineers analyse it in sinusoidal steady state at many frequencies: at 50 Hz the filter must pass the power almost untouched, while at a few hundred kilohertz it must present large impedance or a low-impedance path to ground. The same phasor methods from this lesson are used, just repeated across frequencies.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students add magnitudes instead of phasors, forget to compute impedances at the actual source frequency, mix peak and RMS phasors within one problem, and add phasors from sources of different frequencies. Another error is forgetting to convert sines to cosines before writing phasors. Typical exam questions: find the current and all element voltages in a series RLC circuit and draw the phasor diagram; analyse a series-parallel AC circuit; solve an AC circuit by nodal or mesh analysis; find an AC Thevenin equivalent and the load for maximum power; and use superposition with sources of two different frequencies.

Recap: In sinusoidal steady state, translate sources to phasors and elements to impedances, then use every DC method with complex numbers: Ohm's law V = IZ, KVL, KCL, series and parallel impedances, dividers, nodal, mesh, superposition, source transformation, Thevenin and Norton. The total reactance's sign tells whether a circuit is inductive or capacitive. AC maximum power needs Z_L = Z_Th*. Sources at different frequencies need superposition in the time domain. Next we look at power in AC circuits, where phase angles change how much useful power actually flows.
key_points: In sinusoidal steady state all voltages and currents are sinusoids at the source frequency.
Recipe: sources to phasors, elements to impedances, solve with complex numbers, convert back.
Ohm's law V = IZ; KCL and KVL hold for phasor sums, not magnitudes.
Series impedances add; parallel combine by reciprocals (admittances add); dividers carry over.
Positive total reactance: inductive, current lags; negative: capacitive, current leads.
Nodal, mesh, Thevenin and Norton all work with complex impedances.
AC maximum power: Z_L = Z_Th*.
Sources of different frequencies: superposition, adding results in the time domain.

lessons.title: AC Power and Power Factor
lessons.content:
Order a glass of sugarcane juice from a roadside stall on a hot afternoon. The glass is full, but part of it is foam. You pay for the whole glass, yet only the liquid part actually quenches your thirst. AC power has a very similar story. When voltage and current are out of phase, the source pushes energy into the load during part of each cycle and gets some of it back during another part. The useful part, the "juice", does real work like turning a fan or heating a kettle. The part that just sloshes back and forth, the "foam", still loads the wires and generators without doing useful work. This lesson gives each part its proper name and shows how engineers reduce the foam.

Instantaneous power: At every instant, the power delivered to an element is p(t) = v(t) × i(t), just as in DC. For sinusoidal v = Vm cos(ωt + θv) and i = Im cos(ωt + θi), a trigonometric identity gives p(t) = ½ Vm Im cos(θv - θi) + ½ Vm Im cos(2ωt + θv + θi). The first part is constant; the second part oscillates at twice the source frequency, 100 Hz for Bangladeshi mains. So instantaneous power pulses up and down, and when voltage and current have opposite signs, it is negative, meaning energy is flowing back from the load to the source.

Average power, also called real or active power: Averaging p(t) over a full cycle removes the oscillating part and leaves P = ½ Vm Im cos θ, where θ = θv - θi is the phase difference between voltage and current. In RMS terms, P = Vrms Irms cos θ. The unit is the watt (W). This is the power that is actually converted into heat, light, motion or computation, and it is what your electricity meter counts, in kilowatt-hours, for billing a household.

Power in R, L and C: For a resistor, θ = 0 and cos θ = 1, so P = Vrms Irms = Irms² R = Vrms² / R, all of it absorbed. For an ideal inductor, θ = +90°, and for an ideal capacitor, θ = -90°; in both cases cos θ = 0 and the average power is zero. Inductors and capacitors store energy during one quarter of a cycle and return it during the next. A useful consequence: in any circuit, the total average power equals the sum of Irms² R over all the resistors, since the reactive elements contribute nothing on average.

Reactive power: The part of the power that oscillates between the source and the reactive elements is measured by reactive power, Q = Vrms Irms sin θ. Its unit is the volt-ampere reactive (VAR). Q is positive for an inductive load, where current lags voltage, and negative for a capacitive load, where current leads. Reactive power does no net work, but the current that carries it still flows through wires and transformers, causing real I²R losses and taking up their capacity.

Apparent power: The simple product of RMS voltage and RMS current, S = Vrms Irms, is called apparent power and is measured in volt-amperes (VA). It is what the load "appears" to draw if you only look at a voltmeter and an ammeter. Generators, transformers, UPS units and IPS units are rated in VA or kVA, not in watts, because their heating and capacity depend on the current they must carry, whatever the phase. That is why an IPS might say "1000 VA" but warn that it can supply only about 600 to 800 W of real load.

Complex power and the power triangle: All three powers fit together in one complex number, the complex power S = Vrms × Irms*, where Irms* is the complex conjugate of the current phasor. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q: S = P + jQ, with magnitude |S| = √(P² + Q²). Drawn as a right triangle, P is the horizontal side, Q the vertical side, S the hypotenuse, and the angle between P and S is θ. This picture is called the power triangle, and most AC power problems are solved by drawing it.

Power factor: The ratio of real power to apparent power is the power factor: pf = P / S = cos θ. It ranges from 0 to 1. A pure resistor has pf = 1. A motor might have pf around 0.8. The power factor is described as lagging when current lags voltage (inductive loads, the common case) and leading when current leads (capacitive loads). The angle θ is often called the power factor angle, and for a passive load it equals the angle of the load's impedance.

Worked example 1: A series load of R = 30 Ω and X_L = 40 Ω is connected to 100 V RMS. Z = 50∠53.13° Ω, so Irms = 2 A lagging the voltage by 53.13°. P = Irms² R = 4 × 30 = 120 W. Q = Irms² X_L = 4 × 40 = 160 VAR. S = Vrms Irms = 100 × 2 = 200 VA, and indeed √(120² + 160²) = 200. The power factor is 120 / 200 = 0.6 lagging. Only 60 percent of the volt-amperes delivered become useful power.

Complex power straight from phasors: The same answer comes out in one line with S = V I*. With V = 100∠0° V RMS and I = 2∠-53.13° A RMS, the conjugate is I* = 2∠+53.13°, so S = 100 × 2∠(0° + 53.13°) = 200∠53.13° VA = 120 + j160 VA. The real part is P = 120 W and the imaginary part is Q = +160 VAR, positive because the load is inductive. Forgetting the conjugate would flip the sign of Q, which is why the formula insists on I*.

Worked example 2, a factory motor: A motor runs on 230 V RMS and draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA. P = 2300 × 0.8 = 1840 W. Since sin θ = 0.6 when cos θ = 0.8, Q = 2300 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR. The supply company must provide 10 A of current even though, at unity power factor, the same 1840 W would need only 1840 / 230 = 8 A.

Why low power factor is a problem: For the same real power, a lower power factor means more current. More current means bigger I²R losses in cables and transformers, larger voltage drops along the lines, and more of the generator and transformer capacity used up. For a single household fan this hardly matters, but for a factory with hundreds of motors or for the whole national grid it matters a lot. In many countries, including Bangladesh, large industrial customers can be charged extra when their power factor falls below a set limit.

Power factor correction: Since most industrial loads are inductive (positive Q), we can cancel part of their reactive power by connecting capacitors in parallel, which supply negative Q. The real power P stays the same, but the total Q drops, so S and the line current drop. The capacitor's reactive power needed to move from angle θ1 to θ2 is Qc = P (tan θ1 - tan θ2), and the capacitance is C = Qc / (ω Vrms²).

Correction worked example: Correct the 1840 W motor above from pf 0.8 to pf 0.95. tan θ1 = 0.75 and tan θ2 = tan(arccos 0.95), about 0.329. Qc = 1840 × (0.75 - 0.329), about 775 VAR. With ω = 2π × 50, about 314 rad/s, and Vrms = 230 V, C = 775 / (314 × 230²), about 46.6 µF. After correction, S = 1840 / 0.95, about 1937 VA, and the current falls from 10 A to about 8.4 A. The motor itself does not notice anything; the savings are in the supply system.

Conservation of complex power: In any circuit, the complex power supplied by the sources equals the sum of complex powers absorbed by all the elements. Both real and reactive powers balance separately. This is the AC version of the power check we used in DC, and it is very useful: total P equals the sum of P of each load, and total Q equals the sum of Q of each load, so for several loads in parallel you can simply add their P values and their Q values, then rebuild the power triangle. Apparent powers, however, do not add directly.

Combining loads example: A workshop has a heater taking 2000 W at unity pf and a motor taking 1840 W and 1380 VAR. Total P = 3840 W, total Q = 1380 VAR, total S = √(3840² + 1380²), about 4080 VA, and the overall pf is 3840 / 4080, about 0.94 lagging. The resistive heater has improved the overall power factor simply by adding real power without reactive power.

Real life example 1, the IPS rating at home: A family in Mirpur buys an IPS labelled 1000 VA and plans to run fans, lights, a TV and a fridge during load-shedding. The fridge compressor and fans are inductive, with power factors below 1, while LED lights with cheap drivers can be capacitive or distorted. The family must check both the total watts and the total VA, because the inverter's transistors and transformer heat up according to current, not watts. Understanding VA versus W explains why an IPS can overload even when the wattage seems fine.

Real life example 2, capacitor banks at factories and substations: Garment factories in Gazipur and Narayanganj run thousands of sewing machine motors. Their electrical rooms usually contain automatic power factor correction panels: banks of capacitors switched in steps by a controller that measures the power factor continuously. Power substations on the national grid also use capacitor banks for the same reason. These are large real-world versions of the 46.6 µF calculation above.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students multiply peak values without the factor ½ (or mix peak and RMS), forget to use the conjugate of current in S = V I*, add apparent powers directly, and confuse leading with lagging. Another mistake is thinking a capacitor bank changes the real power drawn by a motor; it changes only Q and the line current. Typical exam questions: find P, Q, S and pf for a load; draw the power triangle; compute complex power from phasors; combine several loads; and find the capacitance needed to correct the power factor to a target value.

Recap: Instantaneous power p = vi pulses at twice the supply frequency. Real power P = Vrms Irms cos θ (W) does useful work; reactive power Q = Vrms Irms sin θ (VAR) sloshes back and forth; apparent power S = Vrms Irms (VA) sets equipment size. Complex power S = V I* = P + jQ forms the power triangle, and pf = cos θ. Low pf means more current for the same work, so industry adds parallel capacitors: Qc = P(tan θ1 - tan θ2). Next we study what happens when inductive and capacitive reactances exactly cancel: resonance.
key_points: Instantaneous power p = vi oscillates at twice the supply frequency.
Real power P = Vrms Irms cos θ (W) does useful work; ideal L and C absorb zero average power.
Reactive power Q = Vrms Irms sin θ (VAR): positive for inductive, negative for capacitive loads.
Apparent power S = Vrms Irms (VA) sizes generators, transformers and IPS units.
Complex power S = V I* = P + jQ; the power triangle links P, Q, S and θ.
Power factor pf = P/S = cos θ, lagging for inductive and leading for capacitive loads.
PF correction with parallel capacitors: Qc = P(tan θ1 - tan θ2), C = Qc/(ωV²).
P and Q add across loads; S does not add directly.
lessons.tip: Draw the power triangle for every AC power question before calculating; it shows instantly which formula links the numbers you have.

lessons.title: Resonance, Filters and Frequency Response
lessons.content:
Push a child on a swing at random moments and not much happens. But push at exactly the swing's natural rhythm, and even small pushes build up into big, high swings. That special rhythm is the swing's resonant frequency. Circuits with an inductor and a capacitor have a resonant frequency too. Drive them at that frequency and something dramatic happens: the inductor's and capacitor's reactances cancel, the current can become very large, and the voltages across L and C can grow far larger than the source voltage. Engineers use this effect to pick one radio station out of hundreds, to build filters that let some frequencies through and block others, and to measure and generate precise signals.

Frequency response: So far we have analysed circuits at one frequency. But reactances change with frequency: X_L = ωL grows, X_C = 1/(ωC) shrinks. So a circuit's behaviour depends on the frequency of the signal. The frequency response of a circuit describes how its output, compared with its input, varies as frequency is swept from very low to very high. It is usually described by a transfer function H(ω) = output phasor / input phasor, a complex number with a magnitude and a phase at each frequency.

Series resonance: Consider R, L and C in series. The impedance is Z = R + j(ωL - 1/(ωC)). At one special frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal and cancel: ωL = 1/(ωC). Solving gives the resonant frequency ω0 = 1/√(LC), or in hertz f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). This is the same ω0 we met in second-order circuits in lesson 18, where it described natural ringing; here it describes forced, steady-state behaviour.

What happens at series resonance: At ω0, Z = R, purely resistive and at its minimum value. So the current is at its maximum, I = V/R, and it is in phase with the source voltage: the power factor is 1. Below ω0 the circuit is capacitive (current leads), and above ω0 it is inductive (current lags). Example: L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF give ω0 = 1/√(10^-8) = 10,000 rad/s, so f0 is about 1592 Hz. With R = 10 Ω and a 1 V source, the current at resonance is 1/10 = 0.1 A.

Voltage magnification and quality factor: At resonance the inductor voltage is I × ω0L and the capacitor voltage is I × 1/(ω0C), equal in size and opposite in phase, so they cancel in the loop. Each can be much larger than the source voltage. Their ratio to the source voltage is the quality factor: Q = ω0L / R = 1 / (ω0 C R) = (1/R)√(L/C). In the example, Q = (10,000 × 0.01) / 10 = 10, so the inductor and the capacitor each have 10 V across them while the source supplies only 1 V. This "magnification" is why components in resonant circuits need voltage ratings well above the supply.

Bandwidth and half-power frequencies: As frequency moves away from ω0, the current falls. The half-power frequencies ω1 and ω2 are where the current has fallen to 1/√2 of its maximum, so the power in R is half its maximum. The bandwidth is BW = ω2 - ω1, and for a series RLC it equals R/L in rad/s. It is also related to Q by BW = ω0 / Q. In the example, BW = 10 / 0.01 = 1000 rad/s, about 159 Hz. For a high-Q circuit, ω1 and ω2 sit roughly symmetrically at ω0 ± BW/2, and in all cases ω0 = √(ω1 ω2), the geometric mean.

Exact half-power frequencies: For a series RLC, setting the current to 1/√2 of its peak gives ω1,2 = ∓R/(2L) + √((R/(2L))² + 1/(LC)). In our example, R/(2L) = 500 and 1/(LC) = 10^8, so the square root is √(100,250,000), about 10,012.5. Then ω1 is about 9512.5 rad/s and ω2 about 10,512.5 rad/s, roughly 1514 Hz and 1673 Hz. Their difference is exactly 1000 rad/s, the bandwidth, and √(ω1 ω2) is exactly 10,000 rad/s, the resonant frequency, confirming both formulas. Notice ω0 is not exactly halfway between them, only close to it, because Q = 10 is moderate.

Q as an energy ratio: There is a deeper definition of Q that works for any resonant system: Q = 2π × (maximum energy stored) / (energy lost per cycle). A high-Q circuit stores a lot of energy compared with what it loses each cycle, so it rings for many cycles if left alone, connecting back to the underdamped circuits of lesson 18. Quartz crystals used for timing in computers, phones and wristwatches behave like resonant circuits with Q values in the tens of thousands or more, which is why they keep such accurate time.

Selectivity: Q measures how sharp the resonance is. A high Q means a narrow bandwidth: the circuit responds strongly only to frequencies very near ω0 and ignores the rest. A low Q means a broad, gentle peak. Lowering R in a series circuit raises Q and sharpens the peak. Radio receivers need high selectivity to separate stations that are close together in frequency, while some audio filters deliberately use low Q for a smooth response.

Parallel resonance: Now put R, L and C in parallel, driven by a current source. The admittance is Y = 1/R + j(ωC - 1/(ωL)). The susceptances cancel at the same ω0 = 1/√(LC). At that frequency, Y = 1/R is at its minimum, so the impedance is at its maximum, equal to R, and the voltage across the circuit peaks. The inductor and capacitor currents are each Q times the source current, circulating between L and C while the source supplies only the small current through R. For parallel RLC, Q = R / (ω0 L) = ω0 R C and BW = 1 / (RC). Notice the dual pattern: in parallel, a larger R gives a higher Q.

Filters: A filter is a circuit designed to pass some frequencies and reject others. A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones. A high-pass filter does the opposite. A band-pass filter passes a band around a centre frequency, and a band-stop (or notch) filter blocks a band. Filters built only from R, L and C are called passive filters; filters that also use amplifiers are active filters, studied in electronics.

The RC low-pass filter: Put R in series and take the output across C. By the voltage divider with impedances, H(ω) = (1/(jωC)) / (R + 1/(jωC)) = 1 / (1 + jωRC). At low frequency, H is close to 1: the capacitor is nearly open and the signal passes. At high frequency, H becomes small: the capacitor is nearly a short and grounds the signal. The cutoff frequency, where |H| = 1/√2, is ωc = 1/(RC). Example: R = 1 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF give ωc = 10,000 rad/s, so fc is about 1592 Hz. At the cutoff, the output phase lags the input by 45 degrees.

The RC high-pass filter: Swap the positions and take the output across R: H(ω) = jωRC / (1 + jωRC). Now low frequencies, including DC, are blocked by the capacitor, and high frequencies pass. The cutoff is again ωc = 1/(RC). This is the circuit used as a "coupling capacitor" in amplifiers to pass an audio signal while blocking a DC level. RL versions also exist, with cutoff ωc = R/L: output across the inductor gives a high-pass, output across the resistor gives a low-pass.

Band-pass and band-stop with RLC: Take a series RLC circuit and use the voltage across R as output. At resonance, all the source voltage appears across R, so H = 1; far below or above, the current and therefore the output fall. That is a band-pass filter, centred at ω0, with bandwidth R/L. Take the output across the L and C together instead, and at resonance their voltages cancel to zero while other frequencies pass: that is a band-stop filter. Such a notch can remove an unwanted 50 Hz hum from a sensitive measurement.

Decibels and Bode plots: Because responses span many orders of magnitude, engineers express gain in decibels: gain in dB = 20 log10 |H|. A gain of 1 is 0 dB, 1/√2 is about -3 dB, 0.1 is -20 dB and 0.01 is -40 dB. That is why cutoff frequencies are called -3 dB points. A Bode plot draws the gain in dB against frequency on a logarithmic scale. For a first-order low-pass filter, the plot is flat at 0 dB below ωc and falls at 20 dB per decade (each tenfold increase in frequency) above it.

Real life example 1, tuning a radio: An AM radio's tuning circuit is an LC resonant circuit, often with a variable capacitor. To tune to a station near 1 MHz with a 100 µH coil, you need C = 1 / ((2π × 10^6)² × 100 × 10^-6), about 253 pF. Turning the tuning knob changes C, which moves the resonance across the band. Every station's signal reaches the antenna at once, but only the one at the circuit's resonant frequency produces a large response. FM receivers, working between 88 and 108 MHz, use the same principle with much smaller L and C values.

Real life example 2, filters in phones and audio: Your phone contains many filters: they separate the frequency bands used for mobile data, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and they keep the radio transmitter from leaking into the receiver. In audio, the bass and treble controls of a speaker system are adjustable filters, and the crossover from lesson 20 is a pair of low-pass and high-pass filters. Even the ECG machines in Bangladeshi hospitals use notch filters to remove the 50 Hz interference picked up from the mains wiring.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students use hertz and rad/s interchangeably, forget that Q and BW formulas differ between series and parallel circuits, believe the source voltage cannot be exceeded inside a passive circuit, and confuse which element's voltage gives a low-pass versus a high-pass filter. Typical exam questions: find ω0, Q, bandwidth and half-power frequencies for a series or parallel RLC; find the current and element voltages at resonance; derive the transfer function and cutoff frequency of an RC or RL filter; and sketch the magnitude response or a simple Bode plot.

Recap: Resonance occurs at ω0 = 1/√(LC), where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel. Series resonance gives minimum impedance R, maximum current, and L and C voltages magnified by Q = ω0L/R; parallel resonance gives maximum impedance R and Q = R/(ω0L). Bandwidth is ω0/Q. RC and RL circuits make first-order low-pass and high-pass filters with cutoff 1/(RC) or R/L, and RLC circuits make band-pass and band-stop filters. Next we see what happens when two coils share a magnetic field: coupled circuits and transformers.
key_points: Resonance at ω0 = 1/√(LC) (f0 = 1/(2π√(LC))) where X_L = X_C.
Series resonance: Z = R (minimum), current maximum and in phase, pf = 1.
Series Q = ω0L/R = (1/R)√(L/C); V_L = V_C = Q × source voltage at resonance.
Bandwidth BW = ω0/Q (= R/L for series); ω0 = √(ω1ω2).
Parallel resonance: Z = R (maximum), Q = R/(ω0L) = ω0RC, BW = 1/(RC).
RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + jωRC), cutoff ωc = 1/(RC); swap for high-pass; RL cutoff = R/L.
Series RLC output across R = band-pass; across L and C together = band-stop (notch).
Gain in dB = 20 log10|H|; the cutoff is the -3 dB point; first-order roll-off is 20 dB/decade.
lessons.tip: Keep a two-column summary of series versus parallel resonance (Z at resonance, Q, BW); exam questions love swapping them.

lessons.title: Magnetically Coupled Circuits and Transformers
lessons.content:
Put two spinning tops close together on a smooth floor and they hardly affect each other. But place two coils of wire close together, run a changing current through one, and something surprising happens: a voltage appears in the other coil, even though no wire connects them. The magnetic field of the first coil passes through the second and "talks" to it. This invisible link is called magnetic coupling, and it powers some of the most important machines in the world: the transformers on every electric pole in Bangladesh, the chargers that turn 220 V into a few volts, and the wireless charging pad that charges a phone without a cable.

Self-inductance, a reminder: In lesson 16 we saw that a coil's own changing current induces a voltage in itself: v = L di/dt. That L is more precisely called self-inductance. When two coils are near each other, each one also feels the magnetic field of the other. The effect of one coil's current on the other coil's voltage is described by a new quantity: mutual inductance.

Mutual inductance: If current i1 flows in coil 1 and changes with time, a voltage is induced in coil 2: v2 = M di1/dt. Similarly, a changing current in coil 2 induces v1 = M di2/dt in coil 1. M is the mutual inductance, measured in henries, and for linear coils it is the same in both directions. Example: if M = 0.1 H and the current in coil 1 rises at 50 A/s, the open-circuit voltage induced in coil 2 is 0.1 × 50 = 5 V. Just like self-inductance, mutual inductance responds only to changing current; a steady DC current induces nothing in the other coil.

The coupling coefficient: How strongly two coils are linked is measured by the coupling coefficient k = M / √(L1 L2). It ranges from 0 (no coupling, coils far apart or at right angles) to 1 (perfect coupling, all the flux of one coil passes through the other). Coils wound on the same iron core can reach k very close to 1; loosely placed air coils may have k of 0.1 or less. Example: L1 = 4 H, L2 = 9 H and M = 3 H give k = 3 / √36 = 0.5. Since k can never exceed 1, M can never exceed √(L1 L2).

The dot convention: Whether the mutual voltage adds to or subtracts from the self-induced voltage depends on how the coils are wound, which a circuit symbol cannot show. So engineers mark one end of each coil with a dot. The rule is: if the current enters the dotted terminal of one coil, the mutual voltage it induces in the other coil is positive at that coil's dotted terminal. In practice: when both currents enter (or both leave) the dotted terminals, the mutual term has the same sign as the self term; when one enters a dot and the other leaves a dot, the mutual term has the opposite sign.

Coupled coils in series: Two coupled coils in series behave like one inductor whose value depends on how they are connected. Series aiding, where the current enters both dotted terminals, gives L = L1 + L2 + 2M. Series opposing, where the current enters one dot and leaves the other, gives L = L1 + L2 - 2M. Example: L1 = 4 H, L2 = 9 H and M = 3 H give 19 H aiding and 7 H opposing. Measuring both is a standard lab method for finding M: M = (L_aiding - L_opposing) / 4 = (19 - 7) / 4 = 3 H.

Energy in coupled coils: The total energy stored in two coupled coils carrying i1 and i2 is W = ½ L1 i1² + ½ L2 i2² ± M i1 i2, with a plus sign when both currents enter dotted terminals and a minus sign otherwise. Because stored energy can never be negative, this formula leads directly to the limit M ≤ √(L1 L2), the reason k ≤ 1.

Coupled circuits with phasors: In AC steady state, each coil's voltage has a self term and a mutual term: V1 = jωL1 I1 ± jωM I2 and V2 = jωL2 I2 ± jωM I1, with signs from the dot rule. Mesh analysis is the natural method, because the mutual terms depend on currents. In each mesh equation, include the extra voltage jωM times the other coil's current, with the right sign. The rest of the analysis is ordinary phasor algebra from lesson 21.

Worked example, a linear transformer: A 100∠0° V source drives a primary coil with ωL1 = 10 Ω. The secondary coil has ωL2 = 40 Ω and feeds a 30 Ω load; the mutual reactance is ωM = 10 Ω, so k = 10 / √(10 × 40) = 0.5. With both mesh currents entering the dotted terminals, the secondary mesh gives 0 = (30 + j40) I2 + j10 I1, so I2 = -j10 I1 / (30 + j40). Substituting into the primary mesh, 100 = j10 I1 + j10 I2, the source sees Zin = j10 + 10² / (30 + j40) = j10 + 1.2 - j1.6 = 1.2 + j8.4 Ω. The extra term (ωM)² / Z22 is called the reflected impedance of the secondary. Then I1 is about 11.8∠-81.9° A, I2 about 2.36 A, and the load power 2.36² × 30, about 167 W, which equals the real power entering the primary, 100 × 11.8 × cos 81.9°. Power balances exactly.

The ideal transformer: A transformer is two coupled coils, the primary (input) and the secondary (output), wound on a common core. An ideal transformer is a model with perfect coupling (k = 1), no losses and very large inductances. Its behaviour is then set entirely by the turns ratio. With N1 turns on the primary and N2 on the secondary, V2 / V1 = N2 / N1 and I2 / I1 = N1 / N2 in magnitude. The voltage goes up by the turns ratio and the current goes down by the same ratio, so power in equals power out: V1 I1 = V2 I2.

Step-up and step-down: If N2 > N1, the transformer is step-up: the voltage increases and the current decreases. If N2 < N1, it is step-down. Example: a transformer to get 12 V from 230 V needs N1 / N2 = 230 / 12, about 19.2. If the 12 V secondary feeds a 6 Ω load, I2 = 12 / 6 = 2 A and the load gets 24 W. The primary current is about 2 / 19.2, roughly 0.104 A, and 230 × 0.104 is about 24 W. The power is the same on both sides; only the balance between voltage and current changes.

Reflected impedance: Seen from the primary, a load ZL on the secondary looks like a different impedance: Zin = ZL × (N1 / N2)². In the example, 6 Ω on the secondary appears as 6 × 19.2², about 2200 Ω, on the primary, and indeed 230 V / 2200 Ω gives about 0.104 A. This is how transformers are used for impedance matching, connecting back to maximum power transfer in lesson 14: to make an 8 Ω speaker look like 800 Ω to an amplifier, you need (N1/N2)² = 100, so a 10:1 turns ratio.

Why transformers need AC: A transformer works through a changing magnetic flux. Connect a DC voltage to the primary and, after an initial transient, the current becomes steady, the flux stops changing, and the secondary voltage is zero. Worse, with only the winding resistance to limit it, the primary current can become very large and burn the coil. This is the deep reason AC won for power distribution: transformers make changing voltage levels simple, efficient and reliable.

Real transformers: Real transformers have winding resistance, causing copper losses that grow with I²; core losses from hysteresis and eddy currents, which is why cores use thin laminated sheets; leakage flux that does not link both coils; and a magnetising current that flows even with no load. Despite these, large power transformers are extremely efficient, often well above 95 percent and close to 99 percent for big units. Small cheap ones are less efficient, which is why an old-style transformer charger left plugged in with nothing connected gets slightly warm.

Isolation and safety: Because a transformer connects primary and secondary only through magnetic flux, there is no direct electrical connection between them. This isolation is a major safety feature: in a well-designed charger, the low-voltage side you touch is isolated from the dangerous mains side. Modern switching chargers still use a small high-frequency transformer for exactly this reason. Cheap, poorly made chargers that skimp on isolation can be dangerous.

Real life example 1, the pole transformer outside your home: Power stations in Bangladesh generate at medium voltages, step up to transmission voltages such as 132 kV, 230 kV or 400 kV, and substations step them down again. In towns and cities, distribution lines commonly run at 11 kV, and the grey transformer on a pole or platform near your building steps that down to about 400 V between phases and about 230 V between a phase and neutral for homes. When that transformer is overloaded on a hot summer evening, its protection may trip, and a whole lane loses power at once.

Real life example 2, wireless charging: A wireless charging pad contains a flat coil driven with high-frequency AC, and the phone contains another flat coil. Placed together, they form a loosely coupled transformer with an air gap. The phone's coil picks up a voltage by mutual inductance, which is then rectified to charge the battery. Because coupling falls quickly with distance and misalignment, the phone must sit in the right spot, and some energy is lost as heat, which is why wireless charging is usually slower and warmer than cable charging.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students ignore the dot convention or apply it backwards, forget the mutual term in mesh equations, use the turns ratio upside down for current, and apply transformer equations to DC. Another frequent error is writing reflected impedance with the turns ratio not squared. Typical exam questions: find k from L1, L2 and M; find the equivalent inductance of coupled coils in series aiding and opposing; write mesh equations for a coupled circuit; find voltages, currents and power in an ideal transformer circuit; and choose a turns ratio for impedance matching.

Recap: A changing current in one coil induces a voltage in a nearby coil through mutual inductance M, with coupling coefficient k = M/√(L1L2) ≤ 1. Dots tell whether the mutual voltage adds or subtracts. Series aiding gives L1 + L2 + 2M, opposing L1 + L2 - 2M. An ideal transformer obeys V2/V1 = N2/N1, I2/I1 = N1/N2, power in = power out, and reflects an impedance by (N1/N2)². Transformers need AC, provide isolation, and make power distribution possible. In the last lesson we put it all together with three-phase power, house wiring and electrical safety.

Coupling coefficient k = M/√(L1L2), between 0 and 1.
Dot convention: both currents into dots → mutual term same sign as self term; otherwise opposite.
Series aiding: L1 + L2 + 2M; series opposing: L1 + L2 - 2M.
Ideal transformer: V2/V1 = N2/N1, I2/I1 = N1/N2, power in = power out.
Reflected impedance: Zin = ZL(N1/N2)²; used for impedance matching.
Transformers need changing flux (AC); they also provide electrical isolation.
Bangladesh distribution: 11 kV lines stepped down to about 400/230 V by local transformers.

lessons.title: Three-Phase Power, House Wiring and Electrical Safety
lessons.content:
A single rickshaw puller pedals with one leg pushing at a time, so the rickshaw surges a little with every push. Now imagine a three-person team pushing a heavy cart, each person pushing a third of a cycle after the other. The push never drops to zero; it stays smooth and strong. Electric power systems use the same idea. Instead of one AC voltage, power stations generate three, each shifted by one third of a cycle. This three-phase system delivers smooth power, needs less copper, and makes motors start and run easily. In this final lesson we study three-phase circuits, follow the power from the pole into your home's wiring, and learn the protection devices and safety rules that keep people alive.

What three-phase means: A three-phase generator has three sets of coils placed 120 degrees apart around the machine. As the magnet rotates, each coil produces a sinusoidal voltage of the same amplitude and frequency, but shifted by 120 degrees from the next. In phasor form, a balanced set is Va = Vp∠0°, Vb = Vp∠-120° and Vc = Vp∠+120° (or ∠-240°), where Vp is the phase voltage. The order in which the phases reach their peaks, a then b then c, is called the phase sequence. For a balanced set, the three phasors add to exactly zero, which you can check by drawing them: three equal arrows 120 degrees apart close into a triangle.

Why three phases: First, for a balanced load, the total instantaneous power of the three phases is constant rather than pulsing at 100 Hz, so large motors run smoothly with less vibration. Second, three-phase transmission delivers more power per kilogram of conductor than single-phase. Third, three currents shifted by 120 degrees in coils around a motor create a rotating magnetic field automatically, so three-phase induction motors start on their own without the capacitor trick used in single-phase ceiling fans. That is why factories, water pumping stations and large buildings use three-phase supplies.

The star (wye) connection: In a star, or Y, connection, one end of each of the three source windings or load impedances is joined at a common point called the neutral. The other three ends connect to the three line wires. The voltage between a line and neutral is the phase voltage Vp. The voltage between two lines is the line voltage VL. For a balanced star, VL = √3 × Vp, and each line voltage leads the corresponding phase voltage by 30 degrees. The line current equals the phase current. For example, with Vp = 230 V, VL = √3 × 230, about 398 V, which is why supplies are described as about 400 V three-phase and 230 V single-phase.

The delta connection: In a delta, or Δ, connection, the three windings or loads are connected end to end in a closed triangle, and the line wires connect to the corners. There is no neutral. Each phase sits directly between two lines, so the phase voltage equals the line voltage: VL = Vp. But each line current is the phasor difference of two phase currents, giving IL = √3 × Ip in a balanced delta, with a 30 degree phase shift. Recall the balanced wye-delta conversion from lesson 8: a balanced delta of impedance ZΔ is equivalent to a balanced star of ZΔ / 3, which is often the quickest way to analyse mixed systems.

Single-phase equivalent: A balanced three-phase circuit can be solved by analysing just one phase, because the other two are identical except for the 120-degree shifts. Convert everything to an equivalent star, solve phase a alone as a simple single-phase circuit using phase voltage and per-phase impedance, then write the other phases by shifting the answers by -120 and +120 degrees. In a balanced star, the neutral current, Ia + Ib + Ic, is zero, so the neutral wire carries no current at all.

Three-phase power: The total real power of a balanced three-phase load is three times the per-phase power: P = 3 Vp Ip cos θ, where θ is the angle of the per-phase impedance. In terms of line quantities, this becomes P = √3 VL IL cos θ, which holds for both star and delta. Similarly, Q = √3 VL IL sin θ and S = √3 VL IL. These formulas appear in every three-phase exam question and on motor nameplates.

Worked example, a balanced star load: Each phase of a star load is Z = 8 + j6 = 10∠36.87° Ω, supplied with a phase voltage of 230 V. The phase current is 230 / 10 = 23 A, which is also the line current, lagging its voltage by 36.87°. Power per phase is 23² × 8 = 4232 W, so the total is 3 × 4232, about 12.7 kW. Check with line values: √3 × 398 × 23 × 0.8, about 12.7 kW. The power factor is 0.8 lagging, and the neutral current is zero because the load is balanced.

The same load in delta: Connect the same three impedances in delta across the same supply, with a line voltage of about 400 V. Now each impedance sees the full line voltage, so Ip = 400 / 10 = 40 A, the line current is √3 × 40, about 69 A, and the total power is 3 × 40² × 8 = 38.4 kW, about three times the star value. This factor of three is exploited by star-delta starters: large motors are started in star to limit the starting current, then switched to delta for full power.

From the pole to your home: The distribution transformer near your building delivers three-phase, four-wire power: three lines plus neutral. Most homes in Bangladesh receive single-phase power, one line plus neutral at about 230 V, while larger buildings, flats with central systems, and shops with heavy loads may receive all three phases. The supply company tries to spread single-phase homes evenly across the three phases so the transformer stays roughly balanced. When the loads are unbalanced, the neutral carries current, and a broken neutral in an unbalanced system can cause dangerous over-voltage in some homes and under-voltage in others.

Inside the home: The incoming supply passes through the energy meter, then a main switch or main breaker, then a distribution board with separate circuits for lights, sockets and heavy appliances such as an air conditioner or water heater. Each circuit has its own protection device. Circuits are wired in parallel, as we saw in lesson 6, so each appliance gets the full voltage. Wire sizes are chosen for the expected current; typical practice uses thinner wire for lighting circuits and thicker wire for sockets and air conditioners, following the I²R heating ideas from lesson 3.

Live, neutral and earth: The live (phase) wire carries the alternating voltage relative to earth. The neutral is connected to earth at the transformer, so it stays close to 0 V. The earth (ground) wire connects the metal bodies of appliances to the ground through an earth electrode. Under the IEC colour scheme, live is brown, neutral blue and earth green-yellow; older installations in Bangladesh often use other colours, such as red for live and black for neutral, so never trust colour alone. Switches and fuses must always be placed in the live wire, so that turning a switch off truly disconnects the dangerous voltage from the appliance.

Protection devices: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit; it must be replaced after it blows. A miniature circuit breaker (MCB) does the same job but can be reset; it trips on overload by a thermal element and on short circuit by a fast magnetic element. A residual current device (RCD), also called an RCCB or ELCB, compares the live and neutral currents, using exactly the KCL idea from lesson 5. If they differ by more than a small amount, typically 30 mA for personal protection, current must be leaking somewhere, possibly through a person, and it trips within a fraction of a second. Fuses and MCBs protect wires and equipment; RCDs protect people.

Why earthing matters: Imagine the live wire inside a metal-bodied washing machine touches its frame because of damaged insulation. Without an earth connection, the frame sits at mains voltage, and anyone touching it while standing on a wet floor completes the circuit through their body. With a good earth connection, a large fault current flows straight to ground, which trips the breaker or blows the fuse, and the RCD trips even faster. This is why three-pin plugs exist and why the earth pin must never be cut off or bypassed.

Electric shock and the human body: The danger of a shock depends mainly on the current through the body, its path, especially across the chest, and its duration. As rough guides, about 1 mA can be felt, around 10 mA or more may cause muscles to clamp so a person cannot let go, and currents of the order of 100 mA through the chest for a short time can disturb the heart's rhythm fatally. Dry skin has a fairly high resistance, but wet skin, sweat and bare feet on a damp floor lower it dramatically, which is why bathrooms, kitchens, rainy seasons and floods in Bangladesh carry extra electrical risk.

Safety rules to live by: Switch off at the breaker before touching any wiring, and check with a tester that it is really dead. Never touch switches with wet hands, and keep electrical devices away from water. Do not overload multi-plugs, and replace damaged cables instead of taping them. Use the correct fuse or breaker rating; never replace a fuse with thicker wire. Stay far away from fallen power lines, especially in floodwater, and report them. If someone is receiving a shock, do not grab them with bare hands: switch off the supply first, or push the person free with a dry non-conducting object such as a dry wooden stick, then call for medical help.

Real life example 1, a garment factory's supply: A factory in Ashulia receives power at 11 kV and has its own transformer stepping it down to about 400 V three-phase. Hundreds of three-phase motors run its sewing, cutting and washing machines, while lighting circuits are spread across the three phases. The electrical engineer balances the phases, installs capacitor banks for power factor correction from lesson 22, and coordinates breakers so that a fault in one machine trips only that machine's breaker, not the whole floor. Every topic from this course appears in that one electrical room.

Real life example 2, a safer home after a scare: A family in Sylhet feels a tingle when touching their refrigerator door during the monsoon. An electrician finds that the socket has no earth connection and the old fridge has slightly damaged insulation. He installs proper earthing, fits a 30 mA RCD in the distribution board, and replaces the frayed cable. The next time a fault occurs, the RCD trips instantly instead of letting current pass through a person. A few hundred taka of protection can save a life.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up line and phase quantities, apply √3 in the wrong place (VL = √3Vp is for star; IL = √3Ip is for delta), forget that P = √3 VL IL cos θ uses the per-phase impedance angle, and add phase currents as magnitudes instead of phasors. In practical questions, they confuse the jobs of fuses, MCBs and RCDs. Typical exam questions: find line and phase voltages and currents for balanced star and delta loads, compute total three-phase power, convert between star and delta, explain the role of neutral and earth, and describe protective devices and safety measures.

Course recap and what comes next: Across these 25 lessons you went from what charge is to analysing three-phase power systems. You learned Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, series-parallel reduction, dividers, nodal and mesh analysis, network theorems, capacitors and inductors, transients, phasors, AC power, resonance, filters and transformers. These tools are the language of all hardware. Next, Electronic Devices adds diodes and transistors to these circuits, Digital Logic Design builds gates and memory from switching circuits, and later courses on microprocessors, embedded systems and computer architecture build whole computers on top of them. Every one of them assumes you can read and solve a circuit, and now you can.
key_points: Three-phase: three equal sinusoids 120° apart; a balanced set sums to zero.
Star: VL = √3 Vp, IL = Ip; delta: VL = Vp, IL = √3 Ip.
Balanced power: P = √3 VL IL cos θ (θ = per-phase impedance angle).
Balanced three-phase circuits can be solved per phase; neutral current is zero in a balanced star.
Bangladesh low-voltage supply: about 400 V line-to-line, 230 V line-to-neutral, 50 Hz.
Live, neutral, earth: switches and fuses in live; earth connects metal bodies to ground.
Fuses and MCBs protect wires; RCDs (typically 30 mA) protect people.
Shock danger depends on body current, path and time; water greatly increases the risk.
